species.note:
THE TWO ROW COUNTS ARE BOTH SOURCED AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME QUANTITY (recorded 2026-07-26). `block_min_rows: 3` is a FLOOR; R-001's claim, mechanism and remedy all say "at least 4 rows", which is a RECOMMENDATION. Neither is a typo for the other and neither should be "corrected" to match.
UMD states both in one sentence, "minimum of three rows side by side (preferably four rows)", and UMN and NC State state only the four ("blocks of at least four rows"). Clemson says "several rows" and quantifies nothing. So 3 is the lowest figure any read source will defend and 4 is what three of the four sources actually advise. All four are quoted in full in R-001's own evidence pointers, read 2026-07-11.
WHY THIS NOTE EXISTS: `block_min_rows` is read by nothing (ISSUES #15), so the divergence has no downstream symptom, and it reads as an error against a grade-A rule that says four three times. The next person to notice it would "fix" it to 4 and silently discard UMD's floor. R-001's trigger fires on `block_min_plants` and does not read rows at all, so no behaviour depends on either number today.
The app quotes the RECOMMENDATION ("a block of 4+ rows"), which is the right advice to give and matches the rule's remedy. If anything ever reads this field, it must not be assumed to be the number the UI is showing.

species.note:
Lima / butter bean, added 2026-07-25. Phaseolus lunatus, a DIFFERENT SPECIES from the common bean (P. vulgaris) and from the runner bean (P. coccineus), all three of which this corpus now models separately. Illinois names the binomials on the same page, which is what makes the split checkable; they share the fabaceae rotation break either way.
NO rhizobia_group, deliberately. This corpus distinguishes symbionts, Bradyrhizobium (cowpea group) for vigna_unguiculata against Rhizobium leguminosarum for bean and pea, and NEITHER source read on 2026-07-25 states which one a lima partners with. UMN discusses inoculant for common beans only and says nothing about limas. A guessed symbiont is a fabricated mechanism, so the field is left absent and is not assumed from the genus.
A SOIL NOTE WORTH KEEPING, and the first sourced texture preference in the corpus: UMN states that "lima bean plants grow best in a coarser-textured, sandier soil", against a clay loam for common beans. Nothing acts on it (soil P0 gates nothing, D-148), but it is exactly the kind of input P2's texture work would use, and it is recorded now while the source is in hand.

species.note:
A climbing warm-season legume like common bean and a real fixer alternative in a Three Sisters. It is grown for both the pods and its showy, pollinator- (and hummingbird-) drawing flowers, and a little more cool-tolerant than common bean. A tender perennial in frost-free climates, grown as an annual. Needs strong support (the corn or a trellis).
SPREAD ESTIMATED, and for a climber the field means something narrower than it does elsewhere. A supported vine's footprint is the base it occupies. Its foliage is up the pole, so the area the foliage reaches doesn't count. Clemson (read 2026-07-25) states the base figure that logic needs (five or six seeds in a 6-8 in circle around a pole) and states nothing about a plant's width. It also never mentions scarlet runner bean; the numbers here are the pole-bean pattern applied to a species Clemson does not cover, which is why the flag stays.

cultivar_groups.note:
The garden pumpkin (carving and pie types), added 2026-07-25. A cultivar group, not a species. UMN states outright that jack-o'-lantern and many pie pumpkins are Cucurbita pepo, the same species as summer squash and zucchini, so it belongs here and inherits the cucurbit rotation (R-011) correctly. Only the GIANT competition types are C. maxima, and those are deliberately not modelled. A 50-plus-pound pumpkin needs 150 sq ft per hill and is a different undertaking.
Appended LAST on purpose. The first group is what an unqualified Cucurbita pepo resolves to (dispatch.resolve's default-cultivar rule), so inserting a group ahead of `bush` would silently re-shape every existing summer squash in the corpus. That is the mistake apple's standard_rootstock group exists to prevent.
NO SUPPORT, unlike the vining group. A squash on a trellis is a routine small-garden technique, a pumpkin on one is not, so this group does not offer optional_strong.

No page read gives its height, spread or spacing, so those are carried over from this species' vining group and flagged estimated, as is its support (a vine that can be trellised, like the vining group). Appended last, like pumpkin: the first group is what an unqualified Cucurbita pepo resolves to.

species.note:
THE ONLY PER-CROP pH CEILING IN THIS CORPUS THAT A SOURCE ARGUES FOR, and the three sources read on 2026-07-25 do not agree where it sits. Every other vegetable's upper bound is the corpus's own (see confidence.sources on any of them); potato's is contested in the literature, which is a better problem to have and is recorded and left unresolved.
All three agree on the MECHANISM. Common scab (Streptomyces scabies) gets worse as soil goes less acid, so potato is grown deliberately sour. They disagree on the number, and UMD names why. species.note: Horseradish, added 2026-08-31, the third species of the perennial-vegetable lane (D-193), and the one that broke the mould. It is MODELLED AS A ROTATED ANNUAL ROOT CROP, not a permanent perennial like asparagus and rhubarb, because that is how it is grown. Extension is explicit: 'horseradish is not recommended for a true permanent bed'; UMN 'Rotate the horseradish planting site, making sure to not plant in the same place more often than every three to four years'; it is lifted every autumn and replanted each spring from root cuttings ('sets'). So `lifespan: annual` records the CULTIVATION, while botanically it is a hardy herbaceous perennial (NC State zone 4-9). The note carries the botany, the field carries the practice, and the planner schedules it as the season-long root crop it is grown as. No hardiness_zone and no R-076 gate, the same as every other annual root. THE BRASSICA-ROTATION CONNECTION, INVESTIGATED AND RESOLVED (the reason this species was sequenced last): horseradish is Brassicaceae, so R-012 (the 4-year brassica rotation rule) fires on it, and that is CORRECT. All Brassicaceae are potential clubroot hosts, and extension prescribes exactly what R-012 warns: rotate horseradish away from cruciferous crops, and off its own ground every 3-4 years. R-012 reads ground history and fires at planting; it imposes no standing rotation on a perennial (that would be R-072's job, and R-072 correctly stays silent here because this is modelled annual, not perennial-in-rotating-ground). No engine or rule change was needed. The interaction is sound, and this note records the investigation so it is not re-opened. INVASIVE, so it is contained and not sited freely. NC State's toolbox flags it '#weedy'/'#colonizing' ('If left unharvested the plant will spread by underground roots and become weedy forming colonies. They can be difficult to eradicate'), and USU's remedy is mechanical: 'some gardeners plant the roots in buried pots or in 12 inch wide and 24 inch long PVC plastic pipes' to stop the spread. This is the mint/comfrey containment concern (cf. R-125); it lives here in prose because the model has no containment field, and horseradish being lifted annually is itself part of the control. VERTICILLIUM SUSCEPTIBILITY IS WITHHELD, deliberately: commercial horseradish literature reports Verticillium wilt (the internal root discoloration Illinois growers fight), but no land-grant home-garden source read here NAMES horseradish as a host. UMN and USU list only 'root rots' and white rust. `verticillium_susceptible` drives R-094/R-095, so setting it on a general-knowledge assertion would fire a disease rule the sources do not support; it stays off until a land-grant source is read, exactly as invariant 4 governs a rule promotion. Every other root crop here omits the flag too (potato relies on R-094's family signal instead), so this is the consistent state. IN NO GUILD. It is grown for its pungent root, lifted and rotated, and invasive if loose, so it holds its own contained ground and has no spot on a guild roster.

species.note:
Arugula / rocket, added 2026-07-25. It is the first NEW species of the expansion arc, and not a cultivar group of one already here. Eruca sativa is its own genus, not a Brassica, so it could not be modelled as a group of anything. What it shares with the cole crops is the FAMILY, and that is what matters here, because R-012's four-year interval and the clubroot pressure behind it are family-level. A fast salad green is not a rotation loophole any more than radish is.
NO BOLT RISK FIELD, deliberately. Arugula bolts hard in heat and every gardener knows it, but lettuce's `bolt_risk.threshold_c` is itself flagged as estimated, and adding a second guessed threshold by analogy to the first would be fabrication compounding fabrication (D-004's rule about GDD, applied to a different number). It stays absent until a source gives a figure.

species.note:
Mustard greens, added 2026-07-25. Brassica juncea: a Brassica, but NOT B. oleracea, B. rapa or B. napus, so it is its own species here and not a group of the cabbage, the turnip or the rutabaga. That distinction is worth stating because this corpus now models four Brassica species and the temptation to file a fifth green under whichever is nearest is exactly how a rotation model rots. All four share the family, which is what R-012 gates on.

image.alt: Rows of curly endive growing

species.note:
Endive and escarole, added 2026-07-25. Two forms of one plant: curly endive (frisee) and the broad-leaved form UMN calls escarole. Asteraceae, like lettuce, so it breaks the big-three rotation the same way and shares lettuce's cool-season habits.
BLANCHING IS PART OF THE CROP, and it is why the days-to-maturity here is derived and not quoted. UMN gives no DTM at all, but it does give the blanching timeline: tie the outer leaves about a month after transplanting or six weeks after direct seeding, and blanching takes about two weeks. Six plus two is eight weeks from seed, which is where 55-70 days comes from. The arithmetic is in confidence.sources; the field is flagged because a number assembled from two sentences is not a number the publication states.
NO SEPARATE CULTIVAR GROUPS for curly vs broad-leaf, deliberately. UMN describes them as forms and gives ONE set of spacings covering both. A group asserting different geometry would be inventing a difference the source does not make.
NO BOLT RISK FIELD, deliberately (checked 2026-08-31). Endive bolts in heat and long days, but no land-grant source read gives a temperature to store: the UMN lettuce/endive/radicchio page and UMD's bolting page describe it only qualitatively, and the only figures found (>85 F, mid-70s F) trace to a commercial content site (harvesttotable.com), the exact source class the R-061 marigold refutation rejects. Adding a threshold_c by analogy to lettuce's or spinach's 24 would be the fabrication-by-analogy the arugula note names (D-004). The field stays absent until a land-grant source gives endive its own figure; the prose here carries the warning meanwhile.

species.note: Radicchio, the heading chicory: a cool-season salad crop sown in spring or in summer for autumn, and cut as a firm, bitter head. The numbers are radicchio's (Cornell, Utah State, UMN); cutting chicory and witloof are the same species with other numbers and are not modelled here. Summer heat sends it to seed, and no source gives the temperature. Left to flower it self-seeds and can escape, so cut it before it does (Wisconsin).

image.alt: Soybean plants growing in a field
image.caption: Edamame is soybean harvested young.

species.note:
Edamame (vegetable soybean), added 2026-07-25. A bush legume that needs NO support, which is what separates it from every other fixer in this corpus. The corn-guild fixer role wants a vine that climbs (predicate: habit vine, support.requires strong), and edamame satisfies none of that. It is a fixer for a bed, with no trellis.
rhizobia_group WAS WITHHELD until 2026-09-02, for the same reason lima bean has none and a sharper one. It is now sourced (see confidence.sources). The original reasoning, kept: UMN says only "Inoculation with Rhizobium may help plant growth and yield", which is the generic word and names no group. A soybean's actual symbiont is not the bean-and-pea Rhizobium this corpus already names, so writing that value would be WRONG, which is worse than unsourced, and writing the right one would be unsourced. Both are worse than leaving it out.
THE HARVEST WINDOW IS THE HARD PART and no field models it. Edamame is picked immature, while the pods are plump and still bright green, and Iowa State records that the window is only a few days. days_to_maturity plans the sow date; it does not warn you that the harvest is over in a week.

cultivar_groups.note:
The shallot is the same species as the onion (Allium cepa), added 2026-07-25, so it inherits the allium rotation break (R-013) and the daylength gate (R-081) correctly, with neither needing to be re-stated.
What differs is the HARVEST. The plant is the same. USU records that wide spacing "results in bulb clusters" of 10-15 bulbs where high-density planting gives one bulb per set. The corpus has no field for multiplier yield, so that difference is kept in prose here. A number would be fabricated.

species.note: Buckwheat, added 2026-09-01, the FIRST species of D-195 (the "plantings for years" breadth tranche) and its T1 lead, a fast summer cover crop that doubles as a top insectary. NOT A LEGUME and NOT a nitrogen fixer. NC State is explicit ("though not a legume, is an excellent cover crop"), so n_fixing is false. Its cover value is a different mechanism from the clover/vetch legume covers already here: a rapid, dense canopy that SMOTHERS weeds (ground_coverage high), phosphorus scavenging, and a month-long nectar flow. It is grown, killed by the first frost (frost_tolerance tender), as a catch crop between main crops, which is exactly the multi-year rotation slot this tranche targets. TERMINATED AT FLOWERING, ~5 weeks after sowing (Cornell: "About five weeks after planting ... It is ready to mow"), which is why days_to_maturity is [35, 42], the flowering/mow window. A buckwheat cover is cut before it seeds, because it "can become a weed if it is allowed to go to seed" (Cornell). Seed maturity is later (~70-90 days) and is not the operational endpoint for a cover. A PREMIER NECTAR PLANT: NC State calls it "A nectar source for honeybees and other beneficial insects" and Cornell "Feeds beneficial insects", so pollinator_value is `high` and it enters the forage lens (R-102) automatically on its bloom_window, the "Door 2" path, with no guild edit needed. Polygonaceae, the family of sorrel and rhubarb. mature_spread_cm omitted: buckwheat is broadcast- sown as a stand, not spaced, and no source read gives a per-plant width. No ph_range: NC State lists a neutral-to-alkaline tolerance (and it is famously grown on poor ground) and no per-crop optimum. No hardiness_zone or R-076 gate, because it is a frost-killed annual, and R-076 gates perennial survival (the phacelia pattern).

species.note: Cereal (winter) rye, added 2026-09-01, a T1 cover crop of D-195 and the first species to use the D-196 scheduling ruling. The classic overwintering cover: fall-sown, survives hard winter (frost_tolerance hardy, the counterpoint to buckwheat's tender), terminated in spring at the heading stage. NOT a legume and NOT a nitrogen fixer. NC State is explicit ("Because rye is not a legume, it does not fix nitrogen"). Its value is a different mechanism from the clover/vetch legume covers: a dense ALLELOPATHIC smother (NC State: "excellent at smothering and outcompeting weeds, perhaps because it releases alleopathic chemicals into the soil"; tagged #allelopathic) plus deep fibrous roots that build soil and scavenge nitrogen. It is wind-pollinated, so pollinator_value is `low` and it carries no bloom_window and no forage role. sow_season fall (D-196): rye is fall-sown and terminated by growth stage in spring, not harvested at a day count, so this marker keeps the calendar from scheduling it as a spring sowing, the same marker garlic uses. days_to_maturity [90,120] is a FLAGGED growing-period figure and is DOCUMENTATION ONLY under D-196. No extension gives cereal rye a garden days-to-maturity (they describe it by stage: tillering, heading, anthesis), so this is the schema-required number (comparable to sorghum, the other cereal cover), not a scheduled one. mature_spread [15,30] is NC State's; ground_coverage `low` matches sorghum (a narrow cereal; the smother comes from dense seeding + allelopathy, not per-plant spread, carried in this note). No hardiness_zone or R-076 gate (annual; winter-hardiness is in frost_tolerance). No ph_range: rye is famously acid-tolerant and grows where wheat will not, so NC State's single "Neutral" band would wrongly exclude the acid ground it thrives on. It is omitted because that band is a tolerance, not a per-crop optimum. spacing_in_row_cm omitted (broadcast/drilled stand).

species.note: Hairy vetch, added 2026-09-01, a T1 cover crop of D-195, under D-196. THE LEGUME cover, the nitrogen-fixing counterpoint to buckwheat and rye: n_fixing true, feeder_class fixer (matching the clover covers), a Fabaceae green manure grown to feed the next crop, so it participates in the corpus's fixer logic (the "Door 2" trait path). Overwintering winter annual, so sow_season fall (D-196) keeps it off the spring DTM calendar. It is often grown WITH cereal rye as a nurse crop it climbs (the tendrils cling to the standing cereal), so support.requires is `none` (no built trellis needed) despite the vining habit. A SPECIALISED, MODERATE BEE DRAW, DELIBERATELY BELOW THE FORAGE THRESHOLD. NC State says "Long-tongued bees and bumblebees are attracted to the nectar", so pollinator_value is `moderate` (specialised to long-tongued bees, not the broad draw of buckwheat or phacelia). It carries a bloom_window as real phenology, but it does NOT enter the forage roster: the lens counts only `high`/`very_high` as forage (engine/forage.py FORAGE_LEVELS excludes `moderate` on purpose), and it is not grown for seed so no pollination.mode is set. So vetch sits in NEITHER forage list, a good illustration that `moderate` is a recorded value the lens intentionally does not count, the opposite end from buckwheat's automatic inclusion at `high`. AGGRESSIVE AND WEEDY: NC State calls it "aggressive, weedy" and "listed as an invasive plant in Oregon", so it carries invasive_status (regions [OR]), the soft-caveat tier (the fennel pattern, W-INVASIVE if a role offers it), NOT the R-082 blacklist, because hairy vetch is a standard, legal, widely-recommended cover crop, invasive only in some western contexts. The caveat and the terminate-before-seed instruction live in the invasive_status note. days_to_maturity [70,100] is a FLAGGED, documentation-only growing-period figure (the rye/crimson- clover treatment): a fall-sown overwinter cover has no clean garden DTM, and sow_season fall means it never drives a schedule. No hardiness_zone or R-076 gate (annual; winter-hardiness in frost_tolerance). No ph_range: NC State's single "Neutral" band is a tolerance, not an optimum. spacing_in_row_cm omitted (broadcast/drilled stand).

species.note: Oats, added 2026-09-01, the last T1 cover crop of D-195, and the third scheduling behaviour in the cover set: buckwheat is frost-killed at once (tender), cereal rye overwinters (hardy), and oats WINTER-KILL (frost_tolerance half_hardy, killed by a hard freeze but taking light frost). That winter-kill is oats' signature cover use: fall-sown, it dies over winter and leaves a weed- suppressing mulch with NO spring termination needed. But oats are also commonly SPRING-sown as a quick cover with a real growing period, so they are modelled as a spring DTM cover, with scheduling_model dtm and NO sow_season fall (that marker, D-196, is for overwintering covers terminated in spring; setting it would wrongly hide oats' legitimate spring sowing). The fall winter-kill mode is recorded here in the note. The schedule does not carry it. NOT a legume, no nitrogen fixation (a grass). Its cover value, like rye's, is a dense ALLELOPATHIC smother. NC State: oats "are excellent at smothering and outcompeting weeds. They release certain chemicals into the soil that inhibit the germination of other plants." WIND-POLLINATED with "small, insignificant flowers" (NC State), so pollinator_value low, no bloom_window, no forage role, the rye pattern. ground_coverage low matches the other cereals (rye/sorghum): a narrow stalk, the smother is a stand property. days_to_maturity [60,90] is a FLAGGED quick-cover figure (NC State gives no DTM); it is a real spring growing period here, not the documentation-only case rye needed, because oats ARE spring-scheduled. No hardiness_zone/R-076 (annual). No ph_range: NC State's single "Neutral" band is a tolerance (oats tolerate acid soils), not an optimum. spacing_in_row_cm omitted.

species.note: Calendula (pot marigold), added 2026-09-01, a T1 insectary flower of D-195. A FORAGE-GRADE insectary: NC State says it "attracts butterflies and pollinators", so pollinator_value is `high` and it enters the forage lens (R-102) on its own traits, the buckwheat "Door 2" pattern, and the point of the insectary sub-lane (a flower a gardener plants once and the engine credits as forage for the whole plant list). A cool-season annual, half_hardy (tolerates light frost; NC State lists it growable across zones 2-11 as an annual), and a long bloomer through spring and summer. Petals are edible (NC State: "give color to soups, custards, and rice"), noted as context, not a modelled field. NOT THE SAME PLANT AS THE FRENCH MARIGOLD next to it in this file: Calendula officinalis (pot marigold, this record) is a DIFFERENT GENUS and role from Tagetes patula (French marigold). The common name "marigold" spans both. Calendula is a bee/beneficial forage plus a culinary flower (pollinator_value high); tagetes is a pest-deterrent (pollinator_value low, its role is volatile/root chemistry, not forage). Recording the distinction so the two are not conflated. days_to_maturity [50,65] is a FLAGGED fast-cool-season figure (NC State gives no DTM). species.note: Sweet alyssum, added 2026-09-01, a T1 insectary flower of D-195. A FORAGE-GRADE insectary and one of the best beneficial-insect plants a gardener can sow: NC State lists it drawing "Butterflies, Moths, Pollinators, Predatory Insects", so pollinator_value is `high` and it enters the forage lens (R-102) on its own traits, the buckwheat "Door 2" pattern. Its predatory-insect draw (hoverflies, parasitic wasps) is the reason it is interplanted through vegetable beds. A low, dense mat (groundcover, 3-10 in), cool-season half_hardy, blooming spring to first frost. IT IS A BRASSICACEAE, and that has a consequence the corpus applies automatically: R-012 (the clubroot rotation, "do not plant Brassicaceae where Brassicaceae grew within 4 years") fires on `family: brassicaceae`, so it now covers sweet alyssum without any per-species edit, the family- driven "Door 2" path. This is CORRECT. Sweet alyssum is a clubroot host, and R-012 gates on GROUND HISTORY (what grew there in prior years), NOT same-season interplanting, so it does not fight alyssum's classic use as a brassica COMPANION (that is same-season adjacency, which R-012 does not see). It fires only if alyssum is planted on ground that carried brassicas within four years, which is a real clubroot-carryover caution. ground_coverage `high` is its carpet habit. days_to_maturity [50,70] flagged (NC State gives no DTM; fast cool-season). No ph_range: NC State lists acid, neutral AND alkaline tolerance, not an optimum. No hardiness_zone or R-076 gate (annual). spacing_in_row_cm omitted.

species.note: Luffa is a long-season tropical vine in the cucumber family. Picked young, its fruit is eaten like summer squash; left to mature, it dries into the familiar sponge. This is the smooth luffa; the angled luffa (Chinese okra) is grown the same way. It wants full sun, steady moisture in well-drained soil and a very sturdy trellis at least 6 feet tall, because fruit lying on the ground rots. Sow after the last frost, or soak the seed for a day and start it indoors 4 to 6 weeks ahead. Pick fruit to eat while it is young, under about 6 inches long. Not known here: how deep to sow it, the soil temperature or days it needs to germinate, how long its seed keeps, or a soil pH of its own.

species.note: Malabar spinach is a fast-growing tropical vine grown for its thick, mild leaves and young stems: a summer stand-in for spinach, which runs to seed in the heat. It is a perennial where it never freezes and is grown here as a one-season crop. Sow it 2 to 3 weeks after the last frost, once the soil is warm (soaking the seed speeds its slow germination), and give it a sturdy trellis or fence. Keep the soil moist: dry soil or extreme heat makes it flower, and the leaves turn bitter. The red-leaved kind (Basella rubra) is mostly grown as an ornamental. No rotation rule names its family, Basellaceae. Not known here: how many weeks ahead to start it indoors, how often to resow it, or how long its seed keeps.

species.note: New Zealand spinach, or warrigal greens, is a sprawling, heat-tolerant leaf crop, not a true spinach: it keeps producing through the summer, when spinach runs to seed. Sow it outdoors after the last frost, or start it indoors 3 to 4 weeks before; soaking the seed for a day speeds its slow, uneven germination. Pick the young tips often and feed it well, or it flowers early and stops growing. The leaves are high in oxalate: Utah State advises blanching them for 3 minutes and pouring the water away, though many people eat them raw. No rotation rule names its family, Aizoaceae. Not known here: the soil temperature it needs to germinate, how much sun it needs, or how often to resow it.

image.alt: A bunch of celery stalks

cultivar_groups.note: The species' own envelope. It is the unqualified default and repeats its numbers with zero new assertion. It exists because celeriac below would otherwise become the default. dispatch.resolve falls back to the FIRST group, so a species that gains groups without a guard silently changes what every existing unqualified planting means.

Celeriac, added 2026-07-26. It is a GROUP and not a species because it is the same plant, Apium graveolens, grown for the swollen hypocotyl instead of the petioles. So it inherits the apiaceous rotation break (R-013) and the family intervals correctly, with neither needing to be restated.
DAYS TO MATURITY IS THE ONLY FIELD THAT DIFFERS, and it is the only one a source distinguishes. Wisconsin A1653 gives celeriac 110 days to first harvest against celery's 100-110, on the same table. Written [110, 110] because the publication states ONE number and this corpus never uses a scalar. The degenerate range is the faithful shape; no range was narrowed by guesswork.
SPACING IS DELIBERATELY IDENTICAL TO CELERY'S. That is a refusal, not an oversight. A1653 gives BOTH crops the same 4-6 in between plants. Giving celeriac its own figure while celery kept the species' 20 cm would assert a difference the source explicitly denies, the ruling endive got, for the same reason. Note this also means A1653's 4-6 in contradicts the corpus's 20 cm for CELERY, which is a celery question and is recorded on the species and not fixed inside a celeriac commit.
HABIT STAYS `stalk` THOUGH A1653 CALLS IT "root celery". In this corpus `root` means carrot at 8 cm of spread, radish at 3 cm of spacing, parsnip, a class of plants a quarter of celeriac's size. Celeriac's above-ground plant is a celery rosette and A1653 spaces it exactly like celery. The swollen part is below ground and `habit` describes the plant, so moving it would misplace the crop to satisfy its common name.

species.note:
Long-season, thirsty, and a heavy feeder. It wants steady moisture and rich soil or the stalks turn stringy. An apiaceous crop, so it breaks the big-three rotation (R-013). Bolts if chilled young.
SPREAD ESTIMATED (read 2026-07-25), and celery is the one species in this pass where a published HEIGHT exists and a width still does not. USU states 18-24 in tall and gives two different in-row spacings on the same page (12 in in the body, 18-24 in in the summary), the tighter one deliberately ("Tight planting helps force long growth and tall petioles"). A spacing chosen to change the plant's shape is the clearest possible case of a spacing that is not a spread.

THE ONE READ FIGURE IS 3x THIS ONE, AND IT IS A DIFFERENT QUANTITY (2026-07-25). Clemson lists a 'Murasaki' sweetpotato with "vigorous vines (grows 20')", which is 610 cm of VINE LENGTH, where the corpus carries 100-200 cm of spread. A 6 m runner does not make a 6 m radius. species.harvest_sign: Calyces should be harvested when they are tender and plump.
species.note: Roselle is a tall, bushy annual hibiscus, a relative of okra, grown for its fleshy red calyces, which make tea, jam and sauce; its young leaves are eaten too. It needs full sun and warmth and is killed by frost. It flowers only as the days shorten, so it crops in autumn and the days to harvest here are only a rough guide; UF/IFAS sows it in spring. In a cool climate the calyces may not ripen at all, though the leaves are still worth eating. Pick the calyces while they are tender and plump. Root-knot nematodes are its main pest, so move it to new ground each year. Not known here: how deep to sow it, how it germinates, how long its seed keeps, its soil pH in numbers, or how to store the calyces.

species.note:
The large winter squashes (hubbard, kabocha, buttercup), completing the three cultivated Cucurbita (with pepo and moschata). A long-season sprawling vine; cucurbitaceae, counts toward the cucurbit rotation (R-011).
SPREAD STILL ESTIMATED AFTER TWO READS (2026-07-25). Four cucurbits, eight publications, and not one states a vine spread; every page states spacing and stops. That is now a finding about the literature as a whole. Home-garden extension guides tell a gardener how far apart to plant, because that is the decision the gardener makes, and the mature footprint of a sprawling vine is not a number they publish. The corpus's 200-400 cm is bracketed by Clemson's large-vined spacing (3-5 ft in rows 6-8 ft) but stated by nobody.
Clemson does state one thing worth keeping even though no field holds it: "Pumpkins have many important feeder roots near the surface and roots grow to about the same spread as vines" (hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/pumpkins-winter-squash, read 2026-07-25, weed-control section). A read source for roots reaching roughly 1x the canopy on a sprawling cucurbit. It lives in the note and NOT in confidence.sources, because this species has no root_spread_multiplier and a citation keyed to a field that does not exist is exactly what E-CONF-REF refuses, correctly. Whether the field should exist here is a corpus decision nobody has made.

storage.shelf_life: two to six months, depending on variety

Large hard-shelled storage squash (Blue / Green Hubbard). A big, long-season sprawling ground-run vine and an excellent long keeper, with the widest footprint of the ordinary (non-giant) types.

Atlantic Giant and competition show pumpkins: enormous fruit on a very long, very late vine; wants roughly 50-60 sq ft per plant and is grown for size alone. Modelled so the footprint gate greys it out of small beds and never silently substitutes.

image.alt: Turnips growing in the ground with their leafy tops

species.note:
Fast brassica root (the greens are edible too). Brassicaceae, so it counts toward the brassica rotation (R-012) and shares clubroot/brassica pressure. It is not a rotation loophole. Brassica rapa, distinct from the cole crops (B. oleracea) and rutabaga (B. napus).
SPREAD ESTIMATED after three reads (2026-07-25). Same root-crop distinction as radish. Every page gives a thinning distance for the ROOT (3-6 in UMN, 2-4 in Illinois, 3-4 in USU) and none gives a top width, and the corpus's 15-20 cm is the top. Note the three thinning bands disagree with each other by a factor of two, which is itself a reason not to promote any of them into a spread.
THE ASIAN GREENS ARE THIS SPECIES (2026-07-25). Bok choy and napa cabbage are Brassica rapa too (UMN gives the binomials outright, `B. rapa chinensis` and `B. rapa pekinensis`), so they are cultivar groups here and not new species, and they inherit R-012's brassica rotation and the clubroot pressure that goes with it. UMN's own planting advice says the same thing in gardener's terms: plant them where you have not grown cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, turnips, rutabaga or Brussels sprouts in four years. Clemson still calls bok choy "Brassica chinensis", an older name for the same plant; the corpus follows the current binomial and records the disagreement and does not silently pick.

cultivar_groups.note: The species' own envelope, and the unqualified default. It repeats the species' numbers except frost tolerance - turnip is hardy, where bok choy and napa cabbage are half-hardy.

Bok choy / pak choi (Brassica rapa chinensis), the same species as the turnip, grown for the leaf stalks. HEIGHT is UMN's, stated per type (dwarf "only six inches tall", full-sized "a foot tall"); spacing is UMN's thinning figure. DAYS TO MATURITY IS THE TURNIP'S and is flagged. UMN says only that bok choy is "quicker to mature" than Chinese cabbage, which is a comparison and gives no number, and Clemson gives none.

Chinese / napa cabbage (Brassica rapa pekinensis), a heading form of the same species. UMN's "about two months to mature" is the DTM, taken as stated; Clemson's "eighteen inches apart for napa types" is the spacing, which is wider than bok choy's and is why the two are separate groups and not one "Asian greens" entry. Height and spread are flagged, because neither source states either for this form, and the figures are carried from the heading habit this species' turnip tops already show.

species.note:
Heat-loving sprawling vine that needs a long warm season; cucurbitaceae, counts toward the cucurbit rotation (R-011).
THE SPREAD IS STILL ESTIMATED AFTER TWO READS (2026-07-25). USU and Clemson both state SPACING and neither states a vine spread or plant width. That is the pattern for vine crops and no accident of these two pages. Spacing is not spread. Growers set vines closer than they run and let them interlock, so a spacing figure is a floor on the ground a plant is given, not a measure of the ground it covers. Know this before anyone "corrects" this number, because mature_spread_cm feeds the R-002 area sum: 400 cm treated as an exclusive circle reserves about 12.6 m2 per plant, where Clemson's own spacing works out to 2.8-4.5 m2 and its rule of thumb to 2.2 m2. That gap is a question about how the engine spends spread, not a demonstration that 200-400 cm is wrong, and it is recorded but not acted on.

cultivar_groups.note: The species' own envelope across seedling/semi-standard rootstocks, and the unqualified default.

A rootstock class, not a scion group. A dwarfing rootstock (M9, Bud9 and M26) holds any apple cultivar to roughly 2-3 m and leaves it poorly anchored, so the tree needs a permanent stake.
ROOT SPREAD (sourced 2026-07-25, and three things came out of it. This is the reference entry; pear, plum and peach carry the same 2.0 and point here).
(1) The published figures are UPPER BOUNDS, not typical values. Illinois says "up to 3 times the canopy spread" in one post and "up to four times (possibly more)" in another. 2.0 sits inside both and is quoted by neither, so the flag stays under D-146.
(2) THE PUBLISHED FIGURE IS SOIL-DEPENDENT and this field cannot express that. Illinois gives 0.5x the canopy width in heavy clay and up to 5x in sand, a TENFOLD range driven by soil texture, which the corpus stores as a single scalar per species. A number that varies by soil is not a species constant, and a better number would not fix it. The fix is either a soil input the engine does not have, or a documented decision that one figure stands for all soils.
RESOLVED 2026-07-25 (D-150, maintainer): ONE FIGURE STANDS FOR ALL SOILS, and the flag says so. A texture-keyed map was the alternative and was rejected for the reason D-149 gives about pH: the two ENDPOINTS are published (0.5x clay, 5x sand) and the middle is NOT, so a map would have had to invent a value for loam (the most commonly declared texture), exactly the way a repeated [6.0, 7.0] once stood in for thirty-three researched pH ranges. Inventing the middle to make a schema look complete is the failure this corpus exists to avoid. The scalar stays, permanently flagged, with the published range recorded here; the flag is not a to-do, it is the answer. This paragraph is the canonical one; pear, plum and peach cite it by reference.
(3) NOTHING IN THE ENGINE READS THIS FIELD. Checked across corpus/, engine/, web/ and e2e/ on 2026-07-25: no rule triggers on it, no placement or footprint code resolves it, no golden contains it. Its only appearance is the Why page's flagged-numbers list, where it renders as "how far the roots reach past the canopy". So the flag drives no output. Know that before anyone spends effort refining the value.
M26 was excluded from this class on 2026-07-24 and PUT BACK on 2026-07-25. The exclusion rested on a search summary saying M26 makes a larger tree and is staked early rather than for life. Read directly, UGA Circular 740 groups M 9 and M 26 together as its dwarf rootstocks and states the support requirement for the class, with no early-only caveat and no separate tier. A read source outranks a summary of one, including when the summary was the basis for a decision made here the day before.
The numbers CORROBORATE but are not quoted: UGA gives a band, not a figure, and 200-300 cm sits inside it. So the fields stay ESTIMATED. A number derived from a published band is not a number the publication states, and the corpus marks the difference. What IS now confirmed from a read source is the staking requirement, which UGA states outright. The quotes, the publication and the read date are in confidence.sources (D-146).

image.alt: Green pears hanging on the tree

species.note:
A pome fruit tree like apple, and a canopy alternative in the fruit-tree guild. Mostly self-incompatible, so plant two cultivars for fruit set (R-080).
NO DWARF GROUP, deliberately (2026-07-25). A quince_rootstock group asserting a 2.5-3.5 m pear was added 2026-07-24 and removed the next day when the claim was checked against extension sources: there are no commercially available dwarfing rootstocks for pear, the home-planting stock is seedling, quince is graft-incompatible with the varieties an American nursery sells, and dwarf pears do not yet exist. A US home gardener buying "a pear" gets a standard or semi-dwarf tree, so the species carries one envelope and the small-space fruit guild prices pear as the big tree it is. If a semi-dwarf group is ever wanted, it is a NEW claim with its own numbers. It would not be this one restored.
Those sources were RE-FETCHED on 2026-07-25, because the original round was read before the [read]/[search] convention existed and recorded no page, no date and no provenance, so none of it met D-146's bar. Penn State, UMaine and WSU are now read citations in confidence.sources. UC's quince page could NOT be re-fetched: it returns 403 from this container, like the Riesselman primary, so UC's fire-blight and alkaline-tolerance points are not carried as citations at all. WSU covers the winter-hardiness and graft-incompatibility halves by direct read and does not discuss fire blight.

species.note: Common (fruiting) quince, added 2026-08-31, the eighth species of the fruit+herb tranche (D-194) and the second of the LOW tier. THE TRUE QUINCE, Cydonia oblonga, a small rosaceous fruit tree grown for its hard aromatic pomes. It is not flowering quince (Chaenomeles), which is an ornamental shrub. It takes the pome-fruit shape of apple and pear with two SOURCED departures from them. SELF-FERTILE, the headline difference. A single quince sets fruit, so pollination.self_incompatible is false and R-080 stays silent, whereas apple and pear are self_incompatible with min_cultivars 2. UGA states it: "Flowers form on the end of new growth in the spring and usually are self-fertile" ("usually" kept on purpose: a 2024 study found some cultivars carry a degree of self-incompatibility, recorded not as a contradiction but as the reason the value is flagged rather than asserted hard). FED LIGHTLY, the second departure: feeder_class is `light`, not apple/pear's `moderate`, because UGA ties feeding to disease: "Fertilize lightly to discourage vigorous growth that may succumb to fire blight." FIRE BLIGHT itself is carried here in prose, with no field or rule. UGA says quince is "subject to many of the diseases that attack apples and pears, including fire blight, but it is generally much less affected." The corpus has no fire-blight field or rule, and adding one would pull in apple and pear too, so it is recorded as a management caveat and not modelled, the same black-walnut/juglone restraint, a hazard noted where the corpus cannot yet enforce it. THE FRUIT IS COOKED, NOT TOXIC. It is "very hard and ... edible when cooked or made into jelly" (UGA), hard and astringent raw but not poisonous, so quince needs NO toxicity rule, unlike elderberry. verticillium host/susceptible are omitted, because no source read names quince among verticillium hosts. No ph_range: USU rates its alkalinity tolerance "High" and UGA calls it "tolerant of a wide range of soils", a tolerance not a per-crop optimum. spacing_in_row_cm omitted.

species.note:
A stone fruit like peach (Prunus, a Verticillium host and itself susceptible, R-094), and another canopy alternative in the fruit-tree guild. Many European plums are self-fruitful, though some cultivars set better with a pollinizer.
THE SPECIES SPREAD IS ESTIMATED AND NO SOURCE STATES IT (checked 2026-07-25). UMaine Bulletin #2034, the one publication read for this species, gives HEIGHT only. 250-450 cm is the corpus's own figure, and the right end state may be a permanent estimate with no citation. The 2026-07-25 pass across 21 species found that home-garden extension publications state spacing and height and almost never state canopy width.

cultivar_groups.note: The species' own envelope on vigorous plum rootstocks, and the unqualified default.

A rootstock class, not a scion group. A Citation-class dwarfing rootstock (a peach-plum hybrid) holds a European plum to roughly 8-12 ft, and the tree wants a permanent stake. Named for the US home grower on purpose. This group first said "Pixy", which is a UK stock an American nursery will not sell them.
Read the framing before trusting the number, and note which source says what: UMaine Bulletin #2034 is why a dwarfing plum stock is the exception rather than the norm, UC ANR is the source for the sizes, and #2034 does not mention Citation at all. Both are in confidence.sources with their quotes and their provenance (D-146).
The numbers stay ESTIMATED, and the provenance is uneven. The UMaine sentences were read off the page, and the UC sizes came from a search summary of it, not a direct read. A human reading UC's rootstock page is what would settle the 8-12 ft.
The SPREAD is weaker still than the height. UC's 8-12 ft is a height figure, and no source found states a Citation-class plum's canopy spread at all, so this group mirrors its own height band. The field is estimated for that reason as well as for UC's provenance.

image.alt: A ripe red raspberry

species.note:
Suckers vigorously; mature_spread is a managed row, not the plant's full reach. The verticillium_susceptible marker blocks establishment where Solanaceae recently grew (R-094).
"A managed row" is now a read source's phrasing as well as ours (2026-07-25), and it comes with a figure the corpus does NOT match: UMN says to keep primocane spread within 12 inches of the row, i.e. 30 cm, where this species carries 60-100 cm. The corpus number tracks UMN's in-row PLANT spacing (2-3 ft) instead. Both are defensible. One is the width of the fruiting hedge a gardener maintains, the other the ground a plant is given.
RESOLVED 2026-07-25 AS NO CHANGE, on the maintainer's approval, and the reason is that the two figures are on the SAME PAGE and would contradict each other. UMN says to space plants 2-3 ft apart AND to keep primocanes within 12 in of the row. Adopting 30 cm as the spread would have the planner pack raspberries at 30 cm, a third of the spacing UMN itself prescribes, and denser than any source supports. The 12-inch figure is a PRUNING instruction for the fruiting wall, not a packing dimension, and mature_spread_cm is what the placement fill packs on (footprint._spread_m takes the max of the range). So the flag stays, the citation records both numbers, and the number stands. Do not "correct" it downward to 30 cm later. That is why this paragraph exists.
IN NO GUILD, AND THE FRUIT-TREE ONE IS WHERE IT WOULD GO (2026-07-26). Raspberry meets temperate_fruit_tree_guild.insectary's stated predicate exactly ({pollinator_value: high, casts_shade: false}) and is deliberately not named among its alternatives. The reason is Verticillium, and it is structural. That guild's canopy role admits prunus_persica and prunus_domestica, both carrying verticillium_host AND verticillium_susceptible, and so does this species. Naming raspberry there would make it the first guild in the corpus to co-plant two Verticillium hosts in one bed.
THE POINT THAT MAKES THIS WORTH WRITING DOWN: neither R-094 nor R-095 would catch it. R-094 fires on a prior SEASON's family and R-095 on a LOGGED prior planting. Both are history rules, and neither looks at what a guild puts in the ground together in the same season. So the guild roster is the only thing standing between a gardener and that bed, and this paragraph is the roster's reason. If a same-bed co-planting check ever exists, this is the case it should be tested on.

image.alt: A ripe blackberry

invasive_status.note: A Weed of National Significance in Australia, and a declared plant in South Australia, where landowners must deal with it on their land. In Tasmania it is a declared weed: importing, selling and growing it are prohibited, though the state's blackberry plan does not cover commercial varieties, such as thornless ones. In New Zealand it is a pest under regional plans, and Auckland bans breeding, selling or releasing the wild kinds. It spreads quickly and forms prickly thickets; rules on growing it differ from place to place.

species.note:
Blackberry, added 2026-07-26, and it took three attempts. Surveyed across seven land-grant publications and REFUSED, because every one of them omitted the single field E-ZONE requires of a perennial. Added now because an eighth publication was found, and the way it was found is the lesson: BOTH OSU URLS HAD BEEN RECORDED AS "403 FROM THIS CONTAINER" AND THE 403 WAS OURS. WebFetch was refused; `curl -sSL` returns HTTP 200 on the identical URL. A species was declined on a negative that was never true. When a fetch tool 403s, try another before recording an absence.
THE ZONE IS THE BEST-SOURCED IN THIS CORPUS AND IS STILL FLAGGED. OSU EC 1303 publishes a table of SIXTEEN NAMED CULTIVARS, each with its own range, which is what every other perennial in this corpus lacks. [5, 9] is not a union artifact spanning plants that do not exist. Five cultivars carry exactly that range ('Caddo', 'Prime-Ark Freedom', 'Galaxy', 'Eclipse', 'Twilight'). It is the WIDEST published range, and narrower ones exist ('Black Gem' 5-8, 'Marion' 6-9). Flagged for consistency with all 25 other perennial zones and because the ceiling's mechanism is still open (ISSUES #13), not because the number is weak.
THE VERTICILLIUM FLAGS ARE NOT ANALOGY TO RASPBERRY, which SPECIES-EXPANSION.md warned against by name for this species. Penn State's bramble page (already R-094's own cited source) says the disease "affects mainly black raspberries and certain cultivars of blackberries", naming this crop DIRECTLY and rating it above red raspberry, which "can be affected, but plants are likely to survive for several years with reduced vigor". Better provenance than rubus_idaeus's own.
NO CULTIVAR GROUPS, THOUGH BLACKBERRY LOOKS LIKE THE TEXTBOOK CASE. The sources do not share a cane-type taxonomy: NC State groups semi-trailing WITH erect at 3-4 ft, Clemson groups it with trailing at 6-8 ft, Illinois puts it at 8-10 ft. Three read sources, three incompatible classifications of the same middle type. OSU's cultivar table cuts across type as well ('Black Gem' is erect at zones 5-8 while 'Kiowa' is erect at 6-9), so type does not predict zone either. Groups here would encode a taxonomy no source shares, which is the ruling endive and sour cherry both got.
SPACING IS THE ERECT FIGURE, and it is the one dimension the sources agree on: 2-4 ft from both Illinois and Clemson independently, 3-4 ft from NC State and UMD, 3 ft from Iowa State. OSU gives 3-5 ft for TRAILING plants, which is a different type and is not what 90 cm represents.
HEIGHT AND YEARS TO BEARING HAVE NO SOURCE IN EIGHT PUBLICATIONS. The one figure that looked like a height is not one: UGA says "Cut these to a height of 40 to 42 inches in early summer to encourage lateral shoot development", a PRUNING INSTRUCTION, the same trap as raspberry's 12 inches, and caught only because this corpus had already recorded that trap.
IN NO GUILD, FOR RASPBERRY'S REASON ONLY MORE SO (the expansion plan requires this be written rather than left silent). The only perennial guilds are the two fruit-tree ones, whose canopy role admits prunus_persica and prunus_domestica, both verticillium_host AND verticillium_susceptible, as is this species. Naming a bramble there would put two Verticillium hosts in one bed, and NEITHER R-094 NOR R-095 WOULD CATCH IT: both fire on prior-season or logged history, never on a same-bed pairing. The case is stronger here than for rubus_idaeus, because Penn State rates blackberry as MORE affected than red raspberry. See rubus_idaeus for the full reasoning and docs/GUILD-MEMBERSHIP.md for why guild membership is editorial rather than computed.

image.alt: A ripe red strawberry

species.note:
Spreads by runners into a matted row; mature_spread is one crown, not the planting's extent. verticillium_susceptible marks it a Verticillium victim (R-094): do not establish where Solanaceae recently grew. Extension also lists strawberry among the crops that BUILD the Verticillium reservoir for later plantings. Modeling strawberry as a reservoir source is a separate rule-level follow-up (the rule triggers on Solanaceae only).
"One crown, not the planting's extent" is exactly what a read source cannot confirm (2026-07-25): UMN publishes three spacings for three systems and no crown width, and it puts the runner problem in the gardener's hands, with up to 120 daughter plants from one crown in a season, so the planting's extent is whatever the gardener permits. 30-45 cm sits inside UMN's 12-18 in general spacing, which is the closest thing to corroboration available.

image.alt: A peach, whole and halved to show the pit

species.note:
Stone fruit. verticillium_host marks it a reservoir SOURCE: a logged peach builds the Verticillium reservoir that later blocks a susceptible perennial (R-094), the third reservoir crop (with strawberry and bramble) that the Penn State source names alongside Solanaceae. verticillium_susceptible makes it a Verticillium victim too (R-094): do not establish where Solanaceae or a logged Verticillium host recently grew. Self-fruitful, unlike apple. One tree sets fruit, so no cross-pollination rule applies (R-080).
The 2.5-4.5 m envelope is a HOME-GARDEN peach and is deliberately not the biggest number in the literature. Checked 2026-07-25 after a USU figure of about 20 feet wide suggested it was too low. That figure is an unpruned tree on a standard rootstock, and standard rootstocks (Guardian, Halford, Nemaguard) run 24-30 ft. A garden peach is trained to an open-centre vase and pruned down, and semi-dwarf rootstocks (Sharpe, MP-29) spread 12-15 ft. 250-450 cm is 8-15 ft, which covers the pruned tree and the semi-dwarf stock, i.e. what a home gardener actually ends up with. Do not "correct" it upward to an orchard-standard spread; the planner would reserve ground for a tree nobody here grows. The three publications behind that reasoning are in confidence.sources (D-146).
NECTARINE is carried as a second common name, not a cultivar group, added 2026-08-31. A nectarine is Prunus persica: the same tree, size, zone, culture and self-fruitful pollination as a peach, differing only in a fuzzless (glabrous) skin, a fruit-surface trait this corpus does not model. The fields a group would carry (height, spread, support, DTM) do not differ, and the size axis is already spoken for by standard_seedling vs genetic_dwarf, either of which a nectarine can be. So a "nectarine group" would either duplicate peach's geometry or collide with that axis; the right form is discoverability: a gardener searching "nectarine" finds and plans the same tree. That is the O117 pattern (a name that resolves to the right species), and no group is minted to assert a difference the model cannot see.

cultivar_groups.note: The species' own envelope on a seedling peach rootstock, and the unqualified default.

A SCION group, not a rootstock class, and the one place this corpus's dwarf trees differ in mechanism. Peach dwarfs by cultivar genetics ('Bonanza', 'Pix-Zee', 'Bonfire' and kin have compressed internodes), not by a dwarfing rootstock, so the tree keeps a normal root system. The no-stake call is the part that has since been checked and held: extension guidance says genetic dwarf fruit trees are sturdier and may not need staking, unlike the dwarf apple and plum, which are staked precisely because a rootstock made them badly anchored. The top of the range moved 2.5 -> 3 m because the sources disagree about how big these get ('Bonanza' is cited at 5-6 ft while genetic dwarf peaches generally are put at 8-10 ft), and the wider envelope covers the disagreement without picking a side. Still ESTIMATED; a human reading a land-grant VARIETY table (not a rootstock chart, which is a different document with a different mechanism) is what would settle it.
THREE land-grant publications have now been read looking for a mature height for a named genetic dwarf peach and none carries one. The negatives are recorded in confidence.sources so the next person does not spend the hour again. Leaving this range estimated with the disagreement written down may be the right end state, and not a gap awaiting a source.

image.alt: Red sour cherries on the branch

species.note:
Sour cherry, added 2026-07-26, and it is the first perennial in the Axis B remainder whose COLD end a publication actually states. Blackberry was surveyed first and declined over exactly this field: seven land-grant publications, not one giving a USDA zone. The difference is not luck. Cold hardiness is the limiting factor for stone fruit, so tree-fruit publications print a zone, while bramble publications write for their own state and have no reason to. Expect that split to hold for the rest of the perennial candidates.
THE FIRST DRAFT OVERCLAIMED THIS, and the correction is the most useful thing in the entry. It said the zone was STATED, BOTH ENDS, unflagged, "which no other perennial in this arc has managed". Illinois does print "4 - 9", so that read as sourced. But its 9 is a nursery COLD-hardiness figure and this corpus gates the field two-sided, making the warm end a chill-hour ceiling as well. Taken literally it made sour cherry the only canopy tree R-076 would offer in HOUSTON. test_hardiness_zone_gates_perennials caught it immediately and the test was not touched. The zone is now [4, 8], flagged, half-sourced like every other zone here. See the citation, which also records that R-076 names no mechanism for the ceiling it enforces (ISSUES.md).
THREE FIELDS ARE UNFLAGGED BECAUSE READ SOURCES STATE THEM AND AGREE: years_to_bearing, full sun (three sources), and self-fruitfulness (two). That last one matters beyond this species, because self_incompatible: false means R-080 correctly does NOT fire, and it is stated rather than assumed: a single sour cherry sets fruit. UMN adds that "a second compatible variety will ensure even better pollination and fruit set", which is the same shape as blueberry's self-fertility note (one plant works, two work better), and is recorded so nobody later reads the false flag as a claim that a second tree is pointless.
THE VERTICILLIUM FLAGS ARE NOT ANALOGY, which SPECIES-EXPANSION.md warned against for exactly this species. verticillium_host rests on Penn State's already-cited sentence naming "stone fruits" as a category to avoid planting after, the same source and the same basis that carries peach and plum, applied to another member of the category it names. verticillium_susceptible rests on a page about this species specifically: Illinois lists "Verticillium wilt (Verticillium dahliae)" among sour cherry's diseases, naming the exact pathogen R-094 models.
NO CULTIVAR GROUPS, AND THE REASON IS A DISAGREEMENT RATHER THAN AN ABSENCE. A genetic_dwarf group is the obvious follow-up. Peach already has one, and the sources name sized cultivars ('North Star' dwarf, 'Meteor' semi-dwarf, 'Montmorency' full size). But the two read sources give the SAME cultivar different heights: UMD calls North Star a "Genetic dwarf, reaches 6-12 ft" while Iowa State says it "commonly grows 8 to 10 feet tall". A group exists to carry a number, and there is no agreed number to carry. The species band spans both instead.
THE HEIGHT IS THE PRUNED TREE, deliberately, and this is the peach ruling applied again. Illinois gives "12-15 Feet (When pruned. Unpruned up to 50 ft)", a 50 ft figure that would have the planner reserve ground for a tree no home garden contains. 250-460 cm is roughly 8-15 ft, which spans the home-garden cultivars every source describes. Do not "correct" it upward toward the unpruned figure later.

species.note: Sweet cherry, added 2026-08-31, the first species of the fruit+herb catalogue tranche the maintainer opened against D-156's new-species cap to answer the /compare/ library gap (D-194, the same scoped-exception shape as D-193's perennial vegetables). The corpus already knew it was missing: R-137's pollination note records "Sweet cherry and Japanese plum are not in the corpus." THE DEFINING CONTRAST WITH SOUR CHERRY IS POLLINATION, and it is why this is a distinct species and not a note on prunus_cerasus: sweet cherry is SELF-UNFRUITFUL (Illinois: "plant two or more different varieties so that they can cross-pollinate"), so pollination.self_incompatible is true and R-080 fires (plant two cultivars), exactly as it does not for the self-fruitful sour cherry, peach and plum. A few modern cultivars ('Stella', 'Lapins', 'Sweetheart') are self-fertile; that is a cultivar exception, not the species default, and is not modelled as a group (no distinct geometry: the nectarine lesson). THE ZONE IS [5, 8], NOT THE NC STATE TOOLBOX'S [3, 8]. The toolbox band is a plant-database survival range and would make sweet cherry HARDIER than sour cherry ([4,8]), which is horticulturally backwards. Sweet cherry is the LESS hardy of the two. Illinois says so directly (sour "can be grown all over the state", sweet only "in central and southern parts") and its Hort Answers page gives the crop zone as "5 - 8". This is the blackberry lesson (a sourced number can still be the wrong number for the crop); the fruiting zone is used and the toolbox figure is recorded and rejected in confidence.sources. THE ENVELOPE IS A HOME-GARDEN TREE, not the orchard standard, the same call peach's record makes. Illinois gives "10-50 feet (depends on the type of rootstock used)"; 300-610 cm (10-20 ft) is the pruned tree on a dwarfing/semi-dwarf rootstock (Gisela, which Illinois names as increasingly popular for sweet cherry, and which, unlike pear, does exist), not the 30-50 ft standard on Mazzard. Do not "correct" it upward; the planner would reserve ground for a tree nobody here grows. VERTICILLIUM: HOST YES, SUSCEPTIBLE WITHHELD, and the asymmetry is deliberate. verticillium_host is true on the same basis sour cherry and peach carry it: Penn State's stated category "avoid land recently planted with ... stone fruits" (R-094's own cited source), and sweet cherry is a stone fruit. So a logged sweet cherry builds the reservoir. But verticillium_susceptible is NOT set: sour cherry's susceptible flag came from its OWN Illinois Hort Answers disease list naming "Verticillium wilt (Verticillium dahliae)", and sweet cherry's Illinois page does NOT list it. A flag that fires R-094/R-095 on this tree as a victim needs a species source, not an analogy; it stays off until one is read, exactly as horseradish's did. The obvious next refinement if a source surfaces. NO ph_range: no sweet-cherry pH figure was read (Illinois gives none), so the field is omitted. Borrowing sour cherry's [6.0, 7.5] would be the borrowed-number failure the cilantro note records. Self-fruitful cultivars aside, it is a canopy alternative in the fruit-tree guild like the other stone fruits.

species.note: Apricot, added 2026-08-31, the second species of the fruit+herb tranche (D-194). A stone fruit like peach and the cherries, and a canopy alternative in the fruit-tree guild. SELF-FRUITFUL, which is why one tree is enough and R-080 does NOT fire, the contrast with the sweet cherry landed just before it. USU: "Apricots are generally self-fruitful", and Illinois lists several self-fruitful varieties; a nearby second cultivar improves set but is not required. So pollination.self_incompatible is false, like peach, plum and sour cherry. THE DEFINING RISK IS EARLY BLOOM, NOT COLD, and it lives in this note because the perennial model has no field for it, the same choice fig's overwintering and peach's spring-spear risk made. Apricot blooms earliest of the stone fruits, so a late spring frost kills the crop even where the tree is hardy; USU reports fruiting "may only occur 3 out of 5 years" in Utah. hardiness_zone is the tree's survival range, not a promise of a crop every year. THE ZONE IS [5, 7], where Illinois Hort Answers and the NC State toolbox agree; USU gives "5 to 8" with hardy cultivars ('Moorpark', 'Goldrich', 'Harglow') to zone 4. Flagged for the warm-end disagreement; the narrower two-source band is used. THE ENVELOPE IS A HOME-GARDEN TREE (370-610 cm, ~12-20 ft) on a semi-dwarf/pruned basis, not the 20-50 ft Illinois gives for the standard on a vigorous rootstock. This is the peach reasoning; do not correct it upward to an orchard tree the planner would over-reserve ground for. VERTICILLIUM: HOST YES, SUSCEPTIBLE WITHHELD, the same asymmetry as sweet cherry. Host is Penn State's stone-fruit category ("avoid land recently planted with ... stone fruits"), so a logged apricot builds the reservoir; susceptible is not set because neither the Illinois nor the USU apricot page names Verticillium (Illinois names brown rot), so no species source fires R-094/R-095 on it as a victim. It stays off until one is read. NO ph_range: no apricot pH figure was read, so the field is omitted and nothing is borrowed.

image.alt: A stand of Russian comfrey foliage

species.cultivar_reason: Sterile. Seeding comfrey is permanent and unwelcome.
species.note:
Russian comfrey, and THE HYBRID IS THE WHOLE POINT (sourced 2026-07-26). `cultivar_required: bocking_14` and its reason were written here before there was evidence for them; there is now. UMN Extension, on Bocking comfrey as an orchard understory cover: "Bocking comfrey is sterile and does not produce seeds", and it "grows in a clumped fashion and only spreads vegetatively when its roots are disturbed through cultivation or intentional cuttings."
THAT IS WHY THIS SPECIES IS SAFE IN A GUILD AND COMMON COMFREY WOULD NOT BE. The same page contrasts Symphytum officinale, "often avoided because of the number of seeds it disperses, making it an aggressive spreader in Minnesota"; Wisconsin files that species under weed identification. This corpus does not model it, and should not: the sterile hybrid is the plant a garden can host. UMN recommends exactly the placement this corpus already gives it: understory under fruit trees.
SO COMFREY IS NOT A CONTAINMENT CASE, and ISSUES #14 was corrected to say so. It spreads VEGETATIVELY but not UNBIDDEN (it moves when you cut or till it, never on its own), which is the distinction that issue now turns on. A rule that flagged "spreads" rather than "spreads unbidden" would evict this plant from the guild an extension service recommends it for.
READ AS OF 2026-07-26: the planner prints `cultivar_required` and `cultivar_reason` on the role line that names this plant, in both fruit-tree guilds, pinned by an e2e check that assembles the expected sentence out of these two fields. Was: the field shipped to the browser in app-bundle.json and no engine, validator or screen consumed it, so a gardener was never told to buy Bocking 14, while this note recorded that seeding comfrey is "permanent and unwelcome". ISSUES #14 keeps only the containment question: naming the safe FORM of a species is not the same as saying a plant needs a barrier.

species.note: Purple coneflower, added 2026-09-01, the last T1 insectary flower of D-195, and the only PERENNIAL one: it lives in perennials.yaml with a hardiness_zone and the R-076 survival gate (frost_tolerance hardy, NC State hardy to zone 3a), unlike the annual insectary flowers (calendula, sweet alyssum). The medicinal Echinacea reputation is not modelled. It is carried here as a flower and pollinator, its garden role.

species.note: Sweet marjoram, added 2026-08-31, the fifth species of the fruit+herb tranche (D-194) and the second of the MEDIUM tier. A TENDER PERENNIAL modelled the way the corpus already models rosemary: NC State lists it as both annual and perennial and calls it "a tender perennial [that] may not survive a winter north of USDA zone 9 where it is typically grown as an annual." So lifespan is `perennial` with a warm floor and `frost_tolerance: tender`, tenderer than rosemary (half_hardy, zone 7), which is why the zone floor is 9 not 7. Across this app's temperate range it is grown as an annual, replanted each spring; the perennial classification records what the plant IS, and R-076 gates it out of gardens too cold for it to overwinter. A LATE-SEASON POLLINATOR HERB: NC State says it "provides late-season nectar for bees" and tags it bee-, butterfly- and pollinator-friendly, so pollinator_value is `high` and it can fill the insectary guild role, like the other flowering herbs. The field shape (habit bush, root_depth shallow, ground_coverage moderate) mirrors its closest corpus relative, oregano (Origanum vulgare). NOT GATED BY R-127, and the restraint is deliberate. This is the closest call in the tranche. R-127 (Mediterranean-herb sharp drainage, grade B verified) plausibly fits marjoram: it is a dry, well-drained Mediterranean herb (NC State: "average, dry to medium moisture, well-drained soil"), and it is the sister species of oregano, which R-127 DOES cover. But R-127 was extended to lavender only because R-127's own verified UMD source NAMES lavender; that source names "oregano," not "marjoram." Extending R-127 to marjoram would rest on marjoram's separate NC State page, which is unverified, and mixing an unverified pointer into a verified rule blurs the grade. The bright line (extend R-127 only to species its verified source names) holds, and marjoram waits outside it until a read source places it under the rule. No ph_range: NC State gives a neutral-to-alkaline tolerance, not a per-crop optimum (the rosemary/lavender pattern). spacing_in_row_cm omitted (no source read gives one; mature_spread carries the footprint).

species.note: English lavender, added 2026-08-31, the third species of the fruit+herb tranche (D-194) and the one herb in it. Lavandula angustifolia is the hardy, culinary lavender (the one used in cooking and the source of most garden cultivars), distinct from the tenderer lavandins and Spanish/French lavenders; the corpus carries the hardy species a temperate gardener actually plants. COVERED BY R-127 ON ARRIVAL, which is the point of adding it as a herb. R-127 (Mediterranean-herb sharp drainage / drought, grade B verified) is species-scoped, and its own UMD source already names lavender: "the 'Mediterranean' herbs, such as basil, thyme, rosemary, oregano, and lavender, grow best on sunny, dry sites in light (sandy) soil", so this species is added to R-127's applies_to in the same commit. Not a new claim: the rule's existing verified source states it, exactly the "R-127's applies_to is the reusable pattern for a one-rule-many-species win" the sweep note called. HARDIER THAN ROSEMARY, which is why it is a garden perennial where rosemary is often potted: NC State gives Lavandula angustifolia zone 5-9, against rosemary's 7-10, so frost_tolerance is `hardy`, not rosemary's `half_hardy`. The zone is the toolbox's, flagged like every zone here. NEUTRAL-TO-ALKALINE AND SHARP-DRAINED, the opposite of the acid-lovers: NC State lists it tolerating "Neutral (6.0-8.0)" and "Alkaline (>8.0)" with "Good Drainage". No ph_range is stored, because that is a tolerance category and not a per-crop optimum (the same reason rosemary and sorrel carry none), and the drainage preference is what R-127 encodes. A PREMIER POLLINATOR PLANT: NC State designates it a pollinator plant (bees and butterflies), so pollinator_value is `high` and it can fill the insectary guild role (pollinator_value high/very_high), a herb that doubles as forage. spacing_in_row_cm is omitted (no source read gives one; mature_spread carries the footprint), as for 26 other species.

image.alt: The lush green leaves of a spearmint plant

species.spreads_unbidden_reason: Runs by rhizome on its own and takes the plot. Give it a buried pot or a bed of its own.
species.note:
Perennial. Spreads aggressively by runners, so mature_spread is a season's reach and not a limit; contain it in a buried pot or a dedicated bed or it takes the plot. Do not rotate (R-072).
A READ SOURCE NOW BACKS THAT CAVEAT (2026-07-25), and it is blunter than the note was: Wisconsin Horticulture describes a mint clump as "unlimited in width". So 60-100 cm is not an envelope the plant respects and no citation will ever make it one. It is a season's fill, which is what the planner needs to reserve and what the note already said. This is the clearest case in the pass of a number that should stay ESTIMATED permanently, rather than one waiting for a document.
IN NO GUILD, AND IT MEETS A ROLE'S PREDICATE EXACTLY (2026-07-26), which is why this is written down and not left to be inferred. brassica_aromatic.masking asks {volatile_aromatic: true, mature_height_cm: {max: 60}}, spearmint satisfies both clauses, and it is still not among that role's alternatives (thyme, oregano, sage, tarragon). Two reasons, and the first is decisive: brassica_aromatic is duration: annual, and R-072 (grade A, ruling BLOCK) forbids siting a perennial in ground that is annually turned or rotated. The predicate match is real and the siting is prohibited, so the role could never have used it.
The second reason is the paragraph above. A clump the source calls "unlimited in width", placed in a guild whose footprint_min_m2 is 1.0, is the guild after one season. Note that a predicate reading mature_height_cm cannot see this: the plant qualifies on HEIGHT and disqualifies on SPREAD, and the role states no spread clause. Do not read the match as an oversight later.
AND THE OTHER ROLE IT MEETS, temperate_fruit_tree_guild.insectary, IS DECLINED ON A DIFFERENT ARGUMENT (2026-07-26, maintainer), because the two above do not reach it. R-072 does NOT block mint there: that guild is duration: perennial. And the size argument does not transfer either. The fruit-tree guild is 25 m2, so mint's 1.0 m2 is four percent of it, far short of the whole bed. Both of the reasons written above are about the aromatic guild specifically.
THE ARGUMENT THAT DOES SURVIVE IS MECHANICAL, AND IT IS ABOUT RHIZOMES RATHER THAN AREA. melissa_officinalis is ALREADY an alternative in that role (same family, and Wisconsin says it "may reseed somewhat aggressively"), so a Lamiaceae spreader is not disqualifying in itself. The difference is HOW: lemon balm spreads by seed, which is pulled or hoed, and mint spreads by rhizome, which has to be dug out. A fruit-tree understory is precisely the place that cannot be done, because excavating rhizomes means tearing through the tree's feeder roots. Wisconsin's own remedy says as much (mint is "best kept in containers to ensure it will remain confined"), and a guild role has no way to say "in a pot".
THE MISSING CONCEPT IS CONTAINMENT, not a mint fact. The corpus has no field for a plant that is fine to grow and must not be let loose in shared ground, and it would serve horseradish and comfrey as well. It is recorded here and not invented, because inventing it for one species is how a schema acquires a field that means one thing.

species.note: Roman chamomile, added 2026-08-31, the fourth species of the fruit+herb tranche (D-194) and the first of the MEDIUM tier. "Chamomile" is TWO different plants and this is the perennial one: Chamaemelum nobile, the low creeping mat grown as a groundcover and lawn. GERMAN CHAMOMILE (Matricaria chamomilla) is the taller ANNUAL usually grown for tea, a distinct species, not carried here; the deliberate-absence note is the endive pattern. Roman was chosen over German because its source data is clean and complete where German's is not (German's NC State spread field is corrupt ("0 ft 8 in - 0 ft 1 in"), and it carries no pollinator or pH data), and because the pollinator designation below is the useful engine hook. A PREMIER POLLINATOR HERB: NC State designates it attracting "bees, other insects and other pollinators", so pollinator_value is `high` and it can fill the insectary guild role (pollinator_value high/very_high), a groundcover that doubles as forage, like lavender. NO mature_spread_cm IS STORED, on purpose. NC State's width figure is "0 ft. 2 in. - 0 ft. 4 in." (5-10 cm), which is implausibly narrow for a plant grown precisely because it spreads into a mat. It describes a single crown, not the footprint. Citing 5-10 cm would be a sourced number that is the wrong number (the blackberry lesson), so the field is omitted and ground_coverage is `high` to carry the mat-former habit instead. NOT gated by R-127 (the Mediterranean-herb sharp-drainage rule). R-127's source names basil/thyme/rosemary/oregano/lavender, not chamomile, and NC State lists Roman chamomile tolerating "Moist" soil, so adding it to R-127 would be analogy, which this corpus does not do. No ph_range: NC State gives a wide tolerance (acid/neutral/alkaline), not a per-crop optimum, the same reason rosemary, lavender and sorrel carry none. spacing_in_row_cm omitted (no source read gives one). LIGHT_MIN CORRECTED 2026-08-31 (part_sun, was full_sun): NC State lists Roman chamomile as "Full sun ... or Partial Shade", so it tolerates less than full sun. full_sun is the corpus's REQUIRES-full-sun value (compiler.py blocks it from shadier sites), which wrongly excluded a shade-tolerant plant; the corpus codes shade-tolerant plants (mint, lemon balm, currants) as part_sun. The error was caught when lovage's identical "full sun or partial shade" listing was read the same day.

species.note: Lovage, added 2026-08-31, the sixth species of the fruit+herb tranche (D-194) and the last of the MEDIUM tier; a hardy perennial umbellifer, a change of pace from the tender Mediterranean herbs before it. Levisticum officinale is a tall (3-6 ft) clump-forming Apiaceae grown for its celery-flavoured leaves and stems, hardy well into cold-temperate gardens (zone 4). Its field shape follows its corpus cousins dill (Anethum graveolens) and fennel (Foeniculum vulgare): habit `stalk`, `casts_shade: true` (a 3-6 ft clump shades low neighbours; it is the tallest of the three), root_depth `deep` and feeder_class `moderate` matching fennel, the largest umbellifer already in the corpus. TOLERATES PART SHADE, so light_min is `part_sun`, not the full_sun of the Mediterranean herbs: NC State lists it "Full sun ... or Partial Shade", and the corpus codes shade-tolerant plants (mint, lemon balm, currants) as part_sun, the minimum light the plant will accept, which is what compiler.py gates on. POLLINATOR VALUE IS `moderate`, NOT `high`, and the gap from its cousins is deliberate. Dill and fennel are graded high on their own umbel/bloom descriptions, and lovage is the same beneficial- insect family (flat Apiaceae umbels are classic hoverfly/parasitic-wasp plants), which would argue for high. But THIS species' NC State page names only "Butterflies" and generic "Wildlife Value", and lacks the bee/pollinator-plant designation lavender, chamomile and marjoram earned their `high` on. So grading lovage high would overclaim against the source read. `moderate` is the source-faithful call, flagged, revisitable upward if a read source gives it the fuller designation. NOT gated by R-127: NC State lists lovage tolerating "Moist" soil, the opposite of R-127's sharp- drainage claim, and R-127's source does not name it. No ph_range: NC State gives a wide acid-to- alkaline tolerance, not a per-crop optimum (the rosemary/lavender pattern). spacing_in_row_cm omitted (no source read gives one; mature_spread carries the footprint).
