image.alt: Blueberries ripening on the bush

species.note:
Highbush blueberry, added 2026-07-25, and it is here for one reason: IT IS THE FIRST SPECIES IN THIS CORPUS WITH A PUBLISHED pH CEILING. D-149 recorded that no source read publishes a per-crop maximum for a vegetable, which is why R-099 gates only the low side. Blueberry is not a vegetable and the acid-loving literature does publish one, so this species is what gives that rule its other half.
`acid_requiring: true` IS THE MARKER THAT DOES IT, and it exists because the obvious mechanism does not work. The plan was "an unflagged ph_range means both ends are published, so gate both sides", with the confidence flag doing double duty. But the two sources read DISAGREE on the ceiling (UMD 5.5, UNH 5.0), so the field must stay flagged, and the flag can no longer carry the gate. The marker separates the two questions: the THRESHOLD is uncertain and flagged, while the EXISTENCE of a consequence above it is not. We do not know a tomato's ceiling; we know a blueberry has one, and what happens past it: iron becomes unavailable and an ericaceous plant goes chlorotic (the mechanism docs/SOIL.md already names, and UF/IFAS HS1207 puts iron deficiency at pH 7.3 and above).
IT IS IN NO GUILD, AND THAT IS A PRODUCT FACT RATHER THAN A GAP. The only perennial guilds are the two fruit-tree ones, whose canopy role wants a tree. But the sharper reason is chemical: blueberry wants 4.5-5.5 and every other species in those guilds sits at 6.0-7.0. ONE BED CANNOT SATISFY BOTH. Acid-lovers are their own bed and not a guild member, which is exactly what the pH gate now tells a gardener who tries.
THE HARDINESS ZONE IS HALF-SOURCED, and the validator is why it exists at all. The first draft omitted it, on the same reasoning that keeps ph_range absent from 31 species: no publication this container fetched gives a range for northern highbush, and nursery pages are not citations. E-ZONE refused it ("perennial with no hardiness_zone (R-076 cannot fire)"), and the check is right, because an ungated perennial is offered in zone 2. So the field carries UMN's cold end and the corpus's own warm end, flagged, with the citation saying which half is which. That is the same shape as every ph_range here: one end published, one end ours.
THREE SOURCES, THREE pH RANGES. UMD 4.5-5.5, UNH 4.5-5.0, UMN 4.0-5.5 (and 4.0-5.0 lower down the same page). They agree on the shape and not on the numbers, which is exactly why this field is flagged and why acid_requiring is a separate marker rather than an inference from an unflagged range.
Also unrecorded for want of a field, but worth keeping: UNH says blueberries "grow best in a well-drained sandy loam" and that Bluecrop "Will not tolerate wet soils". The corpus has no per-species drainage tolerance; R-100 warns about standing water for everything, which covers this case without a new field.

species.note: Asparagus, added 2026-08-05, the first species in asparagaceae and one of two perennial vegetables that open the expansion's Axis C (rhubarb is the other). A NEW FAMILY, and its rotation ruling is SILENT, stated rather than defaulted: no rotation rule names asparagaceae (R-010/011/012/013 name solanaceae, cucurbitaceae, brassicaceae, alliums and apiaceae), and a perennial that holds one spot for 15+ years is not rotated at all. Penn State's "Avoid planting asparagus in fields where it has been grown in previous years" is a do-not-replant note, not a seasonal interval, and there is no field for it here. PERMANENCE NEEDS NO NEW MACHINERY, which is the finding that made this cheap. R-072 (grade A, fatal) already refuses a perennial in ground that is annually turned ("Tillage destroys the crown" is asparagus exactly), and a standing perennial's footprint is already carried as fixed occupancy. So asparagus enters as lifespan:perennial like raspberry and blueberry, and the 15-year lifespan is a note, not a schema change. IT IS IN NO GUILD, a product fact and not a gap, for the same reason blueberry is: a permanent-bed perennial cannot share rotating ground (R-072), so it belongs in a bed of its own, not on a guild roster. Iowa State and Clemson say the same horticulturally ("place the row(s) along a side of the garden space", "a location at the end of the vegetable garden ... that doesn't interfere with annual garden tillage"). THE CROWN IS VERY COLD-HARDY, THE EMERGED SPEARS ARE NOT (Iowa State: winter damage only below -30F without snow cover, but "Late spring frosts can kill emerged spears"). frost_tolerance is the dormant plant's class; the spring-spear risk is a scheduling caution the perennial model has no field for and is recorded here. DIOECIOUS, and modern plantings are all-male hybrids (Jersey series). That is context, not a modelled field. Asparagus is grown for spears, not fruit, so pollination is not a crop concern and pollinator_value is low. Juglone-sensitive per UW-Madison's black-walnut table; that membership is added to juglans_nigra in its own commit, as the walnut record's note pre-recorded.

species.note: Rhubarb, added 2026-08-05, the first species in polygonaceae and the second perennial vegetable of Axis C (asparagus is the first). A NEW FAMILY, rotation ruling SILENT and stated: no rotation rule names polygonaceae, and this is a perennial held in one spot for many years. Permanence needs no new machinery. R-072 (fatal) already refuses a perennial in annually-turned ground, so it enters as lifespan:perennial like asparagus and blueberry. THE SOURCES DISAGREE ON WHETHER TO MOVE IT, and both are recorded because they are answering different questions. UW-Madison: "Because this perennial will remain in the ground for several years, choose a site ... where it can remain undisturbed." UMN: "Because rhubarb takes so many nutrients from the soil, move the plant to a new site every so often. Rotate another crop into the former rhubarb patch." UMN's move is FERTILITY-driven relocation over many years, not the seasonal disease rotation R-010/011/012 model, and it is the same fact feeder_class:heavy records. It does not contradict the permanence R-072 enforces. IT IS IN NO GUILD, the blueberry/asparagus reason: a permanent-bed perennial cannot share rotating ground (R-072). THE TOXIC LEAVES ARE CARRIED BY A RULE, NOT A FIELD (maintainer, 2026-08-05). The leaf blades are poisonous (oxalic acid, and anthraquinone glycosides per NDSU) while the petioles are the edible part; that is a graded claim with a mechanism, so it is R-109, scoped to this species by applies_to.species the way R-108 is, and the species record needs no toxicity field for it to fire. pH IS NOT A CONSTRAINT, and its absence is sourced, not an omission: UMN "Soil pH is not important. Any garden soil ... whether acidic, neutral or basic ... can support a good crop of rhubarb"; Illinois "tolerant of a wide range of soil pH levels." So ph_range is absent by evidence, like the 31 vegetables with no published range. root_depth is likewise absent. The sources give soil-prep depth (UMN "at least two feet") and planting depth (2 in), never a rooting depth, so it is left out. HARDINESS ZONE WARM END IS THE CORPUS'S OWN. Cold end 3 is UMN ("Rhubarb is hardy in USDA Zone 4, and worth trying in Zone 3"); no source read gives a warm-end integer, but the warm LIMIT is a real horticultural fact (UF/IFAS: winters must fall below 40F, "somewhat difficult" in the South). 8 is declared as the corpus's own warm end, flagged, the blueberry precedent. The flag states the number's provenance; a human reading a warm-end source can promote it.

species.note: Globe artichoke, added 2026-08-31, the first species of the perennial-vegetable expansion the maintainer opened against D-156's new-species cap (artichoke, then sorrel, then horseradish; Jerusalem artichoke stays declined per SPECIES-EXPANSION.md, weed-listed by UMN and its NC State guide withdrawn). This record models the edible Scolymus Group, the globe artichoke grown for its immature flower bud. It is NOT cardoon, the other crop under Cynara cardunculus, which is grown for its leaf stalks. ROTATION IS SILENT, stated rather than defaulted: asteraceae carries no rotation rule (R-010/011/012/013 name solanaceae, cucurbitaceae, brassicaceae, and the alliums+apiaceae), and a perennial is not rotated at all. R-072 (grade A, fatal) already refuses a perennial in ground that is annually turned. So artichoke enters as lifespan:perennial like asparagus and rhubarb, and needs no new machinery. THE ZONE IS THE UNPROTECTED PERENNIAL RANGE, the fig/rosemary pattern. It is no claim that it dies elsewhere. NC State's toolbox gives 7-10, and R-076 gates it too-cold below 7. Colder than that it is grown as a half-hardy ANNUAL (USU names 'Imperial Star' for this) or overwintered with heavy mulch/protection ('Green Globe' as a perennial). The note carries that practice because the perennial model has no field for it, the same choice fig's record made. frost_tolerance is `tender` because USU states the plant 'frost and freeze sensitive'; that is the plant's class, and the zone framing above is the where-it-persists story. IT IS IN NO GUILD, a product fact and not a gap, for the same reason asparagus and blueberry are: a permanent-bed perennial cannot share annually-rotated ground (R-072), so it belongs in a bed of its own, not on a guild roster. GROWN FOR THE BUD, so pollinator_value is `low` as a crop: the head is harvested closed, before the flower opens. Left to bloom it is a major bee plant (the big purple thistle flower), but that is not how the crop is grown, the same reasoning asparagus's `low` rests on. NO ph_range, deliberately: neither source read (NC State toolbox, USU growing guide) states a target pH, and 37 other species omit the field rather than carry an unsourced number. The field stays absent until a land-grant source gives artichoke its own figure.

species.note: Sorrel, added 2026-08-31, the second species of the perennial-vegetable lane (D-193), after artichoke and before horseradish. It shares rhubarb's family, POLYGONACEAE, which already exists in the corpus, so it is not a new family. WHICH SORREL, and why: this models Rumex scutatus (French or buckler-leaf sorrel), the culinary perennial. UMN's 'Growing sorrel in home gardens' names the crop as 'Rumex scutatus, R. acetosa' and treats the two as one crop with near-identical culture; R. scutatus is chosen because NC State's toolbox documents IT (a zone band, dimensions, and 'Garden sorrel'/'Sorrel' among its common names), whereas R. acetosa (broad-leaf/common sorrel) has NO toolbox page (404) and UMN gives it only a zone FLOOR ('hardy into USDA Zone 3'), not the two-ended band R-076 needs. So the species modelled is the one the land-grants actually document; the common names carry the plain 'sorrel' a gardener searches for. THE CONFUSION TRAP, stated so it is never walked into: Rumex acetosella (sheep, field, or red sorrel) is a WEED (NC State, UMD and NC State's own publications treat it as one), a different species whose numbers must NEVER be imported into this record. This is the Rumex analogue of the asparagus-fern trap the asparagus record records: a shared common word ('sorrel') spanning a crop and a weed. ROTATION IS SILENT, stated rather than defaulted: polygonaceae carries no rotation rule (the rotation rules name solanaceae, cucurbitaceae, brassicaceae, and the alliums+apiaceae), rhubarb the other polygonaceae triggers none either, and a perennial is not rotated at all (R-072, grade A, fatal, already refuses a perennial in annually-turned ground). NO ph_range, deliberately: NC State's toolbox lists R. scutatus tolerating acid (<6.0), neutral (6.0-8.0) AND alkaline (>8.0) soil. It is pH-indifferent, so there is no optimum band to store, and inventing a narrow one would misrepresent a tolerant plant. The field stays absent, as with artichoke and 37 other species. IT IS IN NO GUILD, the same reason asparagus and rhubarb are: a permanent-bed perennial cannot share annually-rotated ground (R-072), so it holds its own spot. Grown for the leaves, cut young and often; hardy enough to be among the first spring crops, and though perennial it is short-lived and many gardeners resow it (UMN), which is context, not a scheduling field.

species.note: Grape, added 2026-08-05, the 20th family (vitaceae) and the third Axis C item after asparagus and rhubarb. Modelled as a GENUS with the two home-garden types as cultivar groups (maintainer's choice), because American and European grapes are different SPECIES rather than forms of one: the base id is genus-level `vitis_spp` (the narcissus_spp precedent, rendered "Vitis spp."), each group carries its type's binomial here: `american` is Vitis labrusca, `european` is Vitis vinifera. A NEW FAMILY, rotation ruling SILENT and stated: no rotation rule names vitaceae, and a vine held on a trellis for the life of the planting is not rotated. THE SUPPORT-MODEL FEAR WAS UNFOUNDED, which is the finding. SPECIES-EXPANSION.md said grape "needs a support model heavier than support.requires: strong". It does not: `requires: strong` is exactly the signal, and it fires R-040 ("must have an assigned support ... a trellis or cattle panel"), which is what a grape needs. Because grape is NOT n_fixing, the hills/living- support predicate (n_fixing + vine + requires strong) correctly does not grab it. It is a trellised vine like a staked tomato, not a bean on corn. Permanence rides R-072 (fatal) as asparagus's does; the pruning-system geometry the doc also named is a note, not a field, the way raspberry's managed row is. So grape entered on the existing machinery, no new model. IN NO GUILD, the blueberry/asparagus reason. THE AMERICAN ZONE IS DECLARED (maintainer ruling, the blueberry precedent). No extension source gives Vitis labrusca a numeric zone (the NC State Toolbox has no labrusca page, a real 404), only USU's "American bunch grapes ... as a group are the hardiest" and its American-cultivar tables spanning zones 3-7. [4, 8] is declared on that anchor, flagged; the EUROPEAN group's [6, 10] is sourced outright (NC State Toolbox). This is weaker than rhubarb (whose cold end was sourced) and stronger than blackberry was (nothing); the maintainer ruled to ship it declared. NO BOTANICAL HEIGHT OR SPREAD EXISTS for a trellis-trained vine, so mature_height_cm is omitted rather than invented from a cordon-training target, and mature_spread_cm carries the 6-8 ft trellis ALLOTMENT (the managed-row figure, raspberry's pattern) rather than a free-standing canopy. Self-fertile (OSU, Clemson): a single vine sets fruit, so R-080 does not apply.

species.note: Hardy kiwi, added 2026-08-31, the ninth species of the fruit+herb tranche (D-194) and the last of the LOW tier; it is the species the corpus grew a new pollination field to carry. Actinidia arguta is the HARDY, smooth-skinned kiwiberry (grape-sized, eaten skin and all), not the tender fuzzy grocery kiwi (Actinidia deliciosa, zone 7-9), a distinct species with its own record since 2026-10-15 (D-313); Oregon State says to plant a male of the same species as the female vines. It is a big woody deciduous vine (NC State: 25-30 ft, "can grow 30 feet in one year"), so it takes grape's shape: habit vine, casts shade, ground_coverage low, and support.requires `strong` (a lone kiwi will pull down a flimsy trellis). DIOECIOUS, and this is the point: NC State states "A male and female plant is needed for fruit production." Male and female flowers are borne on SEPARATE plants, so a lone vine, or several females with no male, sets no fruit. This is a different mechanism from the S-allele self-incompatibility of apple and pear (R-080), so it is carried by its own rule, R-140, and by a new pollination field, `dioecious: true`, that R-140 reads. The engine now says "needs a male pollenizer", where before it could only have said "plant 2" (which for two females is still no fruit). SELF-FERTILE CULTIVAR EXCEPTIONS exist and are recorded, not modelled: NC State names 'Issai' as "self-pollinating" and 'Chang Bai Giant' as one that "may fruit without male", a cultivar property the species-level boolean cannot express, so the note carries it. VIGOROUS TO THE POINT OF WEEDY (NC State: "Its rapid growth can cause this plant to be somewhat weedy"). That is a management caveat, not a noxious gate (not a woody N-fixer, so R-082 n/a); cats are drawn to its catnip-like scent and can damage young plants. Fruit is a food and not toxic, so there is no toxicity rule. light_min `part_sun` (NC State full sun or partial shade). No ph_range: NC State lists acid, neutral AND alkaline tolerance, not a per-crop optimum. bloom_window [late_spring, early_summer] is FLAGGED and required (an insect-pollinated species needs a window for the forage lens); hardy kiwi flowers late spring into early summer, and NC State's page does not state the month, so the window is the corpus's reading, not a quoted figure. spacing_in_row_cm omitted.

species.note: American elderberry, added 2026-08-31, the seventh species of the fruit+herb tranche (D-194) and the first of the LOW tier. A large (5-12 ft) native fruiting shrub grown for its flower clusters (elderflower) and cooked berries (syrup, wine, jelly), and a strong pollinator/wildlife plant. ITS TOXICITY IS CARRIED BY R-139, NOT A FIELD, following the maintainer's 2026-08-05 ruling that a toxic-part hazard is a rule with a mechanism (R-109 is the rhubarb precedent). Raw and unripe berries and all leaves/stems/roots are toxic (cyanogenic glycosides; cooking inactivates them), so R-139 fires the cook-before-eating caution. R-139 was promoted to verified 2026-09-01 after the maintainer read the NC State and UMN Extension sources (invariant 4); it landed unverified with this species 2026-08-31 and no longer sits in the backlog. SUCKERS INTO THICKETS: NC State calls it "weedy" and notes it "will spread by root sucker and will form thickets if the suckers are not removed". That is a management caveat, carried here and in ground_coverage `high`, and NOT a noxious-weed gate. Elderberry is a native, non-nitrogen-fixing shrub, so R-082 (which gates woody N-fixers against the state noxious list) does not apply to it. CROSS-POLLINATION IS WITHHELD, not asserted: elderberry is widely said to fruit better with a second cultivar, but the NC State page read does not state it, so pollination.self_incompatible is left unset rather than guessed (the sweet-cherry discipline). Verticillium host/susceptible are likewise omitted, since they are not sourced. light_min `part_sun` (NC State: full sun or partial shade). No ph_range: NC State gives an acid-to-neutral tolerance, not a per-crop optimum. spacing_in_row_cm omitted (no source read gives one; mature_spread carries the footprint).

species.note: Currant and gooseberry, added 2026-08-05, the 21st family (grossulariaceae) and the fourth Axis C item. Modelled as a GENUS (`ribes_spp`, the vitis_spp/narcissus_spp precedent) with the three home-garden types as cultivar groups (maintainer's choice): red_currant is Ribes rubrum (the default), black_currant is Ribes nigrum, gooseberry is Ribes uva-crispa / hirtellum. A NEW FAMILY, rotation ruling SILENT and stated: no rotation rule names grossulariaceae, and these are perennial shrubs held in dedicated ground. Permanence rides R-072 as the other perennials do; in no guild, the blueberry reason. THE BLISTER-RUST REGULATION IS CARRIED BY R-110, not a blacklist (maintainer ruling 2026-08-05). Ribes is an alternate host of white pine blister rust and some states regulate planting it, but it is a legal, widely grown crop, unlike autumn olive (BLACKLISTED under R-082 as a banned invasive). So the corpus advises and does not refuse. R-110 is a grade-A ADVISE rule scoped to this species. Black currant is the most susceptible and the most regulated, which R-110 names. UNUSUAL FOR A FRUIT CROP, RIBES TOLERATE PART SHADE. light_min is part_sun, sourced outright (Iowa State 'partial to full sun', UMN 'full sun to partial shade', USU 'morning sun, afternoon part-shade'), so it correctly does not trip the full-sun shade rules. SELF-FERTILE, so mode is `self` (out of the forage lens): red currant and gooseberry set fruit from one plant. BLACK CURRANT self-fertility VARIES BY CULTIVAR ('Consort' is self-fertile, 'Crusader' and 'Coronet' need a pollinizer; UMN, Penn State), which is a cultivar fact this record does not carry as `self_incompatible` (that would wrongly fire R-080 for every black currant); it is recorded here instead. ZONES: gooseberry [3, 6] is sourced outright (USU 'hardy to zone 3 ... perform well in zones 3 to 6'); the two currants carry a SOURCED cold end (USU red currant 'cold hardy to zone 3 or 4') and a DECLARED warm end 7 (the rhubarb precedent: Ribes are cool-climate and do poorly in heat, but no source gives a warm integer), flagged. The NC State Toolbox has no fruiting-Ribes page (all 404); it carries only the ornamental Ribes sanguineum.

species.note: American persimmon, added 2026-09-01, a T2 perennial fruit of D-195, and the SECOND dioecious species in the corpus after hardy kiwi, so it is the first REUSE of the R-140 dioecy feature built for kiwi, which is the point of adding it here. DIOECIOUS: NC State says "Persimmons are dioecious, meaning there are separate male and female trees, and you need both to get fruit", so pollination.dioecious is true and R-140 fires "needs a male pollenizer". R-140's applies_to is extended to name this species in the same change; R-140 stays verified for the GENERAL dioecy claim (the kiwi read), and persimmon's dioecy is a flagged species field sourced from persimmon's own NC State page. This extends the general rule's coverage and does not re-verify it. SELF-FRUITFUL CULTIVAR EXCEPTIONS exist (parthenocarpic American cultivars such as 'Meader' set fruit without a male). They are recorded, not modelled, the kiwi 'Issai' pattern. A hardy (zone 4) native, tolerant of poor soil (feeder_class light), and a strong pollinator + wildlife plant (NC State: bees, butterflies, moths, pollinators; larval host for luna and hickory-horned-devil moths; fruit for birds and mammals), so pollinator_value is high and it also enters the forage lens. The FRUIT is astringent when green and "sweet when soft and ripe and may be eaten raw" (NC State). It is a food and not toxic, so there is NO toxicity rule (unlike elderberry). mature_height/spread are a home-garden ENVELOPE, flagged: NC State's 30-80 ft x 20-35 ft is the wild forest tree, while a grafted garden persimmon is smaller and prunable (the stone-fruit envelope pattern). No ph_range (NC State lists acid/neutral/alkaline tolerance). verticillium host/susceptible omitted, since they are not sourced. years_to_bearing omitted, because no source read gives one; grafted persimmons take a few years to bear, noted here qualitatively, with no number. Ebenaceae is a new family for the corpus (the ebony family).

species.note: Red mulberry, added 2026-09-01, a T2 perennial fruit of D-195, and the THIRD dioecious species in the corpus (after hardy kiwi and persimmon), and the second reuse of the R-140 dioecy feature, which is the point of adding it here. DIOECIOUS: NC State says the "male and female flowers usually appear on separate trees (dioecious)", so pollination.dioecious is true and R-140 fires "needs a male pollenizer". R-140's applies_to is extended to name this species in the same change; R-140 stays verified for the GENERAL dioecy claim (the kiwi read), and mulberry's dioecy is a flagged species field sourced from mulberry's own NC State page. This extends the general rule's coverage and does not re-verify it. DIOECY AND FORAGE ARE INDEPENDENT AXES: mulberry is WIND-pollinated (pollination.mode wind, not insect) with pollinator_value low, so unlike persimmon it fires R-140 but does NOT enter the forage lens. The two kiwi/persimmon features do not travel together. The native M. RUBRA is chosen deliberately over the introduced M. ALBA (white mulberry), which is invasive across much of North America and threatens native red mulberry by hybridization (NC State lists a red x white hybrid cultivar 'Collier'); M. alba is not carried. The FRUIT is edible (NC State: "Ripe fruits are sweet, juicy, and can be eaten raw or made into pies, jellies, or jams"), so there is NO toxicity rule (unlike elderberry). A "can become weedy" management caveat is recorded (NC State: "These trees can become weedy"; "Weedy self-seeding and messy fruit are concerns"). It is noted, not modelled as a blacklist, because weediness of a native fruit tree is a siting tradeoff, not the R-082 noxious-woody-fixer block. mature_height/spread are a home-garden ENVELOPE, flagged: NC State's 25-60 ft x 35-40 ft is the wild forest tree (the stone-fruit / persimmon envelope pattern). No ph_range (not stated by the source), no verticillium (not sourced), no years_to_bearing (no source read gives one). Moraceae is fig's family (already in the corpus).

species.note: Honeyberry (haskap), added 2026-09-01, a T2 perennial fruit of D-195. Its defining planting fact is that it is SELF-INCOMPATIBLE: UW-Madison Extension says it needs "cross-pollination with an unrelated cultivar that blooms at the same time", so pollination.self_incompatible is true with min_cultivars 2 and R-080 fires "plant a different cultivar", the apple/pear pattern, the fourth self-incompatible species in the corpus. This is DELIBERATELY NOT dioecy/R-140: honeyberry plants carry both sexes and reject only same-cultivar pollen (S-allele self-incompatibility), where a dioecious plant is a single sex, the same distinction R-080's mechanism draws against R-140, and the reason honeyberry lands on R-080 not R-140. The one SOURCED numeric contrast is ph_range [5.5, 8.0]: unlike blueberry (acid-loving), honeyberry "tolerate[s] a wide range of soil pH, from 5.5-8" (UW), up to 7.7+ (USU), a real value and not an envelope. It is extremely cold hardy (frost_tolerance hardy; grows in cold zones, flowers hardy to ~20F) but scorches above ~zone 6, so hardiness_zone [2, 7] is a conservative garden band, flagged (sources say the plant survives z1-8). Fruit is edible fresh or processed (UW/USU), so there is no toxicity rule. pollinator_value is `moderate`, flagged: it is insect-pollinated and blooms very early (a real early-season bee plant), but no source read states a forage value, and `moderate` is excluded from the forage lens, so it stays out, which is the right outcome without a forage source. bloom_window is [early_spring] (the earliest the vocabulary carries): honeyberry blooms very early (UW "erupt in early spring", "six weeks before the last frost"), and the forage lens REQUIRES a bloom_window on every insect-pollinated species so it never silently drops one, so it is recorded even though `moderate` keeps honeyberry off the forage roster. years_to_bearing and verticillium omitted (unsourced). caprifoliaceae (the honeysuckle family) is new to the corpus.

species.note: Black chokeberry (aronia), added 2026-09-01, the last T2 perennial fruit of D-195, and the SELF-FERTILE contrast to honeyberry: Iowa State says "Aronia is self-fruitful and does not require a pollinator for fertilization and fruit set", so pollination.self_incompatible is FALSE and R-080 correctly stays SILENT, whereas honeyberry (self-incompatible) and apple/pear need a second cultivar. It is stated rather than assumed (the quince pattern): a single aronia fruits. Cross-pollination can improve set but is not required (UW), a per-planting nicety the boolean does not carry. It is also a real POLLINATOR shrub: NC State lists it attracting "Butterflies, Pollinators" (and birds, small mammals), and UMN lists it among pollinator trees/shrubs, so pollinator_value high, and, being insect-pollinated with a bloom_window, it enters the FORAGE LENS automatically (Door 2), the calendula/echinacea/persimmon path. bloom_window [late_spring, early_summer] from NC State "May to June". A tough zone-3 EASTERN NA NATIVE (frost_tolerance hardy), highly adaptable, needs no fertiliser (Iowa; feeder_class light). Fruit is EDIBLE (astringent raw; NC State "make into jams or jellies", Iowa notes 18-24% sugar when fully ripe), a food, so there is no toxicity rule. It "spreads freely and suckers profusely" (NC State). That is recorded as a siting caveat, NOT modelled as a blacklist: a desirable native that forms a thicket is a placement tradeoff, not the R-082 noxious-woody block. light_min part_sun: both sources list partial shade as suitable (a shade-tolerant native), with full sun "recommended for best crop yields" (Iowa), noted but not the minimum. mature_height/spread are NC State's shrub range (3-10 ft x 3-6 ft), plantable as-is (no forest-tree envelope needed, unlike persimmon/mulberry). ph_range OMITTED: NC State gives only pH CATEGORIES (acid/neutral/alkaline all suitable = broad tolerance) and Iowa "slightly acidic ... preferred". No source read gives numeric bounds, so none are stored (the contrast with honeyberry's explicit UW "5.5-8"); broad tolerance / slight-acid preference noted here. years_to_bearing OMITTED: sources describe a yield RAMP (a small crop within ~2 seasons, mature ~7-8 yr), not a clean first-bearing integer. rosaceae (apple/pear/quince family).

species.note: Anise hyssop, added 2026-09-01, the first T3 species of D-195 (pollinator/culinary herbs). It is BOTH a culinary herb and a premier late-season forage plant, which is the point of it: NC State says "The foliage has an anise or licorice scent and can be used as a flavoring in salads and teas" (the kitchen use) and lists it "Bee friendly", attracting "bees, butterflies and birds" (the forage use). pollinator_value high + a bloom_window puts it in the FORAGE LENS automatically (Door 2), the echinacea/calendula path, and its bloom_window [midsummer, late_summer] is the valuable part: NC State says "Flowering starts in late July and continues until late autumn", so it feeds pollinators in the late-season window when much else has finished (the vocabulary caps at late_summer, so the autumn tail is noted here and not modelled). NO pollination field: the culinary Lamiaceae neighbours (oregano, thyme, lavender, marjoram) carry none, and forage membership comes from pollinator_value, not pollination.mode. Adding mode:insect would only pull in the fruit-set/insect- roster machinery this herb does not use (CLAUDE.md: match the neighbours). A hardy (zone 4) clumping herbaceous perennial (habit stalk, like echinacea); lamiaceae, the mint/herb family. It "will self-seed in the garden" (NC State), a mild spreading caveat noted but not modelled. ph_range OMITTED (not stated by the source); years_to_bearing n/a for an herb. light_min full_sun matches the other Lamiaceae herbs (NC State lists full sun and partial shade; full sun for best bloom).

image.alt: A fig cut in half, showing its red interior

species.note: Fig, added 2026-08-05, the 22nd family (moraceae) and the LAST Axis C item, completing the family expansion. A NEW FAMILY, rotation ruling SILENT and stated: no rotation rule names moraceae, and fig is a woody perennial held on a permanent site. Permanence rides R-072; in no guild, the blueberry reason. THE ZONE-MARGINAL BLOCKER RESOLVED THE ROSEMARY WAY, not with a new "protection extends the zone" concept (which would fabricate survival the plant does not have unprotected). The zone is the plant's real unprotected range, [7, 10], sourced outright from the NC State Toolbox, and R-076 correctly gates it too-cold below 7. The overwintering PRACTICE, which is how fig is grown colder, is carried HERE in prose and not as a rule, because a species-scoped rule reads no field and would fire "wrap your fig" in zone 10 where it is pointless, so the zone-conditional advice stays a note, exactly as rosemary's "grown as a potted plant" does. The practice, all extension-sourced (Rutgers, NC State, Penn State): grow fig in a large CONTAINER and move it to an unheated garage when dormant; or WRAP the plant in burlap/tar paper; or build a chicken-wire CAGE filled with hay/mulch; or MOUND 1-2 ft of soil/mulch over the base. Fig fruits on the CURRENT SEASON'S new wood, so a plant killed to the ground by cold can resprout and still crop, the die-back-and-resprout mechanism NC State, UGA, Penn State and Arkansas all state, and the reason a marginal fig is still worth planting. NO CULTIVAR GROUPS, and that is a sourcing finding, not an omission. The cold-hardy cultivars ('Chicago Hardy', 'Celeste', 'Brown Turkey') are real, but NO extension source gives them a colder USDA zone INTEGER. Extension states their hardiness as degF tolerance (~0-10F with protection) and the die-back/resprout habit, while the "hardy cultivar = zone 6" number is nursery/blog framing only (D-146 excludes it). Encoding a hardy/standard zone split would be the endive/blackberry error: a distinction no read source shares. The named hardy cultivars are in the note as a purchasing steer, not as groups. PARTHENOCARPIC, so mode is `self` (out of the forage lens): common/home-garden figs 'set fruit without cross-pollination' (Clemson, UGA, NC State). The wasp-dependent Smyrna/caprifig types, which need a Blastophaga wasp not present in most of the US, are deliberately not modelled. SIZE IS ROUTINELY RESTRAINED: the toolbox 10-30 ft is the unpruned extent; Clemson notes 'severe pruning can restrict them to a manageable height', and container figs are smaller still.

usda_plants.source: USDA NRCS PLANTS Database, plant profile PUGR2 (https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/PUGR2); record fetched in-container 2026-10-15 from the PLANTS web service (PlantProfile?symbol=PUGR2: Punica granatum L., 'pomegranate', which PLANTS still files in the family Punicaceae, growth habits shrub and tree, no noxious status); quoted in the D-313 packet, which the maintainer read 2026-10-15; unverified until its own promotion commit

species.note: Pomegranate is a dense, thorny, deciduous shrub, 2 to 4 m tall, that suckers from the base and can be trained as a small tree. One plant sets fruit on its own. It wants full sun for fruit and well-drained soil, and once established it takes dry spells, though for a good crop it is watered every 7 to 10 days when there is no rain. It grows in zones 8 to 11 and fruits even in South Florida. It is killed to the ground below about 10 °F (-12 °C), and a dormant plant can be badly hurt at 12 °F (-11 °C); some varieties are hurt at 18 °F (-8 °C), and a late spring freeze harms a plant already in leaf. Where winters are colder than zone 8, grow it in a protected spot or in a container brought indoors for winter. Humid, wet summers bring fruit rot and splitting. It is in the loosestrife family (Lythraceae); older sources, and USDA PLANTS, put it in a family of its own, Punicaceae. Not known here: how deep its roots go.

usda_plants.source: USDA NRCS PLANTS Database, plant profile FESE2 (https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/FESE2); record fetched in-container 2026-10-15 from the PLANTS web service (PlantProfile?symbol=FESE2: Feijoa sellowiana (O. Berg) O. Berg, 'feijoa', family Myrtaceae; a PlantSearch for Acca sellowiana returns nothing, so PLANTS files the plant under its older name); quoted in the D-313 packet, which the maintainer read 2026-10-15; unverified until its own promotion commit

species.note: Feijoa, or pineapple guava, is an evergreen shrub from southern Brazil, Uruguay and northern Argentina (in Uruguay, guayabo del país), grown for its scented green fruit and its edible flowers. It can be kept as a hedge or trained as a small tree, and it takes salt spray and part shade, though it fruits best in sun. It grows in zones 8 to 10: the plant is hurt below about 20 °F (-7 °C) and the fruit below 28 °F (-2 °C). It needs some winter cold to flower, so in a frost-free garden it may bear little; how much it needs depends on the variety. Most varieties crop better with a second variety nearby, though a few, like 'Coolidge' and 'Unique', set fruit alone. Its roots are shallow, so mulch around it rather than dig, and water it in a long dry spell or it drops its fruit. A grafted or named plant first fruits in two to four years; a seedling takes longer. In Montevideo fruit fly is its main pest. Not known here: how many hours of winter chill a given variety needs.

usda_plants.source: USDA NRCS PLANTS Database, plant profile OLEU (https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/OLEU); record fetched in-container 2026-10-15 from the PLANTS web service (PlantProfile?symbol=OLEU: Olea europaea L., 'olive', family Oleaceae, growth habits shrub and tree, introduced in the lower 48 states and Hawaii, no noxious status); quoted in the D-313 packet, which the maintainer read 2026-10-15; unverified until its own promotion commit

invasive_status.note: A declared weed in South Australia; NC State reports it invasive in Australia, New Zealand, Hawaii and southern California. Birds spread the seed, so pick up fallen fruit.

species.note: Olive is a slow-growing evergreen tree from the Mediterranean, grown for fruit that is too bitter to eat off the tree: it is cured or pressed for oil. It wants full sun and well-drained, even poor, soil, and little water once established; wet ground brings root rot and makes the flowers drop. It grows in zones 8 to 10. A hard freeze (about 12 °F, -11 °C) can kill a mature tree to the ground, and it can regrow from the crown; leaves are hurt at about 17 °F (-8 °C), and young trees can die below 25 °F (-4 °C). Some cultivars are said to grow in zone 7. It flowers only after a cool winter, so in a mild-winter garden a tree may grow well and bear little; no source says exactly where that starts. Most varieties crop better with a second variety planted nearby. It is a declared weed in South Australia and birds spread its seed, so no plant team offers it. Not known here: how far apart to plant a single garden tree, its best soil pH (it grows in soils from pH 5.5 to 8.5), and its Spanish name.

Chev.) A. Chev., 'kiwi', rank variety, growth habit vine, an accepted name; a PlantSearch for Actinidia deliciosa returns nothing, so PLANTS files the species as a variety of A. chinensis); quoted in the D-313 packet, which the maintainer read 2026-10-15; unverified until its own promotion commit

species.note: Kiwifruit is the fuzzy, brown-skinned kiwi of the shops, a big deciduous climbing vine from China that needs a strong, permanent arbor or T-bar to carry its weight. Each vine is male or female, and only females bear, so plant at least one male and one female of this same species: Oregon State says to match the male's species to the female's, so a hardy kiwi male is not its partner. One male serves several females. It wants full sun, shelter from wind, steady water and well-drained soil; wet ground rots its roots. It is prone to Verticillium wilt, so do not plant it where strawberries, raspberries, potatoes, tomatoes, peppers or eggplant grew in the last five years. It grows in zones 7 to 9. A dormant vine should survive about 10 °F (-12 °C), but a cold snap after a warm spell can hurt it at warmer temperatures, and new spring shoots are badly damaged by half an hour at 30 °F (-1 °C). It needs some winter chill and a long season ('Hayward' about 225 to 240 frost-free days); no source says how warm a winter is too warm, so zone 9 is only where the range read ends. The first crop comes about three years after planting. Not known here: how deep its roots go, and how much winter chill it needs.

usda_plants.source: USDA NRCS PLANTS Database, plant profile CILI5 (https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/CILI5); record fetched in-container 2026-10-15 from the PLANTS web service (PlantProfile?symbol=CILI5: Citrus ×limon (L.) Burm. f. (pro sp.), 'lemon'; the search hit CILI, Citrus limon (L.) Burm. f., is labelled a 'database artifact' and its profile resolves to CILI5); quoted in the D-313 packet, which the maintainer read 2026-10-15; unverified until its own promotion commit

species.note: Lemon is a small evergreen citrus tree, 10 to 20 feet tall, that can flower and fruit through most of the year. Plant it in full sun, sheltered from wind and frost, in well-drained soil. Water it through flowering and fruit growth, but do not overwater an established tree. It grows outdoors in zones 9 to 11. Its leaves drop at 22 to 24 °F and its wood is badly damaged at 20 °F (the coldest zone 9a winters reach both), and flowers and young fruit die at 29 °F, so in colder places it is grown in a large pot and moved under cover for winter. It still crops where it is hot, but the best lemons come from dry coasts with cool summers: in hot, humid places the peel is coarser and may not colour well. A pruned tree is kept at 7 to 10 feet; a dwarf tree in a pot reaches about 2 metres. Meyer lemon is a lemon and mandarin hybrid, a different plant, and nothing here comes from it. Not known here: a heat or winter-chill limit on fruiting (no source read gives one), or the lemon's own root depth (the shallow roots are citrus in general).

usda_plants.source: USDA NRCS PLANTS Database, plant profile CISI3 (https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/CISI3); record fetched in-container 2026-10-15 from the PLANTS web service (PlantProfile?symbol=CISI3: Citrus ×sinensis (L.) Osbeck (pro sp.), 'sweet orange'; the search hit CISI resolves to it); quoted in the D-313 packet, which the maintainer read 2026-10-15; unverified until its own promotion commit

species.note: Sweet orange is the orange of the grocery store, an evergreen citrus tree 8 to 30 feet tall; navel, Valencia and blood oranges are among its kinds. Plant it in full sun, in deep, well-drained soil. It takes some drought but does best kept moist; do not overwater it. It grows outdoors in zones 9 to 11: mature trees have come through hours below 25 °F (a zone 9a winter), but a brief frost can kill a young tree and the fruit is damaged at 26 to 30 °F, so in colder places it is grown in a pot and moved under cover for winter. The orange is subtropical, not tropical: it still crops in the heat, but humid warmth gives paler peel and sourer, less juicy fruit. Valencia is the orange that does best in the tropics. Not known here: how many years a new tree takes to crop (no source read gives it for the orange), a spacing or soil pH of its own (both are citrus in general), or a heat or winter-chill limit on fruiting.

usda_plants.source: USDA NRCS PLANTS Database, plant profile CIRE3 (https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/CIRE3); record fetched in-container 2026-10-15 from the PLANTS web service (PlantProfile?symbol=CIRE3: Citrus reticulata Blanco, 'tangerine'); quoted in the D-313 packet, which the maintainer read 2026-10-15; unverified until its own promotion commit

species.note: Mandarin (tangerine) is a citrus tree with loose, easily peeled fruit, the hardiest of the four citrus here. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil; it takes drought better than the orange. It grows outdoors in zones 9 to 11: the tree is much more cold-hardy than the sweet orange, but its fruit is tender and readily damaged by cold. Satsuma, a very hardy mandarin (mature trees have come through 14 to 18 °F, zone 8 winters), is not modelled here: the sources disagree about its species, so a satsuma group waits for a source that settles it. Most mandarins set fruit on their own, but some hybrid varieties, such as 'Robinson' and 'Sunburst', need another variety nearby to pollinate them. Mandarins want warm summers for their best fruit, and in humid heat some ripen before the peel colours. Not known here: a size from an extension service (the 3 to 5 m is ABC Gardening Australia's), how many years a new tree takes to crop, a mandarin's own soil pH or spacing (both are citrus in general), or a heat or winter-chill limit on fruiting.

This is the Tahitian (Persian) lime, the lime Sydney and Brisbane gardens plant. The Key lime is a different, more cold-tender plant and is not in the corpus yet. The Tahitian lime is a small evergreen tree, about 15 to 20 feet tall, whose seedless fruit is picked green. Plant it in full sun in the warmest spot you have, in well-drained soil, and water it regularly, above all from flowering to fruit; a sprinkler on a timer can overwater it into root rot. It grows outdoors in zones 9 to 11. Its leaves are damaged below 28 °F and its wood below 26 °F (zone 9b), and below 24 °F a tree can be severely damaged or killed (a zone 9a winter can reach that), so in colder places grow it in a pot. It sets fruit without pollination, often within a year of planting, and it fruits well in the tropics. A garden tree is often pruned to 6 to 8 feet. Not known here: a soil pH range (NC State says only 6.0 or higher), a heat or winter-chill limit on fruiting, or a USDA PLANTS record (PLANTS has none for this lime).

usda_plants.source: USDA NRCS PLANTS Database, plant profile PEAM3 (https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/PEAM3); record fetched in-container 2026-10-15 from the PLANTS web service (PlantProfile?symbol=PEAM3: Persea americana Mill., 'avocado'); quoted in the D-313 packet, which the maintainer read 2026-10-15; unverified until its own promotion commit

species.note: Avocado is a big evergreen tree grown for its fruit. Buy a grafted tree: it starts to bear in about three or four years, while a seedling can take ten. It wants full sun, deep, well-drained soil and steady watering, and it will not stand wet feet, which bring root rot. It is frost-tender, and how much cold it takes depends on its race. Mexican types are the hardiest, taking the low 20s °F once mature; Guatemalan types are hurt in the mid to high 20s; West Indian types take almost no frost and need zone 10. Most garden trees are hybrids of these, and a nursery tag rarely names the race. At the warm end, Mexican types do poorly in the hot, humid lowland tropics. Each flower opens as a female and then as a male at set times of day, and varieties are sold as A or B types by that timing. A lone tree sets some fruit; where no neighbour grows an avocado, a second tree of the other type sets more. Unpruned it reaches 9 to 20 m, and growers often keep it to 3 to 4.5 m. Not known here: a soil pH in numbers, how hungry a feeder it is, or the cold limit of any one variety.

usda_plants.source: USDA NRCS PLANTS Database, plant profile MAIN3 (https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/MAIN3); record fetched in-container 2026-10-15 from the PLANTS web service (PlantProfile?symbol=MAIN3: Mangifera indica L., 'mango'); quoted in the D-313 packet, which the maintainer read 2026-10-15; unverified until its own promotion commit

species.note: Mango is a large, long-lived evergreen shade tree for frost-free gardens. Buy a grafted tree: it starts to bear three to five years after planting, while a seedling can take ten and its fruit is often stringy. It wants full sun and well-drained soil. Water it while it settles in; from about four years old it is drought tolerant and needs water only in long dry spells, and too much water spoils the fruit. It does not harden to cold: mature trees lose leaves and small branches at about 25 °F, young trees can be killed at 29 to 30 °F, and flowers and small fruit are hurt below 40 °F. It crops best where the weather stays dry while it flowers; rain, heavy dew or fog at bloom cut the crop. Unpruned it grows 9 to 18 m tall and 9 to 15 m wide; less vigorous varieties can be kept to about 3 to 4.5 m by pruning every year. Its sap, and for some people its pollen and fruit skin, can bring on a rash like poison ivy's, so wear gloves when pruning. In central and south Florida, UF/IFAS rates it Caution: manage it so it does not escape into the wild. Not known here: a dwarf size from an extension source, or how hungry a feeder it is.

usda_plants.source: USDA NRCS PLANTS Database, plant profile MUSA2 (https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/MUSA2); record fetched in-container 2026-10-15 from the PLANTS web service (PlantProfile?symbol=MUSA2: Musa L., 'banana', rank Genus); quoted in the D-313 packet, which the maintainer read 2026-10-15; unverified until its own promotion commit

species.note: Banana is a giant herb, not a tree. What looks like a trunk is a false stem of tightly rolled leaf bases, growing from an underground rhizome. Each stem fruits once and is then cut to the ground, and a sucker beside it carries the next bunch, so the clump goes on for years; keep about three stems of different ages and remove the other suckers. Garden bananas are hybrids that set their fruit without pollination. The first bunch comes 9 to 24 months after planting. A banana wants full sun, shelter from wind, rich, well-drained soil and plenty of steady water; it will not stand flooding or soggy ground. It is frost-tender: freezing damages it, and below 28 °F it is killed to the ground, but it usually regrows from the rhizome when the weather warms. Fruit needs a long frost-free run to ripen, and cool weather below 60 °F slows the plant and can stall the bunch. In south-east Queensland and northern New South Wales, get plants only from an accredited nursery: moving banana plants spreads Panama disease and bunchy top. Not known here: how cold the rhizome itself can get and survive.

usda_plants.source: USDA NRCS PLANTS Database, plant profile PAED (https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/PAED); record fetched in-container 2026-10-15 from the PLANTS web service (PlantProfile?symbol=PAED: Passiflora edulis Sims, 'purple granadilla'); quoted in the D-313 packet, which the maintainer read 2026-10-15; unverified until its own promotion commit

invasive_status.note: UF/IFAS's 2026 assessment, for all of Florida: 'High Invasion Risk', 'Predicted to be invasive and not recommended by IFAS.' Its older home-garden guides were milder. No rating for Australia could be reached.

species.note: This is the purple passionfruit, the self-fruitful form southern Australia grows ('Nelly Kelly' is one): a single vine can set fruit. Large bees carry the pollen; where bees are scarce, hand pollination with a soft paintbrush works. The yellow passionfruit, and some purple-yellow hybrids, need a second vine of different parentage to fruit. It is a fast evergreen vine that climbs by tendrils, so give it a strong trellis or fence in full sun, sheltered from wind. It has shallow roots and wants well-drained soil with small, frequent waterings; it will not stand drought or waterlogging. Vines fruit within about a year of planting (around 18 months in southern Australia) and crop well for three to six years before they need replacing. Mature vines can take a light frost with some leaf loss, but are killed to the ground in the low to mid 20s °F and may not regrow; a thick insulating wrap around the base can protect it, and new shoots grow back from there. The purple form fruits poorly in hot lowlands. Not known here: a cold limit for the purple form alone, a plant height (it grows as tall as its support), or a rating for Australia.

entities.substitution_note: Fills the support role with zero nutrient competition, zero timing constraint, and effectively unbounded load. Loses biomass, ground cover, and the story.
Fills the cover role. Does not grow food. Sometimes correct.

hazards.note:
Also J. cinerea, J. regia (weaker), and Carya spp. (weaker).
RASPBERRY IS DELIBERATELY NOT ON THE SENSITIVE LIST. UW-Madison's table names BLACKBERRY, and this corpus models rubus_idaeus, the red raspberry - a different species in the same genus. Adding it would be an inference from a genus, and this rule BLOCKS, which is the worst place in the corpus to guess. Recorded so the omission reads as a decision rather than an oversight. BLACKBERRY ITSELF (rubus_fruticosus) entered the corpus later and joined the sensitive list 2026-09-02 (O133 step 9) on the same table's own word; raspberry's reasoning is unchanged.
THE TOLERANT LIST GREW 2026-09-02 (O133 step 9) by what two pages name and this corpus models: UW-Madison's tolerant table (currant; calendula, marigold, zinnia) and Penn State's tolerant fruit trees (cherry, plum, peach, quince). Blueberry is named by neither page read and sits on no list.
ASPARAGUS and RHUBARB were added to this corpus 2026-08-05 (the perennial-vegetable expansion), and this note reserved their place: both are on UW-Madison's sensitive table, so both entered juglone-sensitive and are now on the sensitive_species list above. Like cabbage before them, that membership CHANGES what a gardener is told - R-020 blocks, and asparagus or rhubarb sited within a black walnut's juglone zone previously fired nothing.

effect_radius_m: UW-Madison / Wisconsin Horticulture (Joy, Hudelson & Jull, rev. 2024-02-28), 'Black Walnut Toxicity', hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/black-walnut-toxicity (re-read 2026-07-25): 'The toxic effects of a mature black walnut tree can extend 50 to 80 feet from the trunk of the tree, with the greatest toxicity occurring within the tree's dripline.' 50 ft is 15.24 m and 80 ft is 24.38 m, so [15, 25] is a metric rounding of a stated range - and BOTH BOUNDS ROUND OUTWARD, widening the hazard rather than narrowing it, which is the conservative direction for a rule that blocks. Flagged because a rounded conversion is not the figure the publication states (D-146). The sentence was already quoted in R-020's own evidence.pointers; it was never attached to the FIELD, so the number looked unsourced to anything reading the species entry. [read]

NOTE WHAT THE SAME SENTENCE IMPLIES AND THIS FIELD CANNOT EXPRESS: 'the greatest toxicity occurring within the tree's dripline' makes this a graded effect, strongest near the trunk and fading outward, while effect_radius_m is a flat [15, 25] band that the rule treats as in-or-out. The corpus has no way to say 'worse nearer'. Recorded rather than modelled. [read]
sensitive_species: UW-Madison, same page (re-read 2026-07-25). The prose names the four solanaceous vegetables - 'Vegetables such as tomato, potato, eggplant and pepper ... are particularly sensitive to juglone' - and the page's TABLE is wider. Its sensitive vegetables are 'asparagus, cabbage, eggplant, pepper, potato, rhubarb, tomato'; its sensitive trees include 'apple and crabapple'. brassica_oleracea (cabbage) was added on this table, and it is the one entry here that changes what a gardener is told: R-020 blocks, and cabbage under a walnut previously fired nothing. ASPARAGUS and RHUBARB, named in the same table sentence, were added to this corpus 2026-08-05 and are now on the sensitive list on the same UW-Madison authority. BLACKBERRY is on it and red raspberry is not - see the note. [read]

UW-Madison, same page (re-read 2026-07-25), tolerant table: vegetables are 'beans, beet, carrot, corn, melon, onion, parsnip, squash'. All eight are modelled here except that 'melon' and 'squash' are genus-level in the source - cucumis_melo and cucurbita_pepo are this corpus's nearest entries and are taken as the intended ones, which is why this field STAYS FLAGGED even though the list is now the source's. citrullus_lanatus (watermelon) is NOT added: 'melon' in a Wisconsin vegetable table is muskmelon, and stretching it to watermelon on a rule this strong is a guess. guilds.description: Corn, climbing beans and squash in one bed, the corn holding up the beans while the squash shades the soil below.
guilds.provenance: Haudenosaunee and widespread Indigenous North American polyculture. In the Río de la Plata, INIA Uruguay and the Universidad de la República's garden manual (2018) describes the same planting: corn with poroto beans beside it and zapallo squash.
guilds.planting_source: Cornell Garden-Based Learning, How to Plant the Three Sisters (read 2026-07-14)

roles.alternative_cost: Sunflower can carry the beans, but it is a heavy nitrogen feeder that competes with the beans and casts shade (R-021), and it needs a ~30-day head start or the vines pull it down.

mechanisms.claim: corn provides a living trellis
squash foliage suppresses weeds and retains soil moisture
squash spines and sprawl deter some vertebrate pests
beans pass a small share of their nitrogen to the corn in-season; most of it arrives next year
the corn shades the squash fruit from strong summer sun once the squash plants lose their leaves

guilds.description: The Three Sisters with a fourth plant, Rocky Mountain bee plant, added to bring in the insects that pollinate and hunt.
guilds.provenance: Contested and regional. The fourth sister is variously given as sunflower, Rocky Mountain bee plant, or amaranth, depending on nation and source. Do not present a canonical version.
guilds.planting_source: Cornell Garden-Based Learning, How to Plant the Three Sisters (read 2026-07-14); insectary density estimated (sparse accent)

roles.alternative_cost: A sunflower feeds natural enemies from its extrafloral nectaries as well as from its flowers, and it pays for that twice here: it is a heavy nitrogen feeder set among corn that is already one, and it casts shade over the mounds the squash and beans are working. Borage carries neither cost - it stays short and casts none.

mechanisms.claim: insectary draws pollinators and predatory insects

guilds.description: A small field of corn, beans and squash with pepper and amaranth worked in, the fuller Mesoamerican system the Three Sisters comes from.
guilds.provenance: Mesoamerican. Three Sisters is the northern expression of this system.
guilds.footprint_reason: Milpa is a field system with a fallow cycle. It doesn't fit a bed. Below field scale you are growing Three Sisters and calling it something else.
guilds.planting_source: Ramírez-Vega et al., Maize Intercropping in the Traditional Milpa System, PMC9605515 (read 2026-07-14); chile/amaranth densities estimated (sparse, not in close association)

roles.alternative_cost: Sunflower can carry the beans, but it is a heavy nitrogen feeder that competes with the beans and casts shade (R-021), and it needs a ~30-day head start or the vines pull it down.

mechanisms.claim: corn provides a living trellis
squash foliage suppresses weeds and retains soil moisture
fallow cycle restores fertility at field scale
beans pass a small share of their nitrogen to the corn in-season; most of it arrives next year

guilds.ruling_when_ineligible: Milpa is a field system with a fallow rotation. At your scale you want Three Sisters, which is the same team adapted to a garden.

guilds.description: Beans and squash for a bed too small for a corn block, with a trellis standing in for the corn.

roles.cost: No biomass, no romance. About $20. Reusable across seasons.
roles.alternative_cost: A heavy nitrogen feeder that competes with the beans. It needs a ~30-day head start or the vines pull it down, and it holds up about 2 vines per stalk.

mechanisms.claim: trellis provides vertical support
bush squash suppresses weeds
beans improve the ground for next season

guilds.honesty_note: Label as an adaptation, not as Three Sisters. It keeps the support, weed-suppression and soil mechanisms and drops the crop that made it a subsistence system. The beans climb a trellis instead of corn, so the corn block is gone, along with the pollination mechanism that needs it.

guilds.description: Cabbage-family crops with thyme planted among them, whose scent is meant to hide the cabbages from the pests that hunt them by smell.

mechanisms.claim: less cabbage-worm damage has been reported, and the reason isn't known yet

guilds.effect_size: Reported reductions vary widely; several trials show none. Promise nothing.
guilds.note: The weakest polyculture in the corpus and the one whose grade will move first. If the trials collapse, demote to D and say so in the commit.

guilds.description: Sage and thyme in a bed of their own, where the soil drains fast and they get water only when it is dry.
guilds.provenance: The Mediterranean culinary herbs the extension herb guides group together on one regime (Clemson HGIC 'Herbs'; Univ. of Maryland Extension 'Care of Herbs'; both read for the watering rule), grown as a bed of their own, which is how those guides describe siting them.
guilds.footprint_reason: One shrub-layer herb (sage, rosemary or lavender, spread 60-90 cm) with thyme and oregano at their 30 cm spacing along the sunny edge.

mechanisms.claim: one regime - sharp drainage, full sun and low summer water - which vegetable irrigation breaks

guilds.honesty_note: Nothing here feeds or guards another plant. These five are together because they want the same thing (gritty, fast-draining soil, full sun and water only when dry), and because the vegetables they usually get planted among want the opposite. The pizza garden keeps its herbs for the kitchen; this bed keeps them alive. Marjoram, savory and tarragon stay out until a source read for each of them puts it in this group.

guilds.description: Cucumbers ringed by a border of winter squash that draws cucumber beetles away from the crop, so you can catch them there.
guilds.provenance: Perimeter trap cropping as developed and trialed by UConn Cooperative Extension (Boucher and Durgy, 2003) and recommended by UMass Extension and Univ. of Minnesota Extension for cucumber beetles.
guilds.footprint_reason: Four hubbard plants at their 120 cm spacing make the smallest unbroken ring, around a cucumber center of about 2 m². The crop inside can grow; the ring cannot shrink.

mechanisms.claim: a ring of the cucurbit the beetles prefer draws them to the edge, where they are dealt with, and keeps most of them and the wilt they carry off the crop

guilds.honesty_note: The border does the catching; you do the rest. Beetles gathered on the hubbard have to be removed, by hand, under a cover, or with whatever control you choose. Otherwise the ring becomes a nursery that sends more beetles onto the crop. Plant the hubbard a week or two before the cucumbers so it is up when the first beetles arrive, and keep it unbroken around the crop. The trials behind this were field-scale; a garden ring is the same idea at a size the researchers only say may work.

guilds.description: Corn and climbing beans with sweet potato as the ground cover, for a gardener who wants the Three Sisters without squash.
guilds.provenance: A derived composition (docs/PROPOSAL-35-combinations.md #1, adopted 2026-08-09): the Three Sisters role structure with sweet potato in the cover slot, a milpa for a gardener who does not want squash. Not a documented traditional planting.
guilds.planting_source: corn/bean densities from Cornell's Three Sisters hill method (see three_sisters, read 2026-07-14); sweet-potato cover density ESTIMATED — no interplanted rate read

mechanisms.claim: corn provides a living trellis
sweet-potato foliage suppresses weeds and retains soil moisture
beans pass a small share of their nitrogen to the corn in-season; most of it arrives next year

guilds.description: Climbing beans on a trellis with sweet potato covering the ground, for a bed too small for corn.

roles.cost: No biomass, no romance. About $20. Reusable across seasons.
roles.alternative_cost: A heavy nitrogen feeder that competes with the beans. It needs a ~30-day head start or the vines pull it down, and it holds up about 2 vines per stalk.

mechanisms.claim: trellis provides vertical support
sweet-potato foliage suppresses weeds and retains soil moisture
beans improve the ground for next season

guilds.honesty_note: Label as an adaptation, not as a milpa. The beans climb a trellis instead of corn, so the corn block is gone, along with the pollination mechanism that needs it. Sweet potato remains the ground layer it always was.

guilds.description: Corn with cowpeas climbing it and melons covering the ground, a warm-weather take on the Three Sisters.
guilds.provenance: A derived composition (docs/PROPOSAL-35-combinations.md #2, adopted 2026-08-09): the Sisters role structure with cowpea as the fixer and melon as the cover. Not a documented traditional planting. It is deliberately NOT an alternative on three_sisters, whose 2026-07-26 ruling declined melons there on provenance grounds. A separate guild carries its own provenance.
guilds.planting_source: corn/bean densities from Cornell's Three Sisters hill method (see three_sisters, read 2026-07-14); melon cover density ESTIMATED — no interplanted rate read

mechanisms.claim: corn provides a living trellis
melon vines suppress weeds and retain soil moisture
cowpeas pass a small share of their nitrogen to the corn in-season; most of it arrives next year

guilds.description: Cowpeas on a trellis with melons covering the ground, for a bed too small for corn.

roles.cost: No biomass, no romance. About $20. Reusable across seasons.
roles.alternative_cost: A heavy nitrogen feeder that competes with the cowpeas. It needs a ~30-day head start or the vines pull it down, and it holds up about 2 vines per stalk.

mechanisms.claim: trellis provides vertical support
melon vines suppress weeds and retain soil moisture
cowpeas improve the ground for next season

guilds.honesty_note: Label as an adaptation, not as Melon Sisters. The cowpeas climb the trellis instead of corn, so the corn block is gone, along with the pollination mechanism that needs it. The melon stays the ground layer; on a bed this small, let its vines run over the edges so they don't crowd the roots.

guilds.description: Carrots grown with onions and edged with dill, laid out to make the bed harder for carrot rust fly to find.
guilds.provenance: A derived composition (docs/PROPOSAL-35-combinations.md #22, adopted 2026-08-09), built to give the carrot rust fly mechanism a role-based expression. Before this arc no guild contained carrot at all.

mechanisms.claim: alliums interplanted with carrots reduce carrot rust fly damage

guilds.note: The proposal scored this 2 with an insectary point; the point was dropped as claim-unfaithful. Nothing in this bed fruits, so pollinator visitation has nothing to improve — dill stays as a border herb with no mechanism claimed. One mechanism, honestly stated, is the guild.

guilds.description: Carrots and chives in rows with lettuce filling the soil between them, a small bed you can pick a salad from.
guilds.provenance: A derived composition (docs/PROPOSAL-35-combinations.md #23, adopted 2026-08-09): the carrot-allium pairing at salad scale, with a lettuce canopy on the soil between rows.

mechanisms.claim: alliums interplanted with carrots reduce carrot rust fly damage
a low lettuce canopy shades the soil between carrot rows

guilds.description: Two tomatillo plants, since one alone sets no fruit, with bee plant to draw pollinators and squash covering the ground.
guilds.provenance: A derived composition (docs/PROPOSAL-35-combinations.md #28, adopted 2026-08-09), built around a hard structural fact most plans get wrong. Tomatillo is self-incompatible and needs two plants to set fruit. The guild exists to make that requirement unmissable.
guilds.footprint_reason: the squash in this team is a vining kind, and once it gets going it sprawls well past the edges of a bed this size. A bush squash stays put, which is what the smaller version of this team plants instead.

mechanisms.claim: an insectary beside a fruiting crop improves predator presence
squash foliage suppresses weeds and retains soil moisture

guilds.description: The tomatillo pair fitted to a smaller bed, still two plants so they set fruit, with a bush squash on the ground.

mechanisms.claim: an insectary beside a fruiting crop improves predator presence
bush squash suppresses weeds

guilds.honesty_note: A footprint adaptation, and a mild one. The two tomatillos and the flowers beside them are exactly what they are in the full bed, so this is still the same team doing the same job. What changes is the ground layer. A bush squash sits where a vining one would have run, so you get the weed suppression close in around the plants. You lose the sprawling cover that shades a whole bed and holds moisture in it. If you have four square meters, plant the full version and let the vine run.

guilds.description: An apple tree with a ring of clover, comfrey, daffodils and yarrow planted around it, a planting that stays in place for years.
guilds.provenance: Permaculture design literature. Long informal track record.

mechanisms.claim: bulb ring suppresses turfgrass competition at the trunk
understory insectary improves predator presence
cutting the mulch plant and leaving it where it falls (chop-and-drop) returns its potassium-rich leaves to the surface as mulch
the nitrogen-fixing plant feeds the tree in the same season

guilds.honesty_note: The ring pattern fits any of these trees; the checks on where each tree fits do the sorting. Sweet cherry, persimmon and mulberry need a partner: sweet cherry a second compatible cultivar, persimmon and mulberry a male near a female. The footprint is the minimum for the smallest canopy; a mulberry or persimmon wants nearer 40 m² at maturity. Fig grows only in zone 7 and warmer, and is more a large shrub than a tree; elderberry suckers and is used here as a small canopy, not as a hedge.

guilds.description: The fruit tree ring around an apple on a dwarfing rootstock, sized for a small yard.
guilds.provenance: The fruit-tree guild on a dwarfing rootstock, the standard small-yard adaptation.

mechanisms.claim: a dwarfing rootstock holds the tree to ~2-2.5 m, fitting the whole plant team into a small yard
a dwarf rootstock is poorly anchored, so the tree needs permanent staking
bulb ring suppresses turfgrass competition at the trunk
understory insectary improves predator presence
cutting the mulch plant and leaving it where it falls (chop-and-drop) returns its potassium-rich leaves to the surface as mulch
the nitrogen-fixing plant feeds the tree in the same season

guilds.honesty_note: A footprint adaptation of the same team. The mechanisms are the fruit-tree team's, on a smaller tree. The dwarfing rootstock is what makes it fit, and it also makes the tree dependent on permanent support.

guilds.description: A currant or gooseberry bush with the fruit tree ring of clover, comfrey, daffodils and yarrow scaled down around it.
guilds.provenance: The fruit-tree guild's ring pattern, scaled to a berry shrub.
guilds.footprint_reason: A single currant or gooseberry (spread ~1-1.5 m) with a narrow companion ring.

mechanisms.claim: bulb ring suppresses turfgrass competition at the stem
understory insectary improves predator presence
cutting the mulch plant and leaving it where it falls (chop-and-drop) returns its potassium-rich leaves to the surface as mulch
the nitrogen-fixing plant feeds the shrub in the same season

guilds.honesty_note: Currants and gooseberries tolerate part shade and take the fruit-tree team's companion ring at berry scale. Ribes hosts white pine blister rust, and the planner flags this automatically; where the disease is regulated, black currant may be restricted, so check before planting. Honeyberry needs two different cultivars to set fruit and aronia sets alone; both take the ring at the same scale, aronia the tallest of these shrubs.

guilds.description: A blueberry bush in its own acid bed, ringed with daffodils, the one companion that can share that soil.
guilds.provenance: The ring pattern, reduced to what an acid bed can hold.
guilds.footprint_reason: A single highbush blueberry (spread ~1-1.5 m) with a bulb ring only.

mechanisms.claim: bulb ring suppresses turfgrass competition at the stem

guilds.honesty_note: Blueberry requires an acid bed (pH 4.5-5.5). The team's usual neutral-soil companions (clover, yarrow, comfrey) cannot share it, so this ring carries only an acid-tolerant bulb ring. Site an insectary and a fixer in a separate neutral bed. That constraint is why the ring bands partial where the currant bands backed. The partial band records the acid soil and says nothing against the plant.

guilds.description: A row of blackberry canes along an edge, with clover, comfrey and yarrow planted at their feet.
guilds.provenance: The ring pattern adapted to a cane fruit grown as an edge.
guilds.footprint_reason: A short run of blackberry cane (spacing ~90 cm) with a companion strip.

mechanisms.claim: understory insectary improves predator presence
cutting the mulch plant and leaving it where it falls (chop-and-drop) returns its potassium-rich leaves to the surface as mulch
the nitrogen-fixing plant feeds the canes in the same season

guilds.honesty_note: Brambles grow from canes with no single trunk, so there is no bulb ring here. The turfgrass mechanism is scoped to a trunk or a shrub/vine stem, and a cane is neither. Blackberry is a Verticillium host, so keep it out of any bed that has held tomatoes, potatoes, or other susceptible crops, and don't co-plant another host. The planner gates this. It bands partial on the insectary alone.

guilds.description: A grapevine on an arbor, with a ring of daffodils at the posts and little else in the shade beneath it.
guilds.provenance: The ring pattern around a trellised vine, with a structure at the center.
guilds.footprint_reason: A grapevine on an arbor (spacing ~2.4 m) with a bulb ring at the posts.

mechanisms.claim: bulb ring suppresses turfgrass competition at the stem

guilds.honesty_note: The grapevine needs a trellis or arbor, assigned here as its support, and casts shade once established, so the understory stays sparse, with a bulb ring at the posts and no full insectary. The arbor structure is the center of this team; the vine is trained onto it, so the structure stands where a tree would, which is how this team answers "a ring with no tree at the middle". A hardy kiwi arbor wants a male and a female vine, so plan on about 9 m² and a stouter structure than a grapevine needs; the vine is far heavier.

guilds.description: A pair of hardy kiwi vines, one male and one female, on a strong arbor with daffodils ringed at the posts.
guilds.provenance: The grape arbour's twin (O132 team 5, adopted 2026-09-02): the ring pattern around a trellised vine, with hardy kiwi's pair floor and structure from Penn State, Oregon State, Minnesota, Wisconsin and NC State, read 2026-09-02.
guilds.footprint_reason: A male and a female hardy kiwi on one arbor, planted about 3 m apart, with a bulb ring at the posts.

mechanisms.claim: bulb ring suppresses turfgrass competition at the stem

guilds.honesty_note: The vine is dioecious, so this arbor holds two vines, a male and a female of the same species, and a lone vine or two females sets no fruit; one male serves up to six females if you plant more. It is far heavier than a grapevine, up to 40 lb of fruit on a vine that can grow 30 ft in a year, so the structure is a stout arbor or T-bar on 4 to 6 inch posts. A grape trellis won't hold it. The understory stays a bulb ring at the posts because the canopy casts shade.

guilds.description: Tomato, pepper, tomatillo, onion and cilantro, grown together because they go into the same bowl of salsa.
guilds.honesty_note: None of these plants is known to help another. They go in the same bowl.

guilds.description: A bush tomato, a hot pepper and cilantro, the salsa garden sized for a big pot or a balcony.
guilds.honesty_note: The salsa garden for a large pot or balcony: a determinate (bush) tomato and one hot pepper with cilantro. The cost is the tomatillo. It needs two plants to set fruit (R-080), which a single pot cannot host, so it is dropped. Everything else still goes in the same bowl.

guilds.description: Tomato, basil, pepper, oregano, thyme and rosemary, the plants that go on a pizza, grown in one bed.
guilds.note: Two rules fire and a belief surfaces (R-072, R-076). The single best demo in the corpus: the most clichéd request in gardening, and the user leaves knowing three true things. A guild GATES on rules and SURFACES beliefs. Beliefs never gate.
guilds.honesty_note: Chosen for the kitchen, with one thing it gets wrong. Oregano, thyme and rosemary want dry, lean, sharply drained ground, and the tomato and basil beside them want the opposite. Keep the herbs at the driest edge, or give them the dry herb bed of their own next to this one.

guilds.description: A bush tomato, basil and a pepper, the pizza garden sized for a pot or a sunny windowsill.
guilds.honesty_note: The pizza garden for a pot or sunny windowsill: a bush tomato, basil, and one pepper, all annuals. The cost is the perennial herbs (oregano, thyme, rosemary). They want permanent, unrotated ground (R-072) and rosemary a mild zone (R-076), neither of which a replanted annual pot gives, so they are dropped. As in the full pizza garden, none of these plants is known to help another. They share the bowl.

guilds.description: Lettuce, tomato, cucumber, radish, green onion, arugula, endive, radicchio and mizuna, grown together for the salad bowl.
guilds.honesty_note: None of these plants is known to help another. They're harvested together for the salad bowl. What it teaches is timing. The quick radish and cool-season lettuce come and go (both can bolt, so the plan suggests sowing them in succession) while the warm-season tomato and cucumber are still ripening (R-034). This bed is really two or three successions.

guilds.description: Cucumbers and dill with garlic, onion and beets, everything for a crock of pickles from one bed.
guilds.honesty_note: None of these plants is known to help another. They're harvested together for the pickling crock: cucumbers and dill with garlic and onion, and beets for a second jar. They share a bed because they share a recipe.

guilds.description: Sweet basil and garlic, the two pesto ingredients you can grow yourself.
guilds.honesty_note: The two ingredients of pesto you can grow: sweet basil and garlic. The pine nuts and the cheese come from elsewhere. Neither plant is known to help the other; they're harvested together for the mortar.

guilds.description: Asparagus, rhubarb, sorrel and lovage, vegetables you plant once and harvest from for years.
guilds.honesty_note: Four vegetables you plant once and cut from for years: asparagus, rhubarb, sorrel and lovage. Nothing here feeds or guards another; they are together for one plain reason, that they are all perennial and want a bed of their own. Give them a permanent corner, out of the yearly dig-and- replant that would tear their roots up, and they will come back on their own every spring.

guilds.description: Bok choy, mizuna, green onion, pepper, broccoli, garlic and carrot, grown together for the wok.
guilds.honesty_note: Grouped for the wok: bok choy, mizuna, green onion, pepper, broccoli, garlic and carrot. The plants were picked for the recipe, and one pairing helps as well. The alliums in it (green onion and garlic) reduce carrot rust fly damage on the carrot. It is the one bundle here that is more than a shared recipe.

guilds.description: Malabar spinach, New Zealand spinach, amaranth and sweet potato, greens that keep coming through the summer heat that sends lettuce and spinach to seed.
guilds.provenance: A derived composition (D-310, 2026-10-15): the extension advice to grow heat-tolerant greens in the months lettuce and spinach will not produce (UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions, 'Heat-Tolerant Vegetables' and 'Tropical Spinaches'; UF/IFAS VH021; Utah State, 'How to Grow New Zealand Spinach in Your Garden'), gathered as one bed. Not a documented traditional planting.
guilds.honesty_note: None of these plants is known to help another. They share a season: the summer heat that sends lettuce and spinach to seed is when these grow best, so they keep a gardener in leafy greens until the weather cools. Keep them watered and fed. Dry soil or a hungry plant flowers early, and then the leaves turn bitter. Malabar spinach climbs and wants a sturdy trellis; New Zealand spinach and the sweet potato spread along the ground.
