guilds.description: Zinnias, cosmos, cleome, yarrow and daffodils, grown in one bed to be cut for the vase.
guilds.honesty_note: Grown to be cut for the vase: zinnias and cosmos for the summer, cleome for height, yarrow as the filler, daffodils for spring. There's no recorded interaction between them; they share a bed because they share a purpose. Sunflower, which would be the tallest cut flower in this bed, is deliberately left out, because its residue is recorded as suppressing the germination of small-seeded direct-sown neighbors, and zinnias and cosmos are exactly that.

guilds.description: A season of beans followed by garlic, a rest year that gives a bed a break from its usual crops.
guilds.applicability: ground carrying rotation load from solanaceae, cucurbitaceae, or brassicaceae

mechanisms.claim: residue mineralizes N for next season's crop
low rotation pressure; occupies ground through the off-season

guilds.note: Not a compromise. The bed sheds inoculum and banks nitrogen. Present it as the correct move.

guilds.description: A summer of cowpeas in a bed, ahead of the cool-season crops, so the bed rests from its usual crops through the hot months and banks nitrogen for the ones that follow.
guilds.provenance: A derived composition (D-310, 2026-10-15): UF/IFAS's advice that beans and peas 'make good summer cover crops, enriching the soil for your cool-weather plantings' (Gardening Solutions, 'Heat-Tolerant Vegetables'), with cowpea, the summer cover crop UF/IFAS's Florida Vegetable Gardening Guide names first ('Summer: cowpea, velvet bean, soybean, sunflower, and sunn hemp'). Not a documented traditional planting.
guilds.applicability: a warm place's summer, on ground carrying rotation load from solanaceae, cucurbitaceae, or brassicaceae

mechanisms.claim: residue mineralizes N for the cool-season crop that follows

guilds.note: The warm-season half of a rest year. The cowpeas take the bed through the heat and leave their nitrogen for the cool-season crops planted after them.

guilds.description: Winter rye and hairy vetch, sown together in early fall to cover bare ground over winter and cut down in spring.
guilds.provenance: The grain-and-legume winter cover the extension cover-crop guides all describe (NC State 'Winter Annual Cover Crops'; UMass 'Cover Crop, Hairy Vetch'; Penn State 'Making the Most of Mixtures'; Clemson HGIC 'Cover Crops'; Univ. of Maryland 'Cover Crops for Gardens'; all five fetched and read for this team), sown as a pair in early autumn and cut in spring.
guilds.applicability: any bed that stands empty from autumn to spring

mechanisms.claim: the hardy grain stands up in spring and carries the climbing vetch
the legume's residue mineralizes N for the next crop
the grain takes up the soil nitrogen the legume does not need, holding it against winter leaching
the grain's residue suppresses small-seeded weeds, and the next small-seeded sowing with them

guilds.honesty_note: Two plants doing two jobs on ground that would otherwise sit bare. Rye is the grain that stands the winter; oats die back to a mat at the first hard frost, which is the swap for an early sowing or anywhere spring rye gets away from you. Crimson clover is the shorter legume that does not climb. Either swap gives up the climbing line, which only vetch on rye earns. Cut the rye at least two weeks before you sow anything small-seeded; the plan flags this for you. Hairy vetch is listed as invasive in Oregon and is weedy anywhere it sets seed, so cut it before it does. Buckwheat is the summer cover, grown on its own, and is not part of this pair.

guilds.description: Rice paddies shared with fish and ducks, an old East Asian system recorded here but beyond what a garden planner can plan.
guilds.provenance: East Asian. Documented, ancient and mechanistic.
guilds.reason: Requires paddy hydrology and livestock. Real, and not a raised bed.

guilds.description: Raised growing beds built up out of shallow lake water, a Mesoamerican system recorded here but beyond what a garden planner can plan.
guilds.provenance: Mesoamerican raised-field wetland agriculture.

guilds.description: Lettuce planted where sweet corn shades it through the hottest part of the day, so it keeps going longer into summer.
guilds.provenance: A derived composition (O132 team 7, adopted 2026-09-02): the extension advice to plant long-season lettuce where sweet corn or staked tomatoes shade it in the hottest part of the day (University of Maryland, 'Growing Lettuce in a Home Garden'; NC State Extension Gardener Handbook ch. 16), laid out as one bed.

roles.alternative_cost: A giant sunflower casts the shade, but its residue suppresses the small-seeded greens sown beside it (R-021); an indeterminate tomato needs a stake to stand that tall (R-040) and is a heavy feeder. Neither needs the corn's pollination block.

mechanisms.claim: the tall crop's midsummer shadow shelters the greens from the heat that makes them bolt

guilds.description: A strip of crocus, yarrow and phacelia chosen so something is in flower for insects from early spring to late summer.
guilds.provenance: A derived composition (O132 team 4, adopted 2026-09-02): UNH's and Illinois's early-spring bulbs plus the corpus's own summer forage, chosen so something is in flower from early spring to late summer. Not a documented traditional planting.

mechanisms.claim: something in flower from early spring to late summer keeps pollinators and predatory insects fed and near the beds it borders

guilds.honesty_note: The strip feeds insects; it doesn't summon them, and the planner can't see a bee. It exists for the arithmetic of bloom windows. Crocus opens early spring, yarrow carries late spring through late summer, phacelia backs yarrow up through midsummer. Swap a role and the cover can break; the plan says which season goes dark. Crocus corms are rodent food, so a strip in vole country wants the daffodils nearby. Anise hyssop, echinacea and summer savory can all take the summer bridge in phacelia's place. Mint would flower there too, but it runs on its own roots and a strip has nothing to hold it, so it is left off the swap list. Keep a mint in a pot beside the strip instead.

rules.claim: Corn needs a block of at least three short rows side by side for good kernel set, and four rows is better.
rules.mechanism: Maize is wind-pollinated and protandrous (each plant sheds its pollen before its own silks are ready). Tassels shed pollen that must land on the silks of neighboring plants. In a single row much of the pollen blows out of the row, and each silk it misses is one missing kernel.
rules.remedy: Plant corn in a block of several short rows rather than one long row; four rows is best. For a small patch, shake the stalks gently while the tassels shed pollen, or dust a cut tassel over the silks, every few days. Or leave corn out and give the beans a trellis.

rules.claim: A plant's mature spread must fit its allocated area.
rules.mechanism: Geometry.
rules.remedy: Reduce plant count, or choose a bush cultivar group.

rules.claim: Plants over 120cm mature height belong on the polar side of a bed.
rules.mechanism: Solar geometry. Shadow falls outside the bed, clear of shorter neighbors.
rules.remedy: Move tall species to the polar edge; sort by descending height equatorward.

rules.claim: Sun-requiring species must not sit in the computed shadow of a taller neighbor.
rules.mechanism: Photosynthesis. Compute shadow polygons from latitude, date, and mature height.
rules.remedy: Move the taller neighbor to the polar edge, or move this plant out of its shadow.

rules.title: Don't put full-sun plants where you've marked shade
rules.claim: A full-sun species must not be placed in ground the gardener has marked as shaded.
rules.mechanism: Photosynthesis. A crop whose light minimum is full sun is below that minimum in shade and underperforms. Shade you mark yourself (from a wall, fence or building the planner can't see) is separate from the shade the planner works out from taller neighboring plants (R-004).
rules.remedy: Plant it somewhere you have not marked shaded, or use that ground for a species whose light minimum is part sun.

rules.claim: A bed whose shorter side runs well past ~1.2 m (4 ft) has interior ground that can't be reached from its edges.
rules.mechanism: A comfortable arm's reach is ~0.6 m, so ground more than twice that across can only be tended by standing on the bed. Standing on it compacts the soil and breaks the structure the bed exists to protect.
rules.remedy: Make a wide area into several beds with a path between them, so you never step into a bed. In the planner each bed stands alone and can't be split into parts, so add another bed instead.

rules.claim: A plant that must climb needs an assigned support strong enough to carry it.
rules.mechanism: Mechanical. Unsupported pole beans sprawl, rot, and yield poorly.
rules.remedy: Assign a strong support (a trellis or cattle panel), or choose a bush cultivar group.

rules.claim: Living supports have finite load capacity.
rules.mechanism: Mechanical load on a living stem.
rules.remedy: Put fewer vines on the living support, or use a built support. A cattle panel is effectively unbounded.

rules.claim: Vining cucurbits in beds under about 2 m (6 to 8 ft) escape the bed.
rules.mechanism: Vining squash and pumpkins run along the ground and take up a lot of space: the guides space large-vined ones in rows 6 to 8 feet (1.8 to 2.4 m) apart, so a narrower bed leaves them nowhere to go but out.
rules.remedy: Specify bush habit for beds under 4 sq m, or accept sprawl.

rules.title: Don't plant nightshades where nightshades grew in the last 3 years
rules.claim: Do not plant Solanaceae in ground that held Solanaceae within 3 years.
rules.mechanism: Alternaria solani (early blight) and Septoria lycopersici overwinter on tomato debris and solanaceous weeds; a 2-3 year break plus debris removal starves this inoculum. Fusarium has a very narrow host range, so rotating away from the host is effective. Verticillium is the exception. Its microsclerotia persist ~10 years and it infects 300+ host families, so a garden-scale rotation does not control it.
rules.remedy: Plant Solanaceae in different ground, or wait until 3 years have passed since this ground last held them. Clear and remove the old debris either way, because the inoculum overwinters on it.

rules.claim: Do not plant Cucurbitaceae in ground that held Cucurbitaceae within 2-3 years.
rules.mechanism: Melittia cucurbitae overwinters as a pupa in the soil where its host grew and emerges the next summer; Anasa tristis overwinters as an adult in sheltered sites (plant debris, under boards or rocks) and flies to cucurbits in spring. A host-free break cuts local carryover, but both are strong fliers that re-invade from a distance, so rotation is only partial and works best paired with fall sanitation (destroy spent vines).
rules.remedy: Plant cucurbits in different ground, or wait 3 years. Destroy the spent vines in autumn and clear debris and boards nearby. The pupae overwinter in the soil where the crop grew, the adults in the shelter around it. Rotation is only partial; both pests fly in from a distance.

rules.claim: Do not plant Brassicaceae in ground that held Brassicaceae within 4 years (extension recommends 4-7, and even that is not a cure).
rules.mechanism: Plasmodiophora brassicae forms thick-walled resting spores that survive in soil more than 10 years. They germinate in wet, acidic soil (pH < 7); liming above ~7.2 suppresses infection. Spores outlast any garden rotation, so a host-free break reduces but does not clear inoculum.
rules.remedy: Plant brassicas in different ground, or wait at least 4 years (extension recommends 4 to 7). Rotation alone is not a cure, because the resting spores outlast it. Raising soil pH above ~7.2 suppresses infection.

rules.claim: Alliums and Apiaceae are unrelated to Solanaceae/Cucurbitaceae/Brassicaceae and can break those families' rotation cycles. They are still not "low-pressure" and need their own rotation.
rules.mechanism: They host none of the big-three families' soilborne pathogens, so following those crops with an allium or apiaceous crop breaks the host cycle. They are not inherently low-pressure, though. Allium white rot (Sclerotium cepivorum) is allium-specific, its sclerotia persist 15+ years, and it cannot be eradicated once established; apiaceous crops carry their own soilborne diseases.

rules.title: For rotation, a plant team's crop families count across its whole bed
rules.claim: A plant team's crop families count toward rotation across its whole bed.
rules.mechanism: Soilborne inoculum and overwintering pest stages disperse across the bed. A plant team dominated by one family forecloses that ground for that family's rotation interval.
rules.remedy: Rotate the whole bed the plant team occupied, including rows that family never grew in.

rules.title: Don't follow a Verticillium host with raspberries, strawberries or stone fruit
rules.claim: Do not establish Verticillium-susceptible perennials (raspberries, strawberries, stone fruit) in ground that recently hosted Verticillium dahliae, either Solanaceae or a logged planting of a Verticillium host (strawberry, raspberry or other bramble, or stone fruit).
rules.mechanism: Verticillium dahliae persists in soil as microsclerotia and infects a wide host range spanning Solanaceae and Rosaceae. There is no in-ground cure once a susceptible perennial is planted, so it can wilt and die from inoculum an earlier host left behind. Because the reservoir family may differ from the victim's, the same-family rotation intervals (R-010/R-011/R-012) miss it.
rules.remedy: Site the perennial on ground with no recent Solanaceae, or choose one that is not Verticillium-susceptible. Extension advises growing a non-host (corn or a small grain) for at least two years first, without claiming that clears the soil. Once the perennial is planted there is no in-ground cure.

rules.title: Don't plant raspberries, strawberries or stone fruit where your log shows a wilt host
rules.claim: Do not establish Verticillium-susceptible perennials where the season log records that a Verticillium host (strawberry, raspberry or other bramble, or stone fruit) previously grew. The coarse prior-Solanaceae family signal (R-094) structurally misses this reservoir.
rules.mechanism: The same soil reservoir as the wilt rule for ground that grew the tomato family (Verticillium dahliae microsclerotia). This rule adds the gardener's own record: a logged strawberry, raspberry or other bramble, or stone fruit counts as an earlier host, while a Rosaceae that is not a host, like apple, does not.
rules.remedy: Site the perennial where the log shows no previous Verticillium host, or choose one that is not susceptible. Extension advises growing a non-host (corn or a small grain) for at least two years first, without claiming that clears the soil. Once the perennial is planted there is no in-ground cure.

rules.claim: Legume green manure raises available N for the subsequent crop.
rules.mechanism: A legume fixes atmospheric nitrogen into its tissue as it grows. When the crop is killed and its residue decomposes, soil microbes mineralize that organic nitrogen, converting a form plants can't use into one they can, and release it for the next crop. How much depends on how well the legume grew, and it is lower on sandy soils.

rules.claim: Do not apply fresh high-N fertilizer to root crops.
rules.mechanism: Excess N drives foliage at the expense of root bulking. (Forking is a separate problem, caused by rocks, compaction, or coarse/fresh organic matter in the root path. Nitrogen does not cause it.)

rules.claim: Fertilizer recommendations without a soil test are guesswork. Say so.
rules.mechanism: Whether a soil has enough nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (N-P-K) depends on the site, and there's no way to know it without a test.
rules.remedy: We will not invent an NPK number. A soil lab will test this soil, and the soil card shows how to find one where you garden. Until then, feed heavy feeders, do not feed root crops, and add compost.

rules.title: If soil pH is too low for a plant, we say so and which way to fix it
rules.claim: A measured soil pH below a plant's sourced floor (the lowest pH a published source gives for it) is worth saying out loud, with the shortfall and the direction of the fix. Above the ceiling too, but only for a plant that is documented to require acid soil. For every other plant the upper limit is Milpa's own figure, not a source's, so going over it raises no warning.
rules.mechanism: Nutrient bioavailability is pH-dependent, so below the crop's optimum band phosphorus and molybdenum become less available; below about 5.5 the effect turns acute as aluminum and manganese dissolve fast enough to damage roots directly. Above an acid-requiring plant's range the same curve runs the other way. Iron becomes unavailable and the plant goes chlorotic.
rules.remedy: Lime raises pH. Use the amount your soil lab gives: only its lime requirement test of your own soil measures how much your ground needs, so we do not give a rate. For a plant that needs acid soil and sits above its range, sulfur lowers pH; for how much, ask your lab for its sulfur recommendation, and we give no rate for that either.
rules.response: This bed's measured pH sits below what this plant wants. Near the floor that is a question of yield. Survival isn't at stake. The floor is the pH at which this plant's own source says to lime (for most vegetables, University of Maryland Extension's table). The plant doesn't die there, and the figure is an estimate. Below about 5.5 it becomes a harder problem, because aluminum and manganese dissolve and damage roots. The soil card shows how to reach a soil lab.

rules.claim: Ground the gardener has observed to stand water after rain is a site problem to fix before planting. Selecting plants around it does not solve it.
rules.mechanism: Saturated soil has no air in it, so roots suffocate; and standing water lets Phytophthora release swimming zoospores, which need free water to reach a root or crown at all.
rules.remedy: You told us this ground stands water after rain. Fix the site. Changing the planting list won't solve it. Plant on a mound or berm, or build the bed up. UC IPM puts the mound at 8 to 10 inches for annuals and up to two feet, with a gradual slope, for trees and perennials; WSU asks for at least 12 inches for raspberries. Fruit trees and brambles have the most to lose, and tomatoes, peppers and eggplant are named as susceptible too. Never bury the root crown or graft union when you mound. We are not naming a drainage rate or a tile spacing, because that is an engineering number and this is a garden app.

rules.title: To know how much lime or sulfur to add, you need your lab's recommendation from a test of your soil. We can say which way to go, but the amount has to come from the lab.
rules.claim: A lime or sulfur RATE is the lab's to give, from its test of your own soil; a lime rate comes from a lime requirement test, by a buffer pH or by your pH and your soil's texture. Which way to move the pH we can say; the amount we cannot, and it is never ours.
rules.mechanism: Buffering capacity, which is set by clay and organic matter, decides how much lime moves pH at all, so the same target takes very different amounts in sand and in clay.
rules.remedy: We will not tell you how much lime or sulfur to add, and neither should anything that has not measured your soil. If your report prints a lime or sulfur rate, it is a real one for your ground, whichever lime requirement method your lab used, so use that. If it does not, ask your lab for its lime or sulfur recommendation; for lime, that comes from a lime requirement test, usually part of a routine soil test. Which direction to go we can tell you. Lime raises pH and sulfur lowers it.

rules.title: Don't plant anything sensitive to walnut toxin (juglone) within a walnut tree's root zone. Nightshades are sensitive, and so are apple and cabbage.
rules.claim: Do not plant a juglone-sensitive species within the root zone of Juglans. The plants that count as sensitive come from the walnut hazard's own list, which is wider than the Solanaceae. It also carries apple and cabbage.
rules.mechanism: Juglans roots exude hydrojuglone, oxidized to juglone, a respiration inhibitor. The Solanaceae are highly sensitive; they wilt and die.
rules.remedy: Plant it outside the walnut's root zone, which takes in the whole drip line and beyond. There is no soil treatment for juglone.

rules.claim: Sunflower residue suppresses germination of some small-seeded species.
rules.mechanism: Sunflower tissue and roots release allelochemicals that persist in the soil and inhibit the germination and early growth of sensitive plants. Small-seeded, direct-sown neighbors are the ones at risk. A small seed has little reserve to push through the inhibition, whereas a transplant is already past the germination window and largely escapes.
rules.remedy: Keep small-seeded direct sowings out of last year's sunflower ground, or plant transplants there.

rules.title: Fennel may hold back neighboring vegetables with chemicals it releases. The evidence is thin, from lab tests mostly on weeds.
rules.claim: Fennel is allelopathic; a suppressive effect on neighboring vegetables is plausible but poorly characterized (evidence is weed-directed, in vitro).
rules.mechanism: Reported allelopathic exudates. Effect size poorly characterized.

rules.claim: Tomato fruit set fails when night temperatures persistently exceed ~21C (70F); high day temperatures above 29-32C (85-90F) compound it.
rules.mechanism: Sustained high day (>29-32C / 85-90F) and night (>21C / 70F) temperatures make pollen non-viable ("tacky") and impair its release; flowers go unfertilized within their ~50-hour window and abscise.
rules.remedy: Wait it out. Fruit set resumes on its own once nights cool, and the plants make up the gap. Do not reach for shade cloth. It cools the day, and this failure is driven by the night temperature, which Missouri IPM says shading will not touch. If hot nights are normal where you garden, buy a heat-set cultivar next season.

rules.claim: Pepper fruit set suffers when night temperatures stay above ~21C (70F); the same hot spell's high days compound it.
rules.mechanism: Warm nights above ~21C (70F) weaken pepper growth and, together with hot days, leave flowers poorly pollinated so they drop before setting fruit. Pepper carries a second heat driver this night threshold does not see. Daytime highs above ~34C (93F) also abort the flowers, so this rule catches only the night half of a two-sided problem.
rules.remedy: Wait it out. Pepper sets fruit again once the nights cool. Shade cloth cools the day, but this drop comes from hot nights, so shade cloth will not fix it; keep the plants watered and unstressed so they carry the flush that follows.

rules.title: Don't sow or set out tender crops before your last frost date
rules.claim: Tender species must not be scheduled before the site's last frost date.
rules.mechanism: Ice nucleation in leaf tissue.
rules.remedy: Sow or set out after the last frost date, or start indoors and transplant once it has passed.
rules.data_source: NOAA NCEI 1991-2020 Climate Normals. See docs/CLIMATE.md.
rules.data_source_note: NCEI publishes probability dates of last 32F occurrence at 10/20/30/40/50 percent, not 10/50/90. The original spec said 10/50/90 and was wrong.

rules.title: Don't plant a crop that can't mature before your frost-free season ends
rules.claim: A species must reach maturity within the site's frost-free window.
rules.mechanism: The season's accumulated growing degree days (a running total of its warmth) against the total the crop needs to mature, or the crop's days to maturity against the number of frost-free days.
rules.remedy: Start it indoors and transplant it, choose a variety with fewer days to maturity, or skip this crop at this site.

rules.claim: A vine assigned to a living support must be sown after the support is established, when corn is ~6 in (~15 cm) tall, roughly 2-3 weeks in. Sowing both at the same time is too early.
rules.mechanism: Load. A bean vine on an immature, poorly-anchored stalk pulls it over; extension guides key the delay to the support's height (corn ~6 in) as a proxy for it being rooted enough to bear the climbing load.
rules.remedy: Sow the vine 2-3 weeks after the support, once it is about 15 cm tall.

rules.claim: Succession sowing at intervals of about two weeks extends harvest for short-DTM crops.
rules.mechanism: Sowing the same crop in batches about two weeks apart staggers when each batch matures, so the harvest arrives as a continual succession, with no single glut. It pays off only for short-DTM crops, whose quick turnaround lets several sowings ripen within a single season.

rules.claim: Hardiness zone is the correct variable for perennials, and only for perennials.
rules.mechanism:
Zones encode average annual minimum winter temperature, which governs whether a woody perennial survives to spring. It is the wrong quantity for an annual, which never sees winter.
A zone that is too warm is a second, different mechanism. Mild winters do not kill a perennial; they fail to chill it. Deciduous fruit crops need a winter dormancy period to break bud and set fruit, so in a zone milder than a plant is adapted to it may survive and never crop. Only the cold end is enforced, because only winter survival follows from what a zone measures; the warm end gets advice and is never refused.
That warm limit is a property of the cultivar, and that limits what this rule can do. Chill requirement is published per variety and varies enormously within a species, so a species-level ceiling says "the modeled range does not reach your zone", never "no plant of this kind will crop for you". So above its range the planner still offers the plant, with advice to choose a cultivar rated for your zone.

rules.title: Some plants can't fruit from their own pollen, so they need a second plant of a different variety nearby.
rules.claim: Self-incompatible species require 2+ genetically distinct plants.
rules.mechanism: Many fruit trees carry self-incompatibility alleles at a single locus. When a pollen grain shares an allele with the pistil it lands on, the pistil rejects it and no seed sets. A plant's own pollen always shares its alleles, so it cannot fertilize itself. Neither can a second tree of the identical variety, which is genetically the same. Fertilization needs pollen from a genetically distinct plant.
rules.remedy: Plant at least two, and where the species needs a second cultivar make them different varieties. Two of the same will not pollinate each other.

rules.claim: Onion cultivar group must match site latitude.
rules.mechanism: Bulbing fires when daylength crosses a cultivar's critical threshold (short ~10-12h, intermediate ~12-14h, long ~14-16h). A short-day cultivar grown too far from the equator crosses its low threshold early and bulbs prematurely on small plants, so bulbs stay small. A long-day cultivar grown too close to it never reaches its high threshold and fails to bulb. Changeover is around the 35th-38th parallel, north or south.
rules.remedy: Choose long-day onions far from the equator and short-day near it; the planner picks the group from your plot's latitude.

rules.claim: An insect-pollinated crop depends on an insect to move pollen between its flowers; no arrangement of plants substitutes for one.
rules.mechanism: A monoecious cucurbit bears pollen and ovules in separate flowers, so fertilization requires a vector to carry pollen between them. Neither wind nor self-fertility applies. Ovules that are not fertilized do not develop, and the fruit aborts or forms misshapen.
rules.remedy: Nothing here can guarantee insects, and their absence cannot be diagnosed from a plant list. What you can change is whether anything in the garden is in flower while the crop is. Plants that feed insects near a fruiting crop are a reasonably supported suggestion. They are not a proven fix.
rules.trigger_note: THE TRIGGER IS WEAKER THAN THE CLAIM, ON PURPOSE. The claim is grade A. The condition that fires it - nothing in this garden is in flower while the crop is - guarantees nothing, because bees arrive from outside the garden. Hence severity `suboptimal` (deriving `advise`) rather than `costly` (deriving `warn`): it names a missed opportunity, never a defect. Every source read names WEATHER as the first cause of poor cucurbit set, and D-008 denies this app a weather feed, so weather can never be ruled out - which is the standing reason forage can never be ruled IN. No surface may present this rule as a diagnosis of a failed fruit.

rules.claim: How often to water is a weather question, and your soil answers it better than any schedule. This planner will not invent one.
rules.mechanism: How fast ground dries is set by rainfall, temperature, wind and humidity in your own bed, day by day. Monthly normals describe a usual month and a forecast a coming week, and neither sees your soil, so an interval computed from them is a guess wearing a schedule's clothes.
rules.remedy: Check the soil to decide when to water. Push a finger in to the second knuckle and water if it is dry at that depth. That's a method with no number, and it stands in for a frequency nobody can compute for your week. When you do water, put it on the soil and keep it off the leaves, and water long enough to reach the roots. Darkening the surface is not enough.

rules.title: Blossom-end rot comes from uneven watering, which stops calcium reaching the fruit. It is usually not caused by too little calcium in the soil.
rules.claim: Blossom-end rot is a calcium-transport failure driven by uneven soil moisture. A shortage of calcium in the soil is usually not the cause.
rules.mechanism: Calcium reaches the fruit in the water the roots draw up, carried by the xylem along with that stream. When the supply of water is interrupted the supply of calcium is interrupted with it, and the enlarging fruit runs short at its tip, even where soil calcium is adequate.
rules.remedy: Keep the soil evenly moist, without letting it dry out and then soaking it, and mulch to hold that moisture steady. We are not naming a calcium amendment or a rate, because the sources disagree on whether adding calcium helps at all, and any amendment number would need a soil test first.
rules.trigger_note: THE TRIGGER IS WEAKER THAN THE CLAIM, the same shape as R-102's and for the same reason. The claim is grade A. What fires it is only that a susceptible fruit is being grown - this app cannot see how anyone waters, has no weather feed (D-008), and never learns whether a fruit actually rotted. So it names a RISK carried by the crop, never a diagnosis of a fruit, and severity stays `suboptimal` (deriving `advise`) rather than `costly` (deriving `warn`). No surface may present it as an explanation of damage the gardener is looking at.

rules.claim: Water the soil, not the leaves. A film of water on a leaf is what most fungal spores need in order to germinate.
rules.mechanism: A spore landing on a leaf needs liquid water on that surface to germinate and enter it. Water delivered to the soil never puts a film there; water thrown over the plant does, and the longer it lasts the more of the spores already present can use it.
rules.remedy: Put the water at the base with a soaker hose, a drip line, or a wand held low, so the foliage stays dry. If overhead is all you have, water when the leaves will dry quickly, so they are not wet into the night.

rules.claim: A light sprinkle does not reach the roots. Water long enough to wet the soil to root depth, or the plant gets nothing.
rules.mechanism: Water moves down only as far as the volume applied can wet it. A brief watering darkens the surface and stops there, while the roots that take up water sit well below it, so the water never arrives where it is needed.
rules.remedy: Water until the soil is moist about a hand's depth down. A wet-looking surface is not enough. Push a finger in afterwards to find where the water actually got to. From above, you can't tell a plant watered from a plant dampened.

rules.claim: A container dries out faster than the same plant in the ground, and it is the one place where a day's inattention can cost you the plant.
rules.mechanism: A container holds a small fixed volume of soil, its whole root zone sits above ground, cut off from the soil below, and a porous pot loses water from its sides as well as its surface. The reservoir is smaller and it empties faster.
rules.remedy: Check a container at least once a day, and twice when it is hot, dry or windy. In high summer it may need water more than once a day. A plastic pot holds moisture longer than an unglazed clay one, and a bigger pot longer than a small one.

rules.claim: A tomato transplant goes into the ground deeper than it grew in its pot, buried up to its first leaves. It does not go in at the soil line it came out of.
rules.mechanism: A tomato's stem forms roots along whatever length of it is buried in moist soil. Setting the plant deep therefore converts stem into root, and the plant ends up with a larger root system than the one that came out of the pot.
rules.remedy: When you set it out, bury the stem up to the first leaves, or deeper still if the plant is leggy from being started indoors. This is the one seedling you plant lower than it was growing.

rules.claim: Rhubarb leaf blades are poisonous and must never be eaten. Only the leafstalks (the petioles) are edible. Harvest the stalks and cut the leaves off.
rules.mechanism: The leaf blades hold a toxic concentration of oxalic acid (and, per NDSU, anthraquinone glycosides), which the edible petioles carry only in trace amounts. Oxalic acid binds calcium and can damage kidney function; eating the blades causes cramping, nausea and, in quantity, can be fatal. The stalks are safe because the toxins concentrate in the leaf.
rules.remedy: Cut the leaf blades off and discard them; eat only the stalks. Never cook or eat the leaves.

rules.claim: Elderberries must be cooked before eating. Raw or unripe berries, and all leaves, stems and roots, are toxic; only fully ripe, cooked berries are safe.
rules.mechanism: The plant holds cyanogenic glycosides, highest in the unripe fruit, leaves, stems and roots and lower in ripe fruit. Eaten raw they release cyanide in the gut and cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea; cooking ripe berries drives off and inactivates the compound, which is why cooked elderberry (syrup, wine, jelly) is a traditional food while the raw plant is not.
rules.remedy: Eat only fully ripe berries, and only after cooking. Never eat raw berries, unripe green berries, or any leaves, stems or roots.

rules.title: Some plants come as separate male and female plants, and you need one of each for fruit.
rules.claim: Dioecious species need both a male and a female plant to set fruit.
rules.mechanism: A dioecious species carries male and female flowers on separate plants. Some plants make only pollen, others only fruit. A lone plant, or a planting that is all one sex, sets no fruit at all, because there is no pollen to reach the female flowers. Fruit needs at least one male plant near the fruiting females. This is a different mechanism from the single-locus self-incompatibility of apple and pear. There a plant has both sexes and rejects only its own pollen; here whole plants are one sex. So it is a separate rule and does not widen that one.
rules.remedy: Plant at least one male alongside the female fruiting plant(s). A single plant, or several of the same sex, will never fruit. A few named cultivars are self-fertile and need no separate male; if you grow one of those, one plant is enough.

rules.claim: A self-incompatible pome fruit's pollen partner has to bloom at the same time and make viable pollen. A triploid apple cannot be the pollen source, and a second tree of the same variety is not a second cultivar.
rules.mechanism: Cross-pollination only works while both cultivars' flowers are open together, so their bloom periods must overlap: early with mid, or mid with late. Early and late can miss each other entirely. A normal cultivar makes viable pollen; a triploid apple, with three sets of chromosomes instead of two, makes little or none and cannot fertilize a partner even though it needs one itself. Two plants of a single variety, including a colored sport of it, are genetically identical, so they reject each other's pollen exactly as a lone tree does.
rules.remedy: Pick the second cultivar so its bloom overlaps the first, and do not rely on a triploid apple (Gravenstein, Winesap, Mutsu or Crispin, Jonagold) for pollen. Grow one only beside two other cultivars that pollinate each other. An ornamental crabapple that blooms at the same time will pollinate any apple. Two strains of one variety do not count as two cultivars. The partner does not have to share the bed. Within 50 to 100 feet is close enough for the bees, so a neighbor's tree of a different variety counts. For apple, a crabapple in bloom at the same time does too.

rules.claim: A bed watered for its vegetables is too wet for its Mediterranean herbs. Tomato, pepper, cucumber and basil want the soil kept steadily moist, about an inch a week; rosemary, sage, thyme, oregano and lavender want it to dry between waterings. One bed gets one regime, and whichever way it is watered, half the planting suffers.
rules.mechanism: The vegetables' yield and fruit quality depend on steady soil moisture, so the bed is irrigated to keep it moist. In that same soil the herbs' root zone never dries, oxygen is starved and the roots and stem base rot, the failure the herb rule describes. Watered for the herbs instead, the vegetables run short at fruit set.
rules.remedy: Give the herbs their own bed or container beside the vegetables, with sharp drainage, as a dry herb bed. If they must share, put the herbs at the highest, driest edge and water at the base of the vegetables only.

rules.claim: A border of a more attractive cucurbit (blue hubbard, a Cucurbita maxima), planted a week or two before the crop and kept unbroken around it draws striped cucumber beetles to the edge, where they are dealt with, so most of the beetles, and the bacterial wilt they carry, never reach the cucumbers, melons or summer squash inside.
rules.mechanism: Striped cucumber beetles prefer Cucurbita maxima to C. pepo and C. moschata, and they arrive in one early flush from whatever direction they overwintered. A perimeter of the preferred host intercepts that flush on every side and concentrates the beetles on plants the gardener can treat or strip, so the unsprayed center sees far fewer beetles and far less of the wilt bacterium they transmit. The trap concentrates the beetles and does not kill them. The beetles in the border must be removed, or the ring feeds the crop instead of protecting it.
rules.remedy: Plant hubbard a week or two ahead of the crop in an unbroken ring around it, at no wider than the crop's own row spacing. Check the ring when the beetles arrive and deal with them there, by hand, under a cover, or with whatever control you choose. Keep checking the center. Do not use a border that bacterial wilt kills quickly.

rules.claim: Ground that just carried cereal rye or a sorghum cover crop is a poor seedbed for small seeds for a few weeks. As the residue breaks down it releases chemicals that stop small seeds germinating, and the smaller the seed the worse it fares; transplants and big seeds largely shrug it off.
rules.mechanism: Rye and sorghum roots and residue release allelochemicals (benzoxazinoids from rye, sorgoleone from sorghum) that persist in the surface soil for weeks after the cover is killed. A small seed sown into that layer has little reserve to push through the inhibition; a large seed or a transplant is already past the germination window.
rules.remedy: Wait about two weeks after killing rye and about four after sorghum before sowing small seeds, water an inch to leach the surface, or plant transplants. Big seeds and transplants can go in sooner.

rules.claim: Limed ground is the wrong ground for the next potato crop, because common scab worsens as soil pH rises and lime raises it.
rules.mechanism: Common scab (Streptomyces scabies) infects young tubers through the lenticels and is favored as soil goes less acid; at about pH 5.2 and below it is largely suppressed. Lime raises pH and its effect lasts years, so ground limed for a crop that wants sweet soil carries a scab-prone pH into the seasons that follow.
rules.remedy: This ground has been limed, and potatoes want it sour. Scab is skin-deep and the tubers still eat, but where it has been a problem, put the potatoes on ground you have not limed, choose a scab-resistant variety, keep the soil evenly moist for the four to nine weeks after planting while the tubers set, and never lime or add wood ash where potatoes are going next. A later pH reading at or below about 5.2 on this ground would quiet this. We will not give a sulfur rate to get there, because the amount is your lab's to give: ask it for its sulfur recommendation for your soil.

rules.claim: On ground that has carried brassicas within the rotation interval, a measured soil pH below about 7.2 leaves clubroot's door open; raising it is the lever every clubroot guide we read names, and the direction is all we give.
rules.mechanism: Plasmodiophora brassicae's resting spores germinate in wet soil below about pH 7.0, and alkaline soil with high calcium suppresses the infection; liming to 7.1 to 7.5 slowly reduces severity but is not reliable once an infestation is established.
rules.remedy: Raise this ground's pH toward 7.2 with lime well ahead of planting, using calcitic lime unless your magnesium is low (then dolomitic), and watch for boron shortage on coarse soils once the pH is up. Your lab gives the amount of lime, from a lime requirement test of your soil, and we don't. Rotation stays the first lever; this is the second.

rules.claim: Do not plant alliums in ground that held alliums within 4 years, and know that the worst allium disease outlasts any rotation.
rules.mechanism: Fusarium basal rot (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae) and pink root survive in soil as spores and on other plants' roots, and their inoculum builds where alliums repeat; a four-year break starves them. White rot (Sclerotium cepivorum) is allium-specific and its sclerotia stay viable 15 to 40 years, so rotation reduces but cannot clear it.
rules.remedy: Plant alliums in different ground, or wait until 4 years have passed since this ground last held them. If white rot has ever shown here, treat this ground as lost to alliums and grow them elsewhere.

rules.claim: Do not plant the carrot family in ground that held it within 3 years.
rules.mechanism: The carrot leaf blights (Alternaria dauci, Cercospora carotae and the bacterial blight) and celery's Septoria late blight survive on crop debris and die as it decomposes; a break of two to three years starves them. Alternaria radicina, the black-rot species, infects celery, celeriac, dill, fennel, parsley and parsnip as well, and can persist in soil for up to eight years, which is why the family rotates as one.
rules.remedy: Plant carrot-family crops in different ground, or wait until 3 years have passed since this ground last held them. Either way, remove the old tops or dig them in promptly so they break down, and buy clean seed, because all three carrot blights ride on seed.

rules.claim: Do not plant beets, chard, spinach or amaranth in ground that held them within 3 years.
rules.mechanism: Cercospora beticola, the leaf spot of beet, chard and spinach, survives on infested residue and in soil for up to three years and carries over on lambsquarters and pigweed; spinach downy mildew (Peronospora effusa) leaves oospores in the soil for a few years and rides on seed. A three-year break outlasts both.
rules.remedy: Plant them in different ground, or wait until 3 years have passed since this ground last held them. Bury or remove the old leaves, keep lambsquarters and pigweed out of the bed in between, and buy clean seed.

rules.claim: Do not plant legumes in ground that held legumes within 3 years; the root rots build where they repeat, and the worst of them outlast any garden rotation.
rules.mechanism: Bean and pea root rots (Fusarium solani, Rhizoctonia, Pythium, Aphanomyces) and white mold (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum) survive in soil as spores and sclerotia and build where legumes follow legumes; a three-year break holds the common ones down. Fusarium needs longer, and Aphanomyces oospores and white mold's sclerotia persist for many years, so rotation reduces but cannot clear them.
rules.remedy: Plant legumes in different ground, or wait until 3 years have passed since this ground last held them. Where root rot has shown, make it longer, and keep the ground draining freely, because every one of these rots is worse in wet soil.

rules.claim: Do not plant lettuce or its family in ground that held it within 3 years, and know that lettuce drop's fungi live on most other vegetables too.
rules.mechanism: Bottom rot (Rhizoctonia solani) and lettuce drop (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum and S. minor) survive in soil as mycelium and sclerotia for years and build where lettuce repeats; a three-year break holds bottom rot down. Drop's fungi infect alliums, brassicas, nightshades, cucurbits and legumes as well, so a lettuce rotation slows them without starving them, and only cereals are safe ground.
rules.remedy: Plant lettuce and its family in different ground, or wait until 3 years have passed since this ground last held them. Where drop has shown, the break that counts is one of grains or corn, since most vegetables carry it, and dead plants go in the bin. Keep them out of the compost, because the sclerotia survive it.

rules.claim: Apple, pear and quince share fire blight, and the tree you plant decides most of the fight. Choose a resistant cultivar, hold back on nitrogen, and prune strikes out well below the damage.
rules.mechanism: Erwinia amylovora infects some 75 Rosaceae species, pear worst, and moves between trees on rain splash, on bees and other insects drawn to its ooze, and on pruning tools; soft, fast growth from heavy pruning or excess nitrogen is what it infects most easily.
rules.remedy: Plant a resistant cultivar where you can: apples such as Liberty, Enterprise and Freedom; pears such as Moonglow, Magness and Kieffer. Avoid excess nitrogen. Cut strikes out at least 8 to 12 inches below the damage, in dormancy where possible, and clean the tool between cuts.

rules.claim: Every stone fruit shares brown rot, and it overwinters on the tree. Strip the mummies and prune the cankers before bud break, and keep fallen fruit picked up.
rules.mechanism: Monilinia fructicola overwinters in mummified fruit left on the tree or the ground and in twig cankers; at bloom its spores blow and splash to blossoms, and infected fruit sheds spores that spread to other fruit on the same tree and to neighboring trees, wild Prunus included.
rules.remedy: Before bud break, remove every shriveled fruit still on the tree and cut out cankered twigs. Pick up fallen fruit through the summer, thin so fruit do not touch, and prune for air. Remove wild or volunteer Prunus nearby.

rules.claim: Late blight comes back from last year's potatoes. It does not come back from the soil. Tubers left in the ground carry it through winter as volunteers, so ground that grew potatoes last season needs its volunteers pulled before this year's tomatoes or potatoes go in.
rules.mechanism: Phytophthora infestans needs living tissue to overwinter. Infected tubers left in the ground, in a compost heap that does not freeze, or in a cull pile survive and sprout as volunteers that carry the blight into the new season; tomatoes do not carry it, because frost kills the whole plant and the seed is clean.
rules.remedy: From April to June, walk last year's potato ground and any compost or cull pile, pull every volunteer potato and put it in the bin. Don't compost it. Then plant.

rules.claim: Two kinds of corn tasseling together spoil each other's kernels. Sweet corn pollinated by popcorn, field or ornamental corn goes starchy, and supersweet pollinated by any other corn loses its sugar. Keep different corn types 250 feet apart or 14 days apart in tasseling.
rules.mechanism: Corn is wind-pollinated and the pollen parent sets the kernel's endosperm (xenia), so a sweet-corn ear fertilized by a starchy type stores starch, and a supersweet ear fertilized by any other type reverts to the toughness of field corn. Standard, sugary-enhanced and synergistic sweet corns need no isolation from each other.
rules.remedy: Grow one kind of corn per garden, or separate kinds by at least 250 feet, or stagger sowings so their tasseling is at least 14 days apart; popcorn takes a month longer, so sow it first.

rules.title: Lettuce and spinach do better in a taller neighbor's summer shade
rules.claim: Heat bolters that tolerate part sun, such as lettuce and spinach, are better off in the computed summer shadow of a taller neighbor than in open sun.
rules.mechanism: Leaf temperature. Shade from a taller crop lowers the leaf and soil temperature of the greens beneath it, and high summer temperature is the trigger that sends these species to seed and turns them bitter.
rules.remedy: Put a tall, shade-casting crop such as sweet corn or a staked tomato on the sun side of your greens so its shadow reaches them by midsummer. A 30 to 50 percent shade cloth does the same job where no tall crop fits.

rules.claim: Brambles pick up viruses from other brambles. Aphids carry raspberry mosaic and related viruses from wild raspberries and blackberries, and from older infected plantings, into a new one. Site a new bramble planting at least 600 feet from wild brambles, and keep it away from any bramble planting that shows virus.
rules.mechanism: Aphid vectoring. The raspberry aphids that feed on wild and cultivated brambles pick up the viruses in one probe and carry them to the next plant they feed on, so any bramble within their flight is a source, and there is no cure once a cane is infected.
rules.remedy: Plant certified virus-free stock at least 600 feet from wild brambles, dig out wild brambles nearer than that where you can, and if an older raspberry or blackberry planting in your garden shows mosaic-mottled leaves or crumbly fruit, take it out before planting new canes.

rules.claim: A young apple or stone-fruit tree planted where an old one of its kind stood tends to sulk (stunted, uneven, sometimes dying back), because the ground an orchard tree leaves behind is not neutral for the next tree of the same kind.
rules.mechanism: Apple leaves behind a soil complex of fungi and oomycetes (Rhizoctonia, Ilyonectria, Phytophthora, Pythium) together with the lesion nematode Pratylenchus penetrans; the stone fruits leave the genus-wide version, Prunus replant disease, and in peach the ring nematode with the bacterial- canker organism drives its severe named form, Peach Tree Short Life. Either way a young tree of the same kind meets that loaded soil with a root system too small to outgrow it.
rules.remedy: On old orchard ground, don't drop a new tree of the same kind into the same spot. Have the soil tested for nematodes first; choose a replant-tolerant rootstock where one exists (a Geneva-series apple, a 'Guardian' peach); set the tree in the old grassed row-middles, away from the old tree row; or replace the soil in the planting hole. Waiting alone is not treated as a cure. Many other crops host the same organisms, so a rotation is at best partial and never a guarantee.

rules.claim: A basil dropped back into ground where a basil crop wilted and died young tends to do the same (growing normally to a hand's height, then stunting and suddenly collapsing), because Fusarium wilt leaves that ground infective for years.
rules.mechanism: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. basilici is a soilborne fungus specific to basil (a different fungus from the tomato or watermelon Fusarium); once a planting is infested its resting spores persist in the soil for eight to twelve years. It usually arrives on contaminated seed and is not already present everywhere, so it is a hazard only where infected seed has been sown. Where it is, plants of the mint family carry it without showing symptoms and can hold the ground infective from one year to the next.
rules.remedy: Start from seed tested clean for the fusarium fungus, or hot-water-treat your own (twenty minutes at 133-136 F); where the disease has appeared, grow a resistant variety where one is offered and keep basil, and any standing mint, off that ground for several years. A wait alone is only partial cover, since the spores last the better part of a decade and mints can carry them.

rules.claim: Currants and gooseberries (Ribes) are an alternate host of white pine blister rust, and some states regulate or ban planting them, especially black currant. Check your state's rules before planting, and where white pines are nearby choose a rust-resistant cultivar.
rules.mechanism: White pine blister rust (Cronartium ribicola) needs BOTH a Ribes and a five-needle (white) pine to complete its life cycle. The rust is a minor nuisance on Ribes but can be lethal to white pines, which is why some states restrict Ribes planting. Restrictions are strictest for black currant (Ribes nigrum), the most susceptible type. A rust-immune cultivar breaks the cycle. It cannot host the rust, so it cannot pass it to a pine.
rules.remedy: Check your state's Ribes regulations before planting. A 1900s federal ban was lifted in 1966, but some states still restrict planting, especially of black currant. Where white pines grow nearby, plant a rust-immune cultivar ('Consort', 'Crusader' or 'Titania' black currant, or a resistant gooseberry), which cannot carry the rust to the pine.

rules.title: Pests of one plant family spread more easily through a solid block of it
rules.claim: A specialist pest or pathogen finds and builds on a continuous single-family host patch more readily than one broken by non-host families.
rules.mechanism: Resource concentration. A specialist locates and holds its host more efficiently at higher host density and continuity, so an unbroken run of one family across adjacent beds is an easier target than the same family separated by a non-host (associational resistance).
rules.remedy: Where one family fills adjacent beds in a single season, breaking the run with a non-host family between them lengthens the distance the specialist must travel to the next host. The app discloses this and never docks a score. A continuous single-family block can be the right call anyway (a wind-pollinated crop like corn sets better massed), so the app names the trade-off and leaves the choice to the gardener.

rules.title: Any vegetables planted together help each other
rules.claim_refuted: Any vegetables planted together make a plant team.
rules.what_is_true: Some plant teams rest on a real way one plant acts on another. A kitchen bundle says only that you'll want these things in the same bowl. Both are good ways to plant. Only the first has plants working on each other.

rules.claim: Perennial members must not be sited in ground that is annually turned or rotated.
rules.mechanism: Tillage destroys the crown. Rotation moves the annuals; the perennial cannot move.
rules.remedy: Split perennial members into a permanent border; rotate the annuals around it.

rules.title: A tree or shrub plant team's ground is its drip-line ring, not a bed
rules.claim: A tree or shrub plant team's ground is its drip-line ring, not a bed.
rules.mechanism: A tree's root zone expands for a decade and extends well past the canopy edge.

rules.claim: A bulb ring suppresses turfgrass competition at a fruit tree trunk.
rules.mechanism: Resource competition and physical occupancy of the root collar zone.

rules.claim: Narcissus deters voles and rodents.
rules.mechanism: Narcissus bulbs and tissue contain lycorine and related alkaloids, which are toxic to eat. Rodents avoid them accordingly. Field mice rarely touch daffodils even where they readily eat tulips and crocus, so a ring of narcissus tends to be left alone. It works by avoidance. It discourages feeding on the bulbs but is no barrier and no guarantee against every rodent.

rules.claim: Garlic in a fruit tree's bulb ring deters trunk borers.
A bulb ring suppresses turfgrass competition at the base of a woody perennial shrub or vine.
rules.mechanism: Resource competition and physical occupancy of the root collar zone.

rules.trigger_note: Fires when a guild card renders and declares this mechanism at grade F. Attached, not homeless.
rules.claim_refuted: Beans fix nitrogen that feeds the corn growing beside them, that season.
rules.what_is_true: Rhizobia in legume root nodules do fix atmospheric N. Most of it is incorporated into the legume's own tissue. Some does move to a neighboring non-legume the same season via direct root contact and rhizodeposition, but the amount is small (a few percent of the neighbor's N uptake) and does not meet a heavy feeder's demand. The bulk of the benefit arrives the following season, after residues decompose.
rules.response: Beans will improve this ground for next year. They will not feed your corn this year.

rules.trigger_note: Fires on declared INTENT, not on species adjacency. Scattered marigolds among tomatoes are harmless; nothing in the plan is wrong. What is wrong is the belief that they are doing nematode control. Roles encode intent. That is why this is a rule and B-001 is not.
rules.claim_refuted: Marigolds interplanted among vegetables control root-knot nematodes.
rules.what_is_true: Tagetes patula suppresses Meloidogyne spp. via alpha-terthienyl and related thiophenes. Suppression requires a dense sole-crop stand held for a full season, i.e. a biofumigant cover crop. Scattered marigolds among vegetables do approximately nothing.
rules.response: Marigolds do suppress root-knot nematodes, but only as a solid stand grown for a full season as a cover crop. Dotting them between your tomatoes will not do it.

rules.claim: Comfrey is a dynamic accumulator that mines subsoil minerals and makes them available.
rules.what_is_true: Symphytum has deep roots and produces large potassium-rich biomass that decomposes fast. That is a good mulch plant. The specific mineral-mining claim has very little behind it.
rules.response: Comfrey makes excellent chop-and-drop mulch. The mineral-mining story is unsupported.

rules.claim_refuted: Autumn olive is a good nitrogen fixer for a fruit tree plant team.
rules.what_is_true: It fixes nitrogen. It is also bird-dispersed, forms dense thickets, and is listed as invasive or noxious across much of the eastern and midwestern US.
rules.remedy: Autumn olive will escape your yard. Use white clover, wild lupine, or a native fixer, and check your state noxious weed list before planting any woody nitrogen fixer.

rules.claim: Aromatic species interplanted with brassicas are reported to reduce cabbage-worm damage. The mechanism is unresolved and trial results are mixed.
rules.mechanism: Unresolved, and we don't pick one. Two explanations have been proposed. The herbs' volatile oils (their scent) may mask the cues pests use to find the host plant, or they may disrupt the pests' landing. The trials that report an effect measured damage, which can't separate fewer eggs laid from fewer larvae surviving or more predators arriving. So no mechanism here is established; there are only candidates.

rules.claim: Alliums interplanted with carrots reduce carrot rust fly damage.
rules.mechanism: The carrot rust fly finds its host by the smell of carrot foliage. Onion and other allium volatiles growing among the carrots mask that scent, so fewer flies locate the row to lay eggs. Because the protection is the smell, it lasts only while the alliums are in the ground. Once they are pulled, the masking goes with them.

rules.trigger_note: The claim says NEAR fruiting crops and the trigger now says so too (O71, approved 2026-08-12). `fruiting_crop_nearby` means a fruiting crop in the same bed, or in an adjacent one — adjacency being the engine's stated geometry judgment (beds whose edges sit within a walking path, ~0.6 m), because no read source quantifies an insectary's service radius and this corpus does not invent distances. The same-bed half is what the harmony scoring already enforces (claim-faithful since the bands shipped); the cross-bed half is credited by the plot layer, which is the only place bed adjacency exists. Dispatch fires this rule only where a guild DECLARES it as a mechanism, and every declaring guild carries a fruiting crop.
rules.claim: Insectary plants near fruiting crops increase pollinator and predator visitation.
rules.mechanism: The flowers supply nectar and pollen that adult predators and parasitoids feed on, so a patch of them near a fruiting crop keeps those beneficial insects fed and close by to work the crop. The effect is real but not guaranteed. An insectary patch does not always suppress pests.

rules.claim: Living mulch suppresses weeds and conserves soil moisture.
rules.mechanism: A living cover keeps a leaf canopy over the ground. It intercepts light at the soil surface, so weed seedlings are shaded out before they establish, and it slows surface evaporation, so the soil holds more water. In a Three Sisters planting this is the squash's role. Its broad leaves shade the bed.

rules.claim: Every derived climate value carries the tier, grade, station, and distance that produced it.
rules.mechanism: Frost percentiles exist only at weather stations: NOAA NCEI's published normals in the US, and odds worked out from a station's own daily record in NOAA's GHCN-Daily abroad. Values elsewhere are offsets or model output. A bare date conceals the difference between a measurement and an inference.
rules.response: Estimated from a station {distance_km} km away, adjusted for terrain. Expect error in complex terrain or cold-air drainage.

rules.title: Adjusting a nearby station's frost date assumes average night lows track frost dates
rules.claim: PRISM offset from a nearby station assumes the spatial pattern of mean minimum temperature predicts the spatial pattern of last-frost date.
rules.mechanism: PRISM models orography, temperature inversions, slope aspect, and coastal proximity at 800m. It provides monthly mean/min/max temperature. It does not provide frost exceedance probabilities; those exist only at stations. Combining them is an inference.

rules.claim_refuted: Frost dates can be downscaled by applying a standard lapse rate to elevation.
rules.what_is_true: On clear still nights, which are exactly the nights that produce radiative frost, cold dense air drains downhill and pools. The valley floor is colder than the slope above it. A standard lapse rate predicts the opposite and makes frost dates worse in the terrain where accuracy matters most. That is why the planner uses PRISM, whose model accounts for temperature inversions, and never a lapse rate.
rules.response: Do not implement elevation correction. Fall to ERA5 and grade down.

rules.title: Your own frost records from 3+ seasons outrank any climate model for your plot
rules.claim: Three or more seasons of logged frost outcomes on a plot supersede modeled climatology there, as an offset from the model.
rules.mechanism: Garden-scale microclimate (south wall, frost pocket, raised-bed drainage, urban heat island) lives below 800m resolution and below 80m. No gridded product resolves it. The season log is a direct measurement on the exact ground in question.
rules.limits: Three seasons is Milpa's own threshold: no source we read says how many seasons a garden needs to learn its offset.

rules.title: Where no station or model reaches, 3+ seasons of your own frosts give rough dates
rules.claim: Where no weather station or model answers for a plot, three or more seasons of its logged frost outcomes give it rough frost dates of its own.
rules.mechanism: Each logged frost is a direct observation of when frost reached that ground. With no station or model to correct, the middle of those observations is the plot's only frost estimate, and because frost dates swing from year to year, a middle taken from a few seasons is rough.
rules.limits: Three seasons give a rough middle date; frost-date records are usually built from 10 to 30 years.

rules.claim: Cold-hardy annuals can be sown or transplanted before the last spring frost (hardy crops about three weeks before, half-hardy about two weeks before). Tender crops wait for the frost itself (R-031).
rules.mechanism: Cold hardiness. Hardy crops tolerate hard frost and half-hardy crops tolerate light frost, so they can occupy the ground weeks before frost-tender crops are allowed in (R-031). The offset is measured from the last spring frost.
rules.limits: For spring sowing only. The three- and two-week leads sit inside Colorado State's planting table (hardy 2 to 4 weeks, half-hardy 0 to 2 weeks before the last frost). The two-week lead is that table's earliest edge, so in a cold spring wait a little longer.

rules.claim: Long-season warm crops are started indoors several weeks before the last frost and set out after it. Tomato and tomatillo go about six weeks ahead, pepper and eggplant about eight, basil six.
rules.mechanism: A frost-tender crop with a long days-to-maturity cannot mature if it is only direct-sown after the last frost, because the frost-free window is too short. A head start under cover buys the weeks the season lacks; the seedling is set out only once frost has passed, so the transplant date is still frost-gated (R-031).

rules.claim: A planted bed keeps every plant within arm's reach of a path, edge, or walkable row.
rules.mechanism: You can comfortably reach about 2 feet (0.6 m) into a bed. Soil farther than that from a path or edge can only be tended by stepping on it, which packs it down. So a bed worked from its edges and wider than about 4 feet (1.2 m) is laid out as planting strips no wider than 4 feet, with paths about 20 inches (0.5 m) between them. A field is worked from rows you walk, about 2.5 feet (0.75 m) apart. Raised beds, in-ground beds and containers are worked from their edges; a field is walked.

rules.title: Beans, peas and other legumes only fix nitrogen with the right soil bacteria. Ground that hasn't grown their kind recently may have too few, so they fix less.
rules.claim: A legume fixes atmospheric nitrogen only in symbiosis with rhizobia specific to its cross-inoculation group; ground with no recent history of that group may carry too few of them to nodulate well.
rules.mechanism: Nitrogen fixation happens in root nodules formed by Rhizobium or Bradyrhizobium bacteria specific to each legume group. On ground that has not grown that legume group before (a new bed, a soil-less mix, a long gap in the rotation, a fumigated or strongly acid soil), the matching strain can be absent or sparse, so nodulation and fixation are reduced until a population builds.
rules.remedy: On first-time legume ground, coat the seed at sowing with the inoculant matched to the crop's group (garden peas and beans, soybean, and clover each take a different one). Ground that has grown that legume recently usually needs none. It is a cheap one-time step, advised where the history is absent and never required.

rules.claim: A warm-season bean germinates from warm soil, whatever the calendar says. Sown into cold ground it rots or emerges weak, even after the frost has passed.
rules.mechanism: Warm-season legumes take up water fast at sowing (imbibition), and in cold soil that first rush of cold water injures the seed tissue before the seedling can establish (imbibitional chilling), so the seed rots or comes up damaged. Soil below about 15 C (60 F) at sowing depth is where this bites, and the frost-free date can arrive weeks before the soil is that warm.
rules.remedy: Wait for the soil to warm to about 15 C (60 F) at sowing depth, which a soil thermometer reads in a minute, or start the beans in warm cells and set them out. Peas are the opposite and are out of scope here. Half-hardy, they germinate in cold soil and are sown early on purpose.

rules.claim: Seedlings raised in cool, wet, or reused growing medium can collapse from damping-off, where soil-borne fungi rot the seed or girdle the young stem at the soil line before the plant establishes.
rules.mechanism: Damping-off is caused by soil-borne fungi (chiefly Rhizoctonia and Fusarium species and the water mold Pythium) that infect the germinating seed or the young stem at the soil surface, rotting it so the seedling fails to emerge or topples at the base. The pathogens thrive in cool, wet medium with poor drainage, and anything that slows the seedling's own growth (low light, overwatering, cool soil, high fertilizer salts) widens the window in which they attack.
rules.remedy: Start seed in fresh sterile or soilless mix (never reused mix or garden soil) in clean containers with drainage holes; keep the medium moist but never soggy; give the tray warmth (about 70 F) and air movement; and sow thinly, at the recommended density. Damping-off spreads once it appears in a tray and there is no cure for an infected seedling, so the whole defense is preventive.

rules.claim: A seedling raised indoors is set out gradually, not all at once. Moved straight from a windowsill or grow-light into full sun and wind it suffers sunscald, windburn, or transplant shock, because its soft indoor growth has not hardened to outdoor conditions.
rules.mechanism: Indoor-raised seedlings grow soft, with a thin cuticle and waxy layer, unlignified stems, and high tissue water, because the light, wind, and temperature swings that toughen a plant are absent indoors. Exposed abruptly to direct sun the thin leaves scald, in wind the soft stems break or desiccate, and the whole plant stalls from the shock. Hardening off (a week or two of increasing daily outdoor exposure) thickens the cuticle and waxy layers, develops lignin in the cell walls, builds carbohydrate reserves, and lowers freeze-prone cell water, so the plant can take the move.
rules.remedy: Begin about one to two weeks before setting out. Put the seedlings outside in a sheltered, part-shade spot during the mild middle of the day, a few hours at first, and lengthen the time and the sun each day, bringing them in at night; keep them off exposed spots on windy days and when nights fall below about 45 F, and ease off watering (without letting them wilt) to slow the soft growth. Then transplant.

rules.claim: A cole crop set out too early can bolt or "button". A long spell of cold on a young plant vernalizes it, and instead of a full head it runs to a premature flower stalk or forms a small, misshapen head.
rules.mechanism: Cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower and their kin are biennials, so cold is their signal that a winter has passed and it is time to flower. A young plant that accumulates enough cold (a stretch of weather in the 40s F) is vernalized and switches from building leaves and a head to running up a flower stalk and setting seed. Set out before the weather has settled, a small transplant crosses that cold threshold before it has grown the leafy bulk a head needs, so it buttons (a tiny premature head) or bolts (runs to seed) and never heads properly.
rules.remedy: Aim for cool-but-moderate weather (roughly the 50s and 60s F) through the plant's first weeks, and don't rush an early set-out; a stout transplant with several true leaves shrugs off a cold snap that would vernalize a tiny one, and a row cover holds the cold off if a spell threatens. This is the opposite failure from over-tender growth. Harden the plant (R-115), but do not set it out into a cold that will check it.

rules.claim: A direct-sown root crop left unthinned grows crowded roots that stay small. The seedlings stand far denser than they can mature and compete for the same soil, and the roots twist and intertwine and never size up.
rules.mechanism: Root crops are sown as seed in place and germinate much denser than they can mature. Where the seedlings stand too close, their swelling roots run out of room and compete for space, water, and nutrients, so they stay undersized and are deformed, twisting and intertwining against their neighbors. Thinning the stand while the seedlings are young leaves each remaining root the room to develop. (This is distinct from FORKING, which the sources attribute to rocky or compacted soil and root-knot nematodes. So this rule claims small-and-intertwined roots and makes no claim about forking.)
rules.remedy: Thin while the seedlings are young, about 2.5 cm (one inch) tall, to the crop's spacing. Pull or snip the extras so the row isn't left solid, to roughly one seedling every 2.5-5 cm for a full-size carrot, wider for parsnip and the larger varieties. The pulled thinnings of carrot are edible, tops and all.

rules.claim: A young transplant can be cut off at the soil line overnight by a cutworm, a caterpillar that curls around the tender stem and severs it just above the ground. A collar around the stem blocks it.
rules.mechanism: Cutworms are the soil-dwelling caterpillars of several night-flying moths. They feed after dark, curling the body around a seedling's stem and chewing through it at or just above the soil surface, which topples the whole plant. A young transplant is vulnerable because its stem is small and tender; as the plant grows the stem thickens past what a cutworm can encircle and cut, so the risk is an early-season one. A collar of cardboard, stiff paper, or foil, set around the stem and pushed into the soil, is a physical barrier the cutworm can neither climb over nor tunnel under to reach the stem.
rules.remedy: Around each new transplant, set a collar of cardboard, folded paper, or foil a few centimeters tall, with one edge pushed a few centimeters into the soil and the rest standing above it, so the cutworm cannot get over the top or under the bottom to reach the stem. Once the stem thickens the collar can come off.
rules.limits: The risk is to young transplants with soft stems; once a stem has thickened, cutworms leave it alone.

rules.claim: Potato tubers that catch light while growing (wherever soil settles or washes away and shallow tubers are left uncovered) turn green and become bitter and toxic, so the crop must be kept covered with soil.
rules.mechanism: Tuber tissue exposed to light produces chlorophyll and, in that same tissue, synthesises the toxic glycoalkaloids solanine and chaconine, so soil mounded over the developing tubers keeps light off them and prevents both the greening and the toxin from forming.
rules.remedy: Hill the crop. Once the stems are roughly 8-12 inches (20-30 cm) tall, draw loose soil up around the base of the plants to cover most of the stem and bury any shallow tubers, and repeat two or three times through the season so the tubers stay covered. Green tubers are bitter and should not be eaten; the green signals the toxin is present and is not reliably removed by peeling, so the defense is to keep light off the tubers in the first place, in the ground and again in dark storage.

rules.title: Cure onions and garlic before you store them
rules.claim: Onions and garlic lifted for storage are cured first, dried down in a warm, airy, shaded place for about two to four weeks until the neck is tight and dry and the outer scales are papery. Bulbs stored uncured, or poorly cured, rot in storage.
rules.mechanism: At harvest the bulb's neck and outer scales are still moist living tissue and the neck is an open channel into the bulb, so curing in warm moving air dries the neck shut and the outer scales to a papery protective skin, removing the wet tissue that storage rots colonise and sealing the neck they enter by; an uncured bulb goes into storage with a moist open neck and soft scales, and decays.
rules.remedy: After lifting, spread the bulbs in a single layer or hang them in bundles in a warm, shaded, well-ventilated place out of direct sun and rain, and leave them until the neck is dry and tight and the outer skin is papery. That takes roughly two to four weeks for onions (a warm 75-90 F speeds it) and two to three weeks for garlic. Only then trim, and keep the cured bulbs in mesh bags or shallow boxes in a cool, dry, well-ventilated spot. Handle gently throughout, as bruising also seeds storage rot.

rules.title: Row cover keeps pests off young crops; lift it at bloom for insect-pollinated ones
rules.claim: A lightweight fabric floating row cover laid over a bed at planting keeps flying and egg-laying pests off the crop through its vulnerable early stage (flea beetles, cabbage moths and loopers, cucumber beetles and squash bugs, and the root-maggot flies of cabbage, onion, and carrot). It must come off at flowering for any crop that needs an insect to set fruit, or it excludes the pollinator too.
rules.mechanism: Floating row cover is a gauze-like spun sheet laid loosely over the crop and sealed at its edges to the soil, and it stops damage by physical exclusion (the adult insect cannot reach the plant to feed or lay eggs), so the barrier must be continuous from planting, before the pests arrive, with its edges buried against a walking insect; because the same closed barrier also shuts out the bee, a crop whose fruit depends on insect pollination has to be uncovered once its flowers open.
rules.remedy: Cover the bed at planting with the crop still small, drape the fabric loosely with slack to grow into, and bury or weight every edge so the perimeter is sealed. Leave it on through the early weeks when the pest is active. For a crop that needs insect pollination to fruit (squash, cucumber, melon, pumpkin), remove the cover once female flowers begin to bloom so pollinators can reach them; leafy greens, roots, brassicas grown for heads, and self- or wind-pollinated crops can stay covered to harvest. Where the target pest overwinters in the soil under the bed (root maggots, flea beetles, Colorado potato beetle), cover a bed that did NOT grow the same crop, or the pest emerges trapped inside.

rules.claim: Garlic is planted in autumn, not spring. The cloves go in the ground several weeks before it freezes, root, and overwinter. The weeks of winter cold below about 40 F vernalize the clove, and that cold is what triggers it to form a bulb the following spring as the days lengthen. Planted in spring, garlic misses the cold and bulbs poorly.
rules.mechanism: A garlic clove will not form a bulb until it has been vernalized, held for roughly six to eight weeks below about 40 F. The bulb itself does not develop during that cold; it is only induced by it, and forms in spring as days lengthen and temperatures rise. Fall planting delivers the cold naturally over winter with the clove already rooted, so growth resumes early and a full bulb sizes up by early summer. It is the same biennial vernalization that prematurely bolts a spring-sown cool-season crop, but with the sign reversed. There the accumulated cold buttons the plant into an early flower and ruins it; here, in a crop sown in autumn to be harvested as a bulb, that same cold is the intended trigger.
rules.remedy: Plant cloves in the fall, roughly late September through November in most regions, several weeks before the ground freezes so they root before winter.
