Set them pointed end up, about 1 to 3 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart, using the largest cloves for the largest bulbs. Once the ground has chilled, mulch with a few inches of weed-free straw to blunt winter heaving and injury. Match the type to the winter. Hard-necked garlics prefer cold-winter regions, and soft-necked are better adapted to mild-winter areas.

rules.claim: Potatoes are grown from certified seed potatoes (disease-free seed tubers from a certified source). Don't plant saved tubers or grocery-store potatoes. Large seed tubers are cut into blocky pieces, each with at least one eye, and the cut surfaces left to dry to a tough protective skin before planting. Grocery-store potatoes may be treated to stay dormant and can carry disease that persists in the soil.
rules.mechanism: Potato is propagated vegetatively (the crop grows from a piece of tuber), so any virus or disease in the seed tuber is passed straight to the new plants and can remain in the soil for years; certified seed is inspected, disease-free stock, which is why saving one's own tubers or planting grocery potatoes risks introducing disease. Each planted piece must carry an eye, the bud the new shoot grows from. A freshly cut piece exposes moist flesh that storage and soil rots colonise; holding the cut pieces a few days until the surface dries and forms a corky protective layer (suberises) seals that wound before planting. Grocery tubers may additionally be treated with a sprout inhibitor, so they are slow to grow.
rules.remedy: Buy certified seed potatoes. Cut large ones into blocky pieces of about two ounces, each with at least one or two eyes; leave small tubers whole. Spread the cut pieces at room temperature (about 60-70 F) for a few days until the cut surface has dried and formed a tough skin, then plant. Do not plant grocery-store potatoes (possible sprout inhibitor, and disease that lingers in the soil) and do not replant your own saved tubers year to year (virus and disease build up).

rules.claim: Over-feeding a tomato with nitrogen grows a tall, dark-green, leafy plant that flowers late and sets little fruit. The plant pours its resources into vines and foliage instead of blossoms, so flowering is delayed or sparse and yield drops. It's an imbalance between vegetative growth (leaves and stems) and reproductive growth (flowers and fruit), and it comes from how you fertilize. It is a different problem from the heat that makes already-open flowers fail to hold, so keep the two apart.
rules.mechanism: High available nitrogen biases the plant toward vegetative growth. Abundant nitrogen keeps it building leaves and stems, and that leaf-and-stem growth takes priority over the switch into flowering, so flower initiation is delayed and fewer flowers form. The visible result is lush dark foliage with reduced and later fruit set, with the growth spent on leaves and stems.
rules.remedy: Go easy on nitrogen, especially before fruit set; do not feed a tomato a nitrogen-heavy fertilizer at planting and hold off feeding again until flowers and small fruit have appeared. Let a soil test say what the bed actually needs. The planner doesn't guess at NPK numbers.

rules.title: Keep mint contained. Planted loose in a bed, it takes over
rules.claim: Mint spreads aggressively by underground rhizomes and will colonize a bed, out-competing and crowding its neighbors if grown loose in open ground. Do not plant it directly in a shared bed. Contain it in a pot, or in a bottomless container sunk into the ground, and harvest and pull strays to keep it in bounds.
rules.mechanism: Rhizomatous, and stoloniferous, spread. Mint's horizontal underground stems (rhizomes) and its surface runners root at their nodes and send up new shoots, so an unconfined plant expands outward from the crown each season and reappears wherever a node reaches soil. This vegetative creep is why a loose planting takes over a bed, and why the control is a physical soil barrier. Spacing does not contain it.
rules.remedy: Grow mint in a container above ground, or plant it in a large bottomless pot or buried edging sunk into the bed (roughly 3-4 inches proud of the soil and 10-15 inches below), so escaping rhizomes are forced up over the lip where they show. Cut back and harvest through the season, and pull any runner that clears the barrier before it roots.

rules.claim: Basil is grown for its leaves. Pinch out the growing tips and remove flower buds as they form to keep the plant making tender leaves and growing bushy. Once basil flowers, it turns toward seed and the leaves fall off in quantity and quality. Harvest and pinch from the top regularly, and take the flower buds off as soon as they appear.
rules.mechanism: Apical dominance and the leaf-to-seed switch. Pinching the terminal shoot releases the lateral buds below the cut, so the plant branches and grows bushier with more leaf-bearing stems; and because flowering redirects the plant from building leaves to setting seed, removing the buds before they open keeps it in leaf and the foliage tender.
rules.remedy: Once the plant has several sets of true leaves, pinch or harvest from the top just above a leaf pair on a regular cadence. Don't strip the lower leaves. Watch for flower spikes and pinch or cut them off as soon as they emerge.

rules.title: Rosemary, sage, thyme and oregano like full sun, sharp drainage and lean soil
rules.claim: Rosemary, sage, thyme and oregano are Mediterranean plants that want full sun and sharp, well-drained soil and tolerate drought once established. They are intolerant of wet, heavy or poorly drained soil and are easily over-watered, which invites root and stem rot. They also do better in lean soil than rich, because over-feeding grows lush, low-flavor foliage and encourages disease. So water sparingly and keep feeding light.
rules.mechanism: These species are adapted to dry-climate Mediterranean conditions, with gritty, fast-draining soils and low summer water. In wet or heavy, poorly drained soil the root zone stays waterlogged, starving the roots of oxygen and rotting them; excess water and rich fertility compound the rot risk and, in these aromatic herbs, thin the essential oils that carry the flavor.
rules.remedy: Site in full sun with excellent drainage. Plant in well-drained ground, a raised or gritty bed, or open up heavy clay with coarse material before planting. Let the soil dry between waterings and water sparingly once the plant is established, and keep the soil lean. Don't feed it heavily.

rules.claim: Nasturtiums bloom best in lean, poor-to-average, well-drained soil in full sun. Rich soil or heavy nitrogen feeding pushes the plant into lush leaf growth at the expense of flowers, the familiar 'all leaves, few blooms'. Go easy on feeding, and do not fertilize except on very poor ground.
rules.mechanism: Rich soil and abundant nitrogen bias the plant toward vegetative leaf growth over flowering; lean, low-fertility soil shifts the same balance back toward bloom. It is the foliage-over-flower tradeoff that heavy feeding produces in many plants, here spending the plant on leaves at the cost of the flowers it was grown for.
rules.remedy: Plant in average-to-poor, well-drained soil in full sun. Do not fertilize, and avoid nitrogen-rich feeding; reserve any feeding for very poor ground. The planner doesn't guess at fertilizer numbers.

rules.claim: Borage is an annual that self-seeds freely and returns on its own from dropped seed, so a single planting typically reappears as volunteer seedlings year after year. Expect volunteers in and around where it grew. If you would rather it did not come up, remove the spent flower and seed heads before the seed drops and pull unwanted seedlings while young; otherwise leave a few heads and let it reseed.
rules.mechanism: An annual that sets abundant seed which drops and germinates in place, so one planting reappears and spreads by self-sown volunteers each season without being replanted. The control follows from the same mechanism. Seed that is removed before it drops cannot volunteer.
rules.remedy: To keep borage going, leave a few seed heads to ripen and drop. To limit where it comes up, cut or deadhead the flower heads before the seed sets and drops, and pull volunteer seedlings while they are young and shallow-rooted.

rules.claim: Culinary French tarragon has sterile flowers and sets no viable seed, so it is grown only from division, cuttings, or a bought started plant, never from a seed packet. Seed sold as "tarragon" is Russian tarragon, a taller, coarser plant whose flavor is far inferior. Sow that seed and you get the near-flavorless plant.
rules.mechanism: French tarragon's flowers are sterile and it seldom sets viable seed, so the only way to keep the true culinary plant is to propagate it vegetatively, by division or cuttings from an existing plant. The "tarragon" seed on the market is a different, seed-fertile type, Russian tarragon, which lacks the odor and flavor that make French tarragon worth growing.
rules.remedy: Buy a started French tarragon plant, or propagate by division or cuttings taken from a known French tarragon plant. Do not sow a seed packet labeled "tarragon" expecting the culinary French herb.

rules.claim: Lemon balm self-sows freely and, left to flower and set seed unchecked, spreads and can take over a bed. Cut back or deadhead the flowering stalks before they set seed to keep it in bounds, or grow it in a container. It is a strong self-seeder that can become weedy, though it is not a listed invasive.
rules.mechanism: The spread is chiefly by self-sown seed. A plant left to flower sets abundant seed that drops and germinates in place, so it recurs and expands from year to year. Removing the flowering stalks before seed sets breaks that cycle. Its spread is by seed. It does not travel by the running underground stems that carry its relative mint, though a soil-grown plant can also creep somewhat at its edges.
rules.remedy: Prune or deadhead the flowering stalks before they set seed, and pull self-sown seedlings while young. Grow it in a container to contain it; for a soil-grown plant, cutting around the plant's edges checks the modest edge-creep. A sterile-flowered cultivar sets no viable seed and does not self-sow.
rules.limits: It spreads mostly by seed, unlike mint's underground runners, so stopping the seed keeps it in bounds; one source notes a little creep at the clump's edge.

rules.claim: Blueberries need strongly acidic soil, about pH 4.5 to 5.5. Above about 5.5 the soil is not acidic enough and the plant cannot take up iron, so the new leaves yellow between the veins (iron chlorosis). Test the soil before planting; if it is too high, lower it with elemental sulfur applied several months ahead, then re-test. A foliar iron spray only greens the leaves for a while and does not fix the soil.
rules.mechanism: Blueberries are acid-loving plants adapted to low-pH soils. At soil pH above about 5.5, iron is not available to the roots even when it is present in the soil, and the plant develops interveinal chlorosis (yellowing between the veins) on new growth. Lowering the pH with elemental sulfur makes iron available again; spraying the leaves with iron greens them only temporarily and leaves the soil, and so the plant's long-term health, uncorrected.
rules.remedy: Test the soil pH before planting. If it is above about 5.5, lower it with elemental sulfur applied months before planting (ideally the season or the year before), and re-test before you plant. If the soil is near neutral (above about 6.0) and hard to acidify, choose a different site. Do not rely on foliar iron sprays as a cure; they mask the yellowing without correcting the soil.

rules.claim: Raspberry and blackberry canes are biennial. A cane grows its first year (a primocane), fruits its second year (a floricane), then dies. On summer-bearing types, after harvest cut out only the spent floricanes, at ground level, and keep the current year's primocanes, because they are next year's crop. Cutting every cane down on a summer-bearing plant removes next year's fruit. Ever-bearing (primocane-fruiting) types fruit on first-year canes and, grown for a single fall crop, can instead be cut wholesale close to the ground in winter.
rules.mechanism: Each cane lives two years while the crown persists. A vegetative primocane in year one becomes the fruiting floricane in year two, and a floricane dies after fruiting, and it will not fruit again or survive another winter. Next year's fruiting wood is therefore this year's primocanes, so removing them removes the crop. The spent floricanes are cut at ground level because dead stubs left standing can harbor canker-causing fungi.
rules.remedy: After harvest, or while the plants are dormant, cut the canes that fruited out at ground level and leave the current primocanes standing; thin crowded primocanes so the keepers grow stout. On an ever-bearing type grown for one fall crop, cut all canes very close to the ground in winter instead.

rules.claim: Do not harvest asparagus at all the first year after planting crowns. When harvest begins (the second or third spring, depending on the source you follow), keep it short. Pick for about two weeks in the first harvest year, no more than a month, then let every later spear grow out. From the fourth year on, harvest can run eight to ten weeks. After harvest ends, let the spears grow into ferns and leave them standing, because the ferns are what feed the crown for next year.
rules.mechanism: Every spear is drawn from energy stored in the crown, and the ferns are what refill that store. The fern's photosynthesis is banked underground to produce the following year's spears. A young planting is still expanding its root storage system, so cutting its spears removes the shoots that would have become ferns, and excessive removal of spears weakens the plants. Restraint in the establishment years is what builds a crown strong enough to bear a full harvest for decades.
rules.remedy: Year one after planting crowns: harvest nothing and let everything fern out. In the first year you do harvest, pick for about two weeks only, a month at most, then stop. From the fourth year on, harvest from first spears through May or June, about eight to ten weeks. Every year, once harvest ends, let the remaining spears develop into ferns and take care of them; they are next year's crop being banked.

rules.claim: On a new June-bearing strawberry planting, remove every blossom for the whole first season. Check weekly and pinch or cut them off; flowering stops by early July. Letting first-year flowers set fruit reduces plant growth, runner production, and the size of next year's crop. Everbearing and day-neutral types are handled differently. Remove blossoms only for the first stretch after planting (about four to six weeks, or until early July), then let them fruit. The first berries come in August and keep coming until frost.
rules.mechanism: A first-year plant that ripens fruit spends on berries the resources that would otherwise build the root system, leaf canopy and runners (daughter plants) that make up next year's bed; letting the flowers develop into berries reduces plant growth, runner production and the size of next year's crop, while removing them directs the plant's resources into a large root system and a healthy plant. June-bearers crop once a year, so the whole first season is given to establishment; everbearing and day-neutral types keep flowering, so only the establishment window is sacrificed and later flowers are allowed to fruit.
rules.remedy: June-bearing: pinch or cut off all blossoms weekly through the first growing season. Everbearing or day-neutral: remove blossoms for the first four to six weeks after planting, or until early July, then allow the plants to fruit.

rules.claim: Grapes fruit on new shoots that grow from last season's canes, and only a few well-placed canes are kept. Prune hard every dormant season, in late winter after the coldest weather but before the buds swell. Removing about 80 to 90 percent of the previous year's growth is normal and necessary. Under-pruning is the common mistake and leaves a tangled vine with fewer flower buds and small, poor-quality fruit.
rules.mechanism: Fruit forms only on shoots arising from last season's canes, so a vine left unpruned piles up old wood that no longer fruits while the crop crowds onto too many buds. Cutting back 80 to 90 percent of last year's growth concentrates the vine into a small number of well-placed, productive canes; prune too little and too many buds remain, so the vine over-produces small, poor fruit and becomes a tangled mass.
rules.remedy: Prune while the vine is fully dormant, after the coldest part of winter, before the buds begin to swell, around February to March. Remove roughly 80 to 90 percent of the previous year's wood, keeping a few strong, well-placed canes (and renewal spurs) according to your training system. Do not under-prune.

rules.claim: Tree fruits differ in whether a lone tree can set a crop. Apples and most European pears are self-unfruitful. One cultivar alone will not set a normal crop, so plant at least two different cultivars whose bloom periods overlap. For apple, a flowering crabapple in bloom at the same time also works. European plums are partially to entirely self-fruitful, and a second European plum cultivar makes fruit set reliable. Japanese and hybrid plums will not cross-pollinate them. Peaches and sour cherries are self-fruitful and may be planted alone. Partner trees must stand near each other. The published distances are within 50 to 100 feet, and 300 feet at most.
rules.mechanism: A self-unfruitful tree will not set a normal crop from its own pollen or the pollen of another tree of the same cultivar; it needs pollen from a genetically different, compatible cultivar, carried by bees while both trees are in bloom. That is why the partner must be a different cultivar, must bloom at the same time, and must stand within a bee's working range. It is also why a self-fruitful species like peach or sour cherry, whose own pollen sets fruit, bears alone.
rules.remedy: Check the pollination requirement before buying. For apple and pear, plant two different cultivars with overlapping bloom. Early- and late-blooming cultivars may miss each other, and for apple a flowering crabapple that blooms at the same time also serves. For European plum, pair with a second European plum cultivar. A Japanese or hybrid plum won't do. Site partner trees close together, within 50 to 100 feet where you can and within 300 feet at most. A peach or sour cherry needs no partner.

rules.claim: A seed comes up from the warmth of the soil, not from a date on the calendar. Each kind of seed has a soil-temperature range it germinates in; sown into ground colder than that range it comes up slowly and patchily or rots before it can emerge, and ground hotter than the range stalls it too.
rules.mechanism: Germination is driven by temperature-dependent enzymes that mobilise the seed's stored reserves, so in soil below the species' range those enzymes work too slowly for the seedling to emerge before soil fungi rot the water-swollen seed, and in soil above the range that same enzyme machinery is suppressed. That is why the soil's own temperature is the reliable signal, and the day of the year is not.
rules.remedy: Read the soil to know when to sow. A soil thermometer pushed to sowing depth for a minute gives the number. Sow each crop once the soil sits in its germination range (warm-season crops wait for warm ground even after the frost has passed, and cool-season crops go into cool soil on purpose), or start seed in a warm flat indoors and set the young plants out. Each plant's own range is on its page.

rules.claim: Some seed will not germinate straight from the packet. It carries a built-in dormancy that a pre-sow treatment has to break first. A hard-coated seed is scarified or soaked so water can get in; a seed with internal dormancy is cold-moist stratified (chilled damp for weeks) before it will come up. The treatment has to be started far enough ahead of the sowing date to finish in time.
rules.mechanism: A hard, water-impermeable seed coat holds the seed dormant by blocking imbibition, so nicking, abrading, or soaking the coat is what lets water reach the embryo; a seed with physiological dormancy stays shut until a period of cold, moist chilling lets its germination-inhibiting hormones dissipate. So each treatment takes its own span of time, and starting it late leaves the seed still dormant at sowing.
rules.remedy: Check the plant's page for the treatment it needs. Scarifying (nick, abrade, or a hot-water/acid treatment) and soaking are done right before sowing; cold-moist stratification takes weeks, so start it well ahead. About six weeks before the intended sowing date is a safe general lead, though the exact period is species-specific and is on each plant's page. Fall-sowing outdoors lets winter do the chilling for hardy natives.

rules.claim: A few kinds of seed need light to germinate, and burying them stops them coming up. Sow these on the surface, pressed into firm, moist soil and left uncovered or barely dusted over. Don't sow them at the depth a larger seed would take.
rules.mechanism: These seeds carry the light-sensing pigment phytochrome, which must catch light to switch on the hormone cascade that releases the seed to germinate, so a seed buried past a few millimeters sits in the dark with that switch never thrown and stays dormant.
rules.remedy: Press light-requiring seed onto firmed, moist soil or medium and leave it uncovered or only barely dusted, then keep the surface damp. A seed sitting on top dries out fast, and a fine mist keeps it in place better than a heavy watering. The plant's page says whether it needs light; a seed that needs darkness is the opposite and is covered as usual.

rules.claim: White powdery spots on squash, cucumber, melon or pumpkin leaves are powdery mildew, a fungus that spreads on the wind and strikes the older leaves first. It weakens the plant and the fruit ripens early.
rules.mechanism: The fungus (mainly Podosphaera xanthii) grows on the leaf surface; the spores formed in each spot are carried by the wind to other leaves, and under favorable conditions it spreads until it covers most of the foliage. A plant that loses most of its leaf area to it is weakened, and its fruit ripens prematurely. It takes hold most readily on densely planted vines, plants crowded by weeds, plants in shade and over-fertilized plants.
rules.remedy: Grow varieties with complete or partial resistance, and give the vines air. Space them properly at planting, stake where you can, and keep weeds down. Where powdery mildew has cost a crop before and the variety is susceptible, a fungicide may be needed. Start at the first spots.

rules.claim: Small, soft, pear-shaped insects clustered on a plant, with twisted and curled leaves, are aphids. They feed on the sap; heavy feeding yellows and stunts the plant.
rules.mechanism: Aphids feed on plant sap, injecting saliva into the host as they feed. Severe feeding twists and curls the leaves, yellows the foliage, stunts or kills shoots and slows growth. They secrete a sticky, sugary honeydew that can let sooty mold grow on the leaves, though the honeydew itself does not harm the plant.
rules.remedy: Knock them off with a strong spray of water from the hose, which also washes off honeydew. Protect the lady beetles, lacewings, hover fly larvae and parasitic wasps that eat them. Avoid broad pesticides, and plant flowers that bloom at different times through the season. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil can control aphids where needed.

rules.claim: Brown leaf spots with target-like rings, starting on the lower leaves of tomato or potato, are early blight, a fungus that overwinters in plant debris and soil and reaches the leaves by soil splash.
rules.mechanism: The early blight fungi overwinter in infected plant debris and in the soil. Lower leaves are infected when they touch contaminated soil or when rain splashes soil up onto them; the spores need free water or very high humidity to germinate. Spots enlarge with concentric rings, and fruit can form leathery black spots.
rules.remedy: Mulch the soil under the plants and stake them, to keep soil and leaves apart; water at the base and keep it off the leaves. Remove spotted leaves early, but no more than a third of the plant. Grow resistant varieties (often marked EB), rotate out of tomatoes and their relatives for at least two years, and remove or bury infected plants in the fall.

rules.title: Sudden wilt with sawdust at stem holes means a squash vine borer
rules.claim: A squash or pumpkin runner that suddenly wilts, with sawdust-like frass pushed out of holes in the stem near the wilt, has a squash vine borer inside. The larva feeds in the vine and cuts off its water.
rules.mechanism: The adult is a day-flying moth that lays its eggs singly at the base of the plant, on leaf stalks and on vines. The larvae tunnel into the stem to feed, and their feeding destroys the vine's vascular tissue, stopping water and nutrient movement, and that is the sudden wilt. As they feed they push frass out of holes in the side of the stem.
rules.remedy: At the first sign of frass, carefully slit the vine lengthwise near the damage and remove the larva. On vining types, bury a few nodes along each vine so it roots there and survives an attack at the base. Floating row cover keeps the moths from laying eggs, but only where squash did not grow the previous year.

rules.claim: Lower tomato leaves that yellow after dark spots appear have a fungal leaf disease (early blight or Septoria leaf spot); leaves that yellow without spots, especially in containers, can be short of nitrogen.
rules.mechanism: Early blight and Septoria leaf spot are fungal diseases that begin on the lower foliage in wet weather as deep brown or blackish spots, followed by yellowing or browning of the leaves. Early blight has target-like rings, and Septoria has whitish centers and dark borders. Separately, tomato leaves can yellow from a lack of nitrogen, which is common in containers because frequent watering and low soil fertility leave little of it.
rules.remedy: Where the yellowing began with spots, treat it as leaf disease. Remove the infected leaves, mulch to stop soil splashing onto the lower leaves, space or stake for air, and rotate and choose resistant varieties next year. Where the leaves yellow without spots, nitrogen may be short. Get a soil test before feeding, and do not over-apply.

rules.title: Ragged holes and velvety green caterpillars on cabbage, broccoli or kale are cabbageworm
rules.claim: Large, ragged holes chewed in cabbage, broccoli or kale leaves, with velvety green caterpillars on them, are imported cabbageworm, the larva of the white butterflies that lay on cole crops.
rules.mechanism: The adult is a white butterfly with black spots on its forewings that lays its eggs on cole crops. The caterpillars grow to about an inch, velvety green with faint yellow stripes, and the larger ones chew large, ragged holes in the leaves, leaving the big veins.
rules.remedy: Handpick the caterpillars into a pail of soapy water. To stop the eggs being laid, cover the crop with floating row cover from seeding or transplanting until harvest. Where caterpillars are many and still young, a Bt product is an option.

rules.claim: A winter cover crop is sown in autumn a set time before the first fall frost (about six to eight weeks for crimson clover, 30 to 45 days for hairy vetch, four to six weeks for cereal rye), so it roots and grows before winter.
rules.mechanism: The plants need time to germinate and grow before the first hard frost and short days force them into dormancy; sown too late, a cover crop neither covers the soil through winter nor survives to grow again in spring. Sown too early, crimson clover can go to seed in the fall and not regrow until the soil warms. Cereal rye tolerates the latest sowing of the three.
rules.remedy: Sow within the crop's window before your typical first fall freeze: crimson clover six to eight weeks before it, hairy vetch 30 to 45 days before, cereal rye four to six weeks before (rye can go in later and still overwinter, with less growth before winter).

rules.claim: Very tender crops go out about two weeks after the average last spring frost: tomato, pepper, eggplant, lima beans, melons, watermelon, pumpkin and winter squash. Tender crops go in at the frost itself (R-031).
rules.mechanism: Chilling. A very tender crop is hurt by cool weather as well as by frost: it needs daytime temperatures above 60 F, and a week of days below 55 F can stunt it. Setting it out about two weeks after the average last frost gives the days time to warm.
rules.limits: Two weeks after your last frost is the earliest the guides we read allow (one says two weeks or more, another about two and a half), so this date leans early. In a cool spring, setting out later still follows the guides.

rules.title: Lettuce and spinach that ripen in hot, long days run to seed.
rules.claim: A lettuce or spinach sowing that comes ready in a month whose normal daytime high reaches the crop's bolting temperature (about 24 C, 75 F), while days are longer than nights, is likely to bolt before it can be picked.
rules.mechanism: Long days and several days in a row above about 24 C (75 F) switch lettuce and spinach from making leaves to making a flower stalk, which turns the leaves bitter and ends the harvest.
rules.remedy: Sow so the crop is picked before the hot months begin, or wait and sow for fall: lettuce about three months before your average first fall frost, spinach about two. Spinach sown for fall grows under shortening days and does not bolt.
rules.limits: It reads each month's normal daytime high, so it cannot see a heat wave in a mild month, and the monthly average stands in for 'several days in a row'. 'Long days' means days longer than nights (UMN: 'During May, the days are much longer than the nights'). A hot month after the autumn equinox does not count: UMN's fall spinach 'will not bolt'.

rules.claim: A bed under a roof, a patio cover or indoors gets no rain, so all of its water comes from you, whatever the weather.
rules.mechanism: The roof or ceiling stops the rain before it reaches the soil, so a wet week outside adds nothing to the water in the bed.
rules.remedy: Water it by its own soil and never by the weather outside: a rainy week is no reason to skip it. Push a finger in to the second knuckle and water if it is dry there, and when you water, soak it down to the roots.
rules.limits: It knows only what you tell it about the bed, and it treats a bed as all open or all covered. A bed that sits partly under an overhang has a dry side it cannot see.

rules.title: Vegetables need about an inch of water a week, and what the rain doesn't bring, you do.
rules.claim: A growing vegetable garden needs about an inch of water a week (25 mm), rain and watering counted together. In a month whose normal rain falls short of that, an open bed's watering makes up the difference, and where the rain falls below a quarter of it, nearly every drop is yours.
rules.mechanism: Growing plants draw water out of the soil, and sun and air dry it from the top. What the rain does not put back, the soil loses until it is watered.
rules.remedy: Read the month's normal rain beside the inch a week to see how much of it is yours, and let the soil pick the day: water when it is dry at the second knuckle, and water long enough to reach the roots. An inch over a 4 by 8 foot bed is about 20 gallons, and over a square meter about 25 liters.
rules.limits: It reads each month's normal rainfall, so it cannot see this week's weather, and a month's rain can come in one storm and run off. NC State words the inch as 'excluding rainfall', though it also says to pause watering in rainy weeks; this follows UMN and Arizona, which count the rain toward it.

rules.title: In the hottest months, expect to water every day or every other day.
rules.claim: In a month whose normal days run above 90 F (32 C) and whose normal nights stay above 70 F (21 C), a vegetable garden may need water daily or every other day.
rules.mechanism: Heat speeds both the water plants draw from the soil and the water the soil loses to the air, so after each watering the soil is dry again sooner.
rules.remedy: In those months check the soil every day, and expect to water daily or every other day, early in the morning, at the soil and down to the roots. The soil still decides: if it is moist at the second knuckle, wait.
rules.limits: It reads each month's normal highs and lows, so it marks the months that are usually this hot and cannot see a heat wave in a milder month. UMN gives these numbers for 'extremely hot weather'; the monthly normal stands in for the weather itself.

rules.claim: In hot weather, water early in the morning, before the heat of the day.
rules.mechanism: Less water evaporates from the soil in the cool of the morning than in the heat of the day, so more of what you give soaks in and reaches the roots.
rules.remedy: Water as early in the morning as you can, and put the water on the soil, low and close to the plants.
rules.limits: It says when in the day, never how often or how much. NC State also names the late evening as a good time; this follows UMN and Arizona's morning.

rules.title: Mulch can cut a bed's watering by around half.
rules.claim: A layer of organic mulch over the soil cuts the water a bed loses from its surface, and with it the watering the bed needs, by around half in Colorado State's figure.
rules.mechanism: Mulch covers and shades the soil, so less of its water evaporates from the surface and the moisture below stays more even.
rules.remedy: Spread 2 to 3 inches of a coarse organic mulch, such as straw or bark, over the soil between the plants. Grass clippings go no deeper than 1 inch.
rules.limits: Around half is Colorado State's general figure; the saving in your bed depends on the mulch, the soil and the weather. Organic mulch also tends to keep the soil cooler in summer.

rules.title: Beans that bloom in the hottest weeks drop their flowers.
rules.claim: A bean sowing that comes ready in a month whose normal daytime high is 90 F (32 C) or more is likely to drop its flowers and set few pods.
rules.mechanism: Above about 90 F the pollen turns sticky and pollination fails, so the flowers fall without setting pods.
rules.remedy: Sow so the beans bloom before the hottest weeks, or wait and sow for fall once the hottest month has passed. Keep the soil from drying out while they bloom.
rules.limits: It reads the normal high of the month the crop comes ready, standing in for bloom a few weeks earlier, so it cannot see a heat wave in a mild month. Dry soil makes the drop worse; it does not read soil moisture.

rules.title: Frost can form on a night the forecast low is a few degrees above freezing.
rules.claim: On a night whose forecast low is 36 F (2 C) or colder, tender and very tender crops can be frosted, because the forecast is the air's temperature a couple of meters up and, on a clear, still night, the plants run colder. Half-hardy and hardy crops take a light freeze, and can be hurt at 28 F (-2 C) or colder.
rules.mechanism: On a clear, still night leaves lose heat to the open sky, so a leaf can fall to freezing and ice can form in it while the thermometer, a couple of meters up, still reads a few degrees above.
rules.remedy: The evening before, cover the crops at risk with a sheet or frost cloth, never plastic, reaching the ground and loose at the bottom so the soil's warmth can rise under it, and take it off in the morning. A cover helps least in a long, hard freeze.
rules.limits: It reads the forecast low for a spot about 10 km across, so a garden in low ground, where cold air pools on still nights, can frost on a night the forecast says it won't: look to your low ground first. A forecast can be off by a few degrees, and it cannot say whether the night will be clear and still, so from 33 to 36 F it says frost is possible, not certain. Guides sort crops into tiers differently: the tiers are Colorado State's, and South Dakota State puts some of that hardy tier (lettuce, spinach, peas) among the crops that take only a light freeze, so hardy crops share half-hardy's 28 F line, though the cabbage family usually takes a few degrees more.

rules.title: A cover buys cool-season crops a week or two at the ends of the season.
rules.claim: A row cover, low tunnel or cold frame lets cool-season crops go in earlier in spring and keep growing later in autumn: about a week earlier under a row cover, and about two weeks at each end under a low tunnel or a cold frame.
rules.mechanism: Soil warmed by the sun by day is the heat source at night; a covering low to the ground traps that heat around the plants on calm, clear nights, keeping them a few degrees above the open air through the light frosts at each end of the season.
rules.remedy: Sow or set out cool-season crops under the cover that many weeks ahead of the open-ground date, and keep autumn crops covered past the usual last call. Vent on sunny days, keep plastic off the leaves, and close the cover before sunset.

rules.title: When lettuce and spinach bolt, summer greens keep growing
rules.claim: In the months a place's lettuce and spinach run to seed in the heat, Malabar spinach, New Zealand spinach, amaranth and sweet potato leaves keep producing leaf, given steady water and feeding.
rules.mechanism: Heat is what sends lettuce and spinach to seed. These four are warm-season leaf crops that grow best in the heat that ends a lettuce crop, so the same months are their season. Dry soil or a hungry plant sends them to flower too, and then the leaves turn bitter and growth stops.
rules.remedy: In the months your lettuce bolts, grow one of these for your greens instead. Keep the soil moist and feed them.

rules.title: Corn shades the squash fruit from sunscald at the end of summer
rules.claim: Late in the season, when squash plants lose leaves and their fruit lies uncovered, corn grown with them shades the fruit from strong summer sun.
rules.mechanism: Sun scald. As a squash plant ages its leaves die back and leave the fruit uncovered, and strong summer sun burns the exposed rind. Corn standing in the same bed casts shade over that fruit.
rules.remedy: Grow your squash beside corn, so the corn's shade reaches the fruit late in the summer.

rules.title: Where frost is rare, sow so the crop grows through months that suit it.
rules.claim: Where frost does not end the season, a crop does best sown so that the months it grows through average between its lowest and highest temperature, long enough for it to reach harvest. Where every month is warmer than a cool-season crop's highest, its coolest months are its best chance, with care.
rules.mechanism: A crop grows and makes its harvest within a band of warmth: in months colder than its band it grows too slowly to finish, and in months hotter than it a cool-season crop bolts and turns bitter while a warm-season crop drops its flowers.
rules.remedy: Sow in the months the app names. Outside them, grow a crop whose months they are, or a variety bred for the heat or the cool.
rules.limits: It reads each month's normal mean, the average of its normal daily high and low, so a cold snap or a heat wave is not seen. Its crop limits come from one table that does not say what its numbers measure; they are read as monthly averages, so every date it gives is an estimate. It does not read the wet season.

rules.title: Tomatoes, peppers and eggplant set little fruit while the nights stay cool.
rules.claim: Tomato and eggplant set little fruit while nights stay below about 13 C (55 F), and pepper below about 15.5 C (60 F).
rules.mechanism: Low temperatures cut the pollen's viability and slow the growth of the pollen tube, so the flowers drop without setting fruit.
rules.remedy: Time the planting so it flowers in months whose nights are warmer than that, and grow a cool-season crop through the coldest months.
rules.limits: It reads each month's normal low, which stands in for the nights, so a cold snap in a mild month is not seen. Ontario's table states that its numbers are daily highs and lows in the field, the measure the normal lows are made of.

rules.title: A banana grows slowly through cool months.
rules.claim: A banana grows slowly through months that average below about 16 C (60 F) and stops below 10 C (50 F), and a bunch that starts in a cool month may fail to come out of the stem.
rules.mechanism: Cool weather slows the plant's leaf and shoot growth, and chilling at flowering stops the bunch from emerging from the stem.
rules.remedy: Choose a variety known to handle cool weather, and plant it in the warmest, sunniest sheltered spot you have.
rules.limits: It reads each month's normal mean against air temperatures the source does not call monthly averages; they are read as monthly averages, so the months it names are an estimate. No place in Milpa's data has a month below 10 C.

rules.title: Where frost is rare, plant a young fruit tree as the rains begin.
rules.claim: Where frost is rare and the year has a dry season, a young fruit tree or banana sucker is best planted as the rains begin; where it has none, plant it whenever you can water it.
rules.mechanism: A new tree's roots have not yet reached deeper moisture, so it settles in on steady rain or watering, and planting into the rains gives it that water.
rules.remedy: Plant at the start of the wet season. Planted earlier, water it every two to three days until the rains come.
rules.limits: It reads the place's dry months, so the month it names is a normal year's, not this year's first rain. Where a place has no dry month, the sources give no month, and none is named.

rules.title: Hardy crops can go in later, counted back from the freeze they can't stand
rules.claim: Hardy and half-hardy crops stand a light freeze, so a planting of one has until the date it could still mature before the first night of about 28 °F (-2 °C). Where a night that cold comes in fewer than a quarter of winters, frost closes no window for them.
rules.mechanism: A hardy or half-hardy crop's tissue survives the ice of a light freeze down to about 28 °F (-2 °C), so its season ends at the first night that cold, which comes after the first 32 °F frost, and later still where winters are mild.
rules.remedy: Sow or set out hardy crops up to the date the app gives. After it, choose a faster variety or wait for the spring sowing.
rules.limits: It reads the median date of the first 28 °F night at a US station (NCEI 1991-2020) and the share of winters that reach it; abroad the model's cell gives only that share, so a hardy crop there keeps the first 32 °F frost unless the night comes in under a quarter of winters, so one year's cold snap is not seen. Days to maturity are counted at their usual pace; in short, cool days crops grow more slowly, and the extension calendars close later than this count for slow crops and earlier for quick ones. The 28 °F line is where every source's tiers meet; several cole crops stand colder (kale, Brussels sprouts and cabbage to about 24 °F), so for them it is cautious. The calendars disagree: for Houston's cabbage, Texas A&M AgriLife's last optimum date is Sep 20 or Oct 20 and LSU's south Louisiana column runs to Nov 30.

rules.title: We check a soil pH against a plant's range only when it was measured in water, the way the ranges are written. A reading in calcium chloride is kept and shown, and never converted.
rules.claim: Milpa reads every soil pH range and threshold it checks plants against as water pH. A pH a lab measured in calcium chloride, or in another salt solution, is recorded and shown with its method. It is never compared with those numbers, and never converted to water pH by a fixed amount.
rules.mechanism: A pH read in a calcium chloride solution is commonly 0.5 to 1.0 unit lower than the same soil read in water, by an amount that changes with the soil's type and salt content, so a range written in water pH cannot be compared with it or reached by adding a fixed number.
rules.remedy: Ask your lab for the pH in water. Many labs measure both, and some print a water figure they worked out themselves; that one counts, because it is the lab's. Enter the water pH and the plants are checked against it.
rules.response: This reading wasn't taken in water, or the report doesn't say how it was, and the ranges here are in water pH. Readings in calcium chloride usually run half a unit to a unit lower than in water, and the gap moves with your soil's salt, so we keep the reading without checking plants against it.

rules.title: Where frost sets the season, a crop still needs enough warm months to reach harvest.
rules.claim: Where frost sets the season, a crop reaches harvest outdoors only where enough months in a row average at least its lowest monthly temperature to cover its days to maturity. Where fewer do, or none, it is a crop to grow with care: under cover, from an early start indoors, or as its quickest variety.
rules.mechanism: A crop grows at the pace its days to maturity assume only in months at least as warm as the low end of its band, and in cooler months it grows too slowly to finish, so a frost-free season of cool months can end before the crop is ready.
rules.remedy: Grow it under cover, in a greenhouse, tunnel or cloche; start it early indoors and choose its quickest variety; or grow a crop whose months these are.
rules.limits: It reads each month's normal mean, the average of its normal daily high and low, so a warm summer, a sheltered wall or a cold snap is not seen. Its crop limits come from one table that does not say what its numbers measure; they are read as monthly averages, so its verdict is an estimate. Away from a weather station the model's monthly highs run cooler than the towns' own, so it can read a place's summer cooler than it is. Days to maturity are counted at their usual pace, and cool months slow a crop down.

beliefs.belief: Basil improves the flavor of adjacent tomatoes.
beliefs.what_is_true: No proposed mechanism. One garden trial is known: a 2004 West Virginia University study whose blind taste tests over three years found no consistent preference for tomatoes grown with companions. Extremely widely believed.
beliefs.response: The one trial we know of found no difference in flavor, and nobody has proposed how it would work. Plant basil next to tomatoes anyway. You'll want them at the same time in the kitchen.

beliefs.belief: Companion planting charts encode real relationships.
beliefs.what_is_true: Companion-planting charts are not a record of tested relationships. The idea is old. Plants were once matched by the four elements and the signs of the zodiac, and later by pseudoscientific methods such as sensitive crystallization of plant extracts, and there is no scientific basis for any of the lists. A minority of pairings do have real, named mechanisms: mixed plantings confuse pests hunting for their host plant by sight and smell, a squash canopy works as a living mulch, and diverse plantings keep beneficial predators and parasitoids around. Those are recorded here as a good hunch. Most chart entries have nothing behind them.
beliefs.response: Most companion-planting advice you'll find online is folklore, and the charts have no scientific basis. A few pairings do have real mechanisms. Here's what we can actually defend, and why.

beliefs.belief: Planting by lunar phase improves germination and yield.
beliefs.response: No mechanism anyone can name, and the few small trials we found disagree with each other. Plant when the soil is warm and the frost risk has passed.

beliefs.belief: Epsom salts prevent blossom-end rot.
beliefs.what_is_true: Blossom end rot is a localized calcium shortage in the fruit, driven by uneven water uptake. Calcium rides the transpiration stream, so erratic watering starves the fruit tip even when soil calcium is adequate. It is not a magnesium deficiency. Epsom salts add magnesium, not calcium, and the calcium is usually already in the soil, so they do nothing for BER. The levers are even watering and mulch; get a soil test before adding any nutrient.
beliefs.response: Epsom salts won't stop blossom-end rot. BER is a calcium-transport problem caused by uneven watering. A magnesium shortage doesn't cause it, and Epsom salts add magnesium, not calcium. Water evenly, mulch to buffer soil moisture, and soil-test before adding anything.

beliefs.belief: Crushed eggshells deter slugs.
beliefs.what_is_true: The claim is that sharp shell edges form a barrier slugs won't cross, but crushed eggshells have not been shown to deter slugs. Nor are the shells much use for their calcium, because they break down too slowly to supply it, and many soils already have plenty. Their real value is as organic matter in the compost. For slugs, what works is trapping, hand-picking at night and iron- phosphate bait, and bait alone will not control them in the long term.
beliefs.response: Crushed eggshells haven't been shown to deter slugs. Use beer traps, hand-pick at night, or put down iron-phosphate bait, which is safer around pets and wildlife. Put the shells in the compost for the organic matter. Their calcium releases too slowly to matter.

beliefs.belief: Coffee grounds acidify soil.
beliefs.what_is_true: Coffee grounds have not been shown to consistently lower soil pH, so they will not durably acidify soil to blueberry range. They make a good compost input, carrying carbon and nitrogen that feed soil organisms. To actually lower pH, use elemental sulfur guided by a soil test.
beliefs.response: Coffee grounds haven't been shown to reliably lower soil pH, so they won't durably acidify your soil or make it blueberry-friendly. Put them in the compost, where they feed soil life; to lower pH, use elemental sulfur guided by a soil test.

beliefs.belief: You must rotate every crop to new ground every single year.
beliefs.what_is_true: Rotation works by starving a pathogen out of the soil, so the right interval depends on how long that pathogen survives, and for many diseases that cannot be stated precisely. Extension advice is to keep a crop family out of the same soil for three to five years; clubroot of the mustard family can survive seven years, bacterial spot needs at least two years without a host, and soil-dwelling soft-rot bacteria are not managed by rotation at all. Moving families every year is a sensible habit. It isn't a law, and Milpa's rules carry the intervals that have named mechanisms. Perennials are the exception. Asparagus and rhubarb stay in one spot for years, and cultivating too deep damages asparagus crowns (R-072).
beliefs.response: You don't have to move every crop every single year by rule. What matters is keeping each crop family out of the same soil long enough to starve its diseases, commonly three to five years. Rotating yearly is a good habit. It isn't a law, and perennials like asparagus and rhubarb stay put for years.

beliefs.belief: Adding sugar or molasses to the soil makes tomatoes and other fruit sweeter.
beliefs.what_is_true: The sugar in a ripe tomato is made in the leaves by photosynthesis and moved into the fruit as it matures; extension sources call sugar-in-the-soil sweetening fiction. How sweet a tomato gets depends on the variety, on ripening on the plant, and on the balance of leaves to fruit, and holding back water as the fruit ripens can raise its sugars. The usual explanation that roots cannot absorb sugar at all is too strong. Roots do have sugar transporters, and in a lab a genetically engineered tomato line grown in glucose-fed soil made sweeter fruit. But nothing we have read shows sugar or molasses sweetening an ordinary garden tomato.
beliefs.response: Sugar in the soil won't sweeten your tomatoes. Fruit sugar is made in the leaves by sunlight. For sweeter fruit, you want a sweet variety, full sun, healthy foliage, and ripening on the plant (a little less water as it ripens helps concentrate it).

beliefs.belief: A layer of gravel or pot shards at the bottom of a container improves drainage.
beliefs.what_is_true: This one is contested. The popular "it's a myth" answer rests on the perched water table. Water held in the fine mix by capillarity was predicted not to cross into a coarse layer, so a gravel bottom would raise the saturated zone and hold more water. A 2025 controlled experiment, using the potting mixes and drainage materials home gardeners actually use, found the opposite. A drainage layer almost always reduced or did not change the water a container held, and almost never increased it. In soil-less coir mixes every layer drained the mix; in loam-based compost most made no difference. Thicker layers did more, and 60 mm of coarse sand worked best across every mix. The study grew no plants, so whether a given plant benefits is still open.
beliefs.response: The old "never put gravel in the bottom of a pot" rule is overstated. A 2025 controlled test found a bottom layer usually drained soil-less mixes better and almost never made things worse, though in loam-based compost it mostly made no difference. It's one study and it grew no plants, so treat a layer as an option. It isn't a fix. If you use one, a thicker layer of coarse sand did best.

beliefs.belief: Burying banana peels feeds plants potassium (roses in particular).
beliefs.what_is_true: A banana peel's potassium is not locked away until the peel rots. Potassium in plant tissue is dissolved in water, so it washes out of plant residues quickly. In one study, 90% of a straw's potassium was released within three days. The weakness in the belief is the dose. Nothing we have read shows buried peels supply meaningful potassium to roses or anything else, and a soil test is how to find out whether a plant is short of it.
beliefs.response: Banana peels do give up their potassium quickly, but a few peels are an unknown and probably small dose, and nothing shows roses need it. If you think a plant is short of potassium, get a soil test; otherwise just compost the peels.

beliefs.belief: Marigolds repel most garden pests and protect the whole garden.
beliefs.what_is_true: Marigolds are not a garden-wide shield. Their best-established effect is on root-knot and some other nematodes in the soil. A dense stand of the right Tagetes, planted at least two months before the crop, suppresses them (R-061). Whether that is through the root compound alpha-terthienyl or because marigold is not a host is not settled. Dotting marigolds among the vegetables does not appear to work, and a susceptible variety can make nematodes worse. Against insects the evidence is mixed. Studies have found fewer thrips, cabbage worms (in mixed plantings) and squash bugs, and a glasshouse study found marigold scent slowed whiteflies, but marigolds do not deter Colorado potato beetles and there is little research behind the flea-beetle claim.
beliefs.response: Marigolds don't protect the whole garden. Their best-known trick is underground. A dense planting of the right kind, grown at least two months before your crop, suppresses root-knot nematodes. Dotted among the vegetables, it doesn't work. Against insects the results are mixed. Some pests, like thrips and whiteflies, drop in trials; others, like Colorado potato beetles, don't budge. Grow them for color and treat any pest help as a bonus.

beliefs.belief: Watering plants in the midday sun scorches the leaves (water droplets focus sunlight like lenses).
beliefs.what_is_true: Water droplets on a leaf do not focus the sun into a burn. On smooth, hairless leaves, sunlit drops of every shape caused no burn damage in a controlled optics study, and wet foliage is not prone to sunburn. The rare exception is a leaf whose water-repellent hairs hold a round drop just above the surface, as on a floating fern. There the drop can focus light and, out of contact with the leaf, no longer cools it. Hundreds of studies of leaf scorch have never pinned it on midday watering. What timing does affect is efficiency. Watering in the heat of the day loses more to evaporation than morning or evening watering, though evening watering can help fungal disease take hold. That is one more reason to put the water on the soil and keep it off the foliage.
beliefs.response: Watering in the midday sun won't scorch your leaves. Droplets don't focus sunlight on ordinary leaves. Water whenever the plant needs it, and aim at the soil and keep the leaves dry, because wet foliage invites fungal disease. Morning or evening watering just loses less to evaporation than the middle of the day.

beliefs.belief: Talking to your plants, or playing them music, makes them grow better.
beliefs.what_is_true: There is no definitive evidence that talking to plants helps them grow. The exhaled-carbon- dioxide idea fails on scale. You would have to talk to a plant for several hours a day to raise photosynthesis enough to matter. Sound itself is a live research question. Plants do respond to sound in lab studies, and one found seed germination affected at 92 decibels, far louder than speech. But the early music experiments lacked proper controls and results remain hard to reproduce, so nothing shows that music grows a garden plant better. What reliably helps is the basics of light, water and mineral nutrition.
beliefs.response: Talking to your plants won't grow them faster. You'd need to talk for hours a day for your breath to make a difference. Plants do respond to sound in the lab, but the music experiments are shaky and nothing shows a playlist helps a garden. Give them light, water and nutrients; chat to them if you enjoy it.

beliefs.belief: Sprinkling human hair, soap shavings, or urine around the garden reliably keeps deer and rabbits out.
beliefs.what_is_true: Hair, soap and similar home remedies are unreliable. Extension services call them questionable at best, deer have been seen eating the soap, and what works in one garden can fail where deer are more numerous. Hair and soap bags have to be renewed monthly, and deer and rabbits get used to repellent smells. A fence is what dependably keeps them out. For deer, the conventional deer- proof fence is 8 feet of woven wire, and for rabbits fencing is the most effective protection. Commercial repellents are more reliable than home remedies, but most cannot be used on edible crops and their effect is temporary.
beliefs.response: Hair, soap and other home-remedy scents aren't a reliable way to keep deer or rabbits out. They need renewing, the animals get used to them, and deer have even eaten the soap. A fence is the dependable fix, and for deer it has to be tall. Store-bought repellents do better than home remedies, but most can't go on food crops.

beliefs.belief: Mixing sand into clay soil improves its drainage.
beliefs.what_is_true: A modest amount of sand in clay does the opposite of what is intended. The fine clay fills the gaps between the sand grains, giving a dense, poorly-draining mix closer to concrete than to loam. To actually shift the texture you would need sand in huge volumes (over half by volume), which is impractical for a bed. What does open clay is organic matter. Compost and mulch build aggregate structure and the pore space that drains. (Whether a gravel layer helps a container drain is a separate and more equivocal case; here the mechanism, clay filling the pore space between the sand grains, is well established.)
beliefs.response: Don't add sand to clay to "loosen" it. In the amounts anyone actually adds, the clay fills the gaps and you get a denser, worse-draining mix. Work in compost and mulch instead; organic matter is what builds the structure that drains.

beliefs.belief: Household vinegar is an effective weed killer.
beliefs.what_is_true: Household vinegar is about 5% acetic acid, a contact herbicide. It burns only the parts of a plant it touches, fastest in bright sun, and gives excellent control of very small annual broadleaf weeds. It does not move to the roots, so larger and perennial weeds can regrow a week or so later, and it is non-selective, injuring any plant it lands on. Stronger products are more dangerous to the person using them. At 11% acetic acid or more, vinegar can burn skin and cause severe eye injury, and 20-30% formulations call for protective gear. It is most useful for weeds in gravel and on patios and sidewalks. It is not a general weed killer.
beliefs.response: Vinegar only burns the parts of a weed it touches, so it works on tiny seedlings, but bigger and perennial weeds grow back from the roots. It also harms any plant it hits, crops included. The strong "horticultural" kinds can burn skin and eyes. Use it for seedlings in paving cracks. It isn't a garden weed killer.

beliefs.belief: Dish soap makes a safe, effective homemade insecticide, the same as insecticidal soap.
beliefs.what_is_true: Dish detergents are not insecticidal soaps. Insecticidal soaps are potassium salts of fatty acids made for use on plants; detergents are degreasers that can damage plants by dissolving the waxy cuticle that protects the leaf, so the "safe homemade version" framing is exactly backwards. If you want a soap spray, use a labeled insecticidal soap, which works on contact against soft-bodied pests such as aphids.
beliefs.response: Dish soap isn't the same as insecticidal soap. Detergents strip the leaf's protective wax and can damage foliage, so the "safe homemade spray" idea backfires. If you want a soap spray, use a real insecticidal soap; it works on contact against soft-bodied pests like aphids.

beliefs.belief: Crushed eggshells in the planting hole prevent blossom-end rot.
beliefs.what_is_true: Blossom end rot is rarely a soil-calcium shortage. It is usually a calcium-transport failure inside the plant, driven by uneven watering (calcium rides the water stream, so erratic moisture starves the fruit tip even when soil calcium is fine; see the belief that Epsom salts prevent blossom-end rot). The real levers are even watering and mulch, and a soil test before adding any amendment.
beliefs.response: Eggshells in the planting hole won't stop blossom-end rot. BER is a calcium-transport problem caused by uneven watering. It's rarely a soil-calcium shortage, and adding calcium to the soil is generally ineffective. Water evenly, mulch to steady the moisture, and soil-test before adding anything.

beliefs.belief: Compost tea (or manure tea) greatly boosts growth and suppresses plant disease.
beliefs.what_is_true: Compost tea, made by steeping mature compost in water, is a source of nutrients, but its disease claims are weak. Batches vary widely; results that look good in the laboratory are more variable in the field; aerated teas have no scientifically documented effect as pathogen suppressors, while non-aerated teas show a trend to reduce how often foliar diseases appear, though not how severe they are. There is a real food-safety downside too. Sugars and other additives commonly put into aerated teas can feed E. coli and Salmonella, so unless the brewing method keeps human pathogens down, extension advice is to save the tea for plants you will not eat. Using the compost itself as mulch is simpler, and composted mulch has documented disease suppression of its own.
beliefs.response: Compost tea isn't the tonic or disease cure it's sold as. The effects in the field are patchy, and aerated teas have no documented disease protection. Additives like molasses can grow E. coli and Salmonella, so keep it off food crops unless you're sure of the method. Spreading the compost itself as mulch is the better bet.

beliefs.belief: Radishes deter flea beetles.
beliefs.what_is_true: Radish does not repel flea beetles; it draws them. Radish is among the brassicas flea beetles find most attractive, and they damage it at every stage, which is why radish and daikon are planted as a deliberate trap crop, to pull flea beetles away from seedlings of other brassicas such as broccoli and cabbage. That is the opposite of a deterrent, and a trap crop only helps if you then deal with the beetles on it. Extension advice is to destroy, spray or harvest the trap crop once the main crop has outgrown the danger. Where wild mustards are common, the trap may make little difference.
beliefs.response: Radishes don't repel flea beetles. Flea beetles love radish, which is why some gardeners plant it as a trap crop to lure them off their broccoli and cabbage. That only works if you then deal with the beetles on the radish. If your radish leaves are riddled with tiny holes, that's flea beetles doing exactly what they do.

beliefs.belief: Chives or garlic planted under a fruit tree prevent apple scab.
beliefs.what_is_true: A widely repeated permaculture plant-team claim with no trial of the planting itself behind it (the trials found test a garlic spray) and no proposed mechanism for how an allium's roots or scent would reach a leaf fungus. Apple scab (Venturia inaequalis) overwinters in fallen leaves and infects in wet spring weather; it is managed by resistant cultivars, raking up and removing the leaf litter, and where needed spray timing. An allium ring at the trunk does none of those things. It is the same shape as the garlic-deters-borers claim Milpa already records as having no evidence.
beliefs.response: There's no evidence that chives or garlic under an apple tree prevent scab, and no mechanism for it. Scab lives in last year's fallen leaves and infects in wet spring weather. Choose a scab-resistant variety, rake up and bin the dropped leaves, and you've done the things that actually work.

beliefs.belief: Cinnamon or chamomile tea prevents damping-off in seedlings.
beliefs.what_is_true: Cinnamon contains compounds with antifungal activity in a lab dish, which is where this remedy comes from, but there is no reliable evidence that dusting cinnamon, or watering with chamomile tea, prevents damping-off on a seed tray. What prevents damping-off is the setup: fresh sterile mix, clean containers with drainage, warmth and airflow, and not overwatering. A remedy sprinkled on top does not fix a cold, wet, overwatered tray, which is where damping-off comes from.
beliefs.response: Cinnamon and chamomile tea are popular anti-damping-off remedies because cinnamon is antifungal in a lab dish. But there's no good evidence either one saves a seed tray. What prevents damping-off is the setup: fresh sterile mix, clean pots with drainage, warmth and airflow, and going easy on the water.

beliefs.belief: Bone meal helps transplants and bulbs put down roots.
beliefs.what_is_true: Bone meal is mainly phosphorus and calcium, and phosphorus can increase root growth in a roundabout way, through the mycorrhizal fungi that roots partner with, and that is where the belief comes from. But both elements are rarely short in garden and landscape soils, so adding more usually does nothing for rooting. Phosphorus barely moves in soil, about an eighth of an inch a year, and bone meal releases its phosphorus mainly in acidic soil, taking little part in the soil's phosphorus cycle over a short time. Too much phosphorus backfires, because roots stop forming mycorrhizal connections. Get a soil test before adding it.
beliefs.response: Bone meal isn't a rooting tonic. It's phosphorus and calcium, which most garden soils already have enough of, and phosphorus hardly moves in soil anyway. Too much can even stop roots teaming up with the helpful fungi they rely on. Get a soil test before adding any.

beliefs.belief: Sprinkling baking soda around tomato plants makes the fruit sweeter.
beliefs.what_is_true: How sweet a tomato tastes comes from the sugar the plant makes in its leaves and moves into the fruit as it ripens, balanced against the fruit's acids; variety, sunlight, healthy foliage and ripening on the plant set it. Baking soda offers no route to change that. It is sodium bicarbonate, and sodium in quantity damages soil structure, leaving clay sealed when dry and hard for water and roots to get through. There is no path from baking soda in the ground to a sweeter tomato. It is the same physiology as the belief that sugar in the soil makes fruit sweeter.
beliefs.response: Baking soda won't sweeten your tomatoes. Sweetness is sugar the plant makes in its leaves. Nothing added at the roots has been shown to sweeten a garden tomato, and baking soda adds sodium, which in quantity damages soil. For sweeter fruit, you want a sweet variety, full sun, healthy leaves, and ripening on the plant.

beliefs.belief: Coffee grounds scattered around plants repel slugs, snails, and other pests.
beliefs.what_is_true: This comes from caffeine. Oregon State reports that a 1% to 2% solution drenched into soil drove slugs out and killed them by caffeine poisoning, and it promotes liquid coffee as a slug killer. But that is a drench. Used grounds keep only small amounts of caffeine, and there is no published evidence that coffee grounds repel or kill any garden pest. Grounds are finely textured and compact easily, so on the surface they can dry out and shed water unless covered with leaves or bark. They are a fine compost ingredient and soil amendment. (The separate claim that grounds acidify soil is checked on its own page, and so is the claim that crushed eggshells deter slugs.)
beliefs.response: Coffee grounds scattered around plants haven't been shown to repel slugs or other pests. The idea comes from caffeine, which does kill slugs in a strong enough soil drench, but used grounds hold very little of it. Use beer traps, hand-pick at night, or put down iron-phosphate bait; put the grounds in the compost.

beliefs.belief: Spraying diluted milk on the leaves prevents or cures powdery mildew.
beliefs.what_is_true: Unusually for a home remedy, this one has some real trials behind it. In a University of Connecticut field trial on pumpkins, diluted milk sprayed before symptoms appeared gave significantly less powdery mildew than no spray, though a chemical fungicide did as well or better; in the greenhouse, milk matched the chemical. The EU has approved cow milk as a basic substance against powdery mildew on grapevines. But extension services still doubt it (UW-Madison counts it among home remedies it debunks), so treat it as a preventive that may help. It is not a cure. What reliably comes first is resistant varieties and spacing that keeps the air moving.
beliefs.response: Milk spray for powdery mildew is one of the few home remedies with some trials behind it. Diluted milk sprayed before symptoms cut mildew on pumpkins, though a fungicide did as well or better in the field. It's a preventive at best. It won't cure mildew, and some extension services still doubt it. Start with resistant varieties and spacing for airflow.

beliefs.belief: Burying rusty nails adds iron that greens up plants and turns hydrangeas blue.
beliefs.what_is_true: Two separate claims ride on this, and both miss. Yellowing leaves (chlorosis) usually don't mean a shortage of iron in the soil, which typically holds plenty. The cause is iron that a high pH has turned into solids the roots cannot take up. Iron released from rusty nails or shavings forms those same unavailable solids at once, so it does nothing for the yellowing. Hydrangea color is not an iron effect either. Blue comes from aluminum, which acidic soil makes available to the roots and neutral or alkaline soil locks away. Start with a soil test. Lowering pH with sulfur is worth trying only where the soil has no free lime, and iron sprays on the leaves act fast but are spotty and temporary. To blue a hydrangea, work sulfur into the soil or water it with aluminum sulfate.
beliefs.response: Rusty nails won't green up your plants or turn hydrangeas blue. Yellow leaves usually mean high pH has locked the iron up. It isn't missing, and iron from a nail gets locked up the same way. Hydrangea blue comes from aluminum in acidic soil, not iron. Soil-test first; for yellowing, sulfur (where there's no free lime) or an iron leaf spray as a stopgap; to blue a hydrangea, add sulfur to the soil or use aluminum sulfate.

beliefs.belief: Spraying plants with dissolved aspirin boosts their immune system and health.
beliefs.what_is_true: There is a real phenomenon underneath this. Salicylic acid is a signal plants use to switch on systemic acquired resistance, a real defense response, and that role was first found when salicylic acid and aspirin made tobacco resist a virus. But that is a long way from "dissolve an aspirin and spray." Applied from outside, salicylic acid is often toxic to the plant, is broken down quickly and does not last; the same dose does not act the same way from one crop to another; and field-scale studies are still needed to judge whether it works. It is an interesting real mechanism. It is not a garden tonic to count on.
beliefs.response: Aspirin spray isn't a proven plant tonic. There's a real kernel. Salicylic acid does switch on a plant defense response, and aspirin did it in the lab. But sprayed on, it's often toxic to the plant, it breaks down fast, and a dose that works on one crop won't carry to another. Treat aspirin as a curiosity, and don't make it a routine.

beliefs.belief: Spreading cornmeal on soil or lawns cures fungal disease.
beliefs.what_is_true: This traces to a real observation. Trichoderma and other fungi that attack plant pathogens grow vigorously on cornmeal, and it is those fungi that do the suppressing. Cornmeal itself is no fungicide. It feeds many fungi (labs use it to culture pathogens such as Rhizoctonia), and no published research supports using it for this or any other garden purpose. (Don't confuse it with corn gluten meal, a different product sold as a pre-emergent weed suppressant, whose real-world results have been inconsistent.) What actually limits fungal disease in a lawn is the setup: good drainage, no overwatering, and air movement.
beliefs.response: Don't use cornmeal as a fungicide. The idea comes from beneficial fungi that grow on it, but cornmeal itself feeds many fungi, pathogens included, and no published research backs it. Manage fungal problems with good drainage, sensible watering and airflow. Don't confuse it with corn gluten meal, a separate weed product.

beliefs.belief: Watering with hydrogen peroxide oxygenates the roots and cures root rot.
beliefs.what_is_true: Hydrogen peroxide does break down into water and oxygen, which is where the idea comes from, but it is no lasting supply to the roots. In soils it breaks down within hours (measured half-lives run from about one to seven hours), fastest where there is more organic matter. It is not harmless to the soil either. It can damage or destroy soil organisms, and large treatments can harm mycorrhizal fungi. Peroxide is a real broad-spectrum fungicide, used as a soil drench, but it does not fix what causes root rot. The water molds behind it live in practically all cultivated soils and kill roots when poor drainage or overwatering keeps the soil wet. Good drainage and water management are what control it.
beliefs.response: Hydrogen peroxide won't oxygenate your roots in any lasting way. It breaks down in soil within hours, and it can harm the helpful life in the soil. It can kill some fungi, but root rot comes from waterlogged soil, and peroxide doesn't change that. Fix the drainage and ease off the watering.

beliefs.belief: Fresh manure is a safe, ready-to-use fertilizer you can spread straight onto the garden.
beliefs.what_is_true: Fresh manure is not a ready-to-use fertilizer, for two separate reasons. It burns. Fresh manure is higher in ammonia and can be high in salts, which can burn roots and foliage, and weathering and rain reduce both. And it can carry human pathogens (Listeria, Salmonella and E. coli O157:H7), which aging does not reliably remove. Storing manure in a pile is not regarded as a reliable way to destroy them, though a compost pile that reaches 140F reduces the risk further. Raw manure should never go on growing food crops, and guidance puts at least 120 days between raw manure and harvest for crops that touch the soil, and 90 days for those that do not. Composting can concentrate salts, so even composted manure can be salty.
beliefs.response: Fresh manure isn't a ready-to-use fertilizer. It can burn plants with ammonia and salts, and it can carry E. coli, Salmonella and Listeria. Leaving it in a pile doesn't reliably kill those; hot composting helps. Never put raw manure on growing food crops, and leave at least 120 days between raw manure and harvest for anything that touches the soil.

beliefs.belief: More fertilizer means bigger, healthier plants.
beliefs.what_is_true: Fertilizer helps a plant by supplying nutrients that are in short supply. More is not better. Overapplied, synthetic and organic fertilizers alike can burn leaves and dry out roots as salts build up, and excess nitrogen gives lush leaf growth at the expense of fruit and leaves plants more open to pests and disease. Too much of one nutrient can cause shortages of another; excess phosphorus brings on iron and zinc deficiencies. What the plant cannot use is carried off by leaching and runoff and pollutes nearby water. The amount to apply comes from a soil test and the plant's needs.
beliefs.response: More fertilizer doesn't mean bigger, healthier plants. Past what the soil is short of, the extra burns roots, pushes leafy growth at the expense of fruit, invites pests, and washes off into streams and lakes. Get a soil test and feed what it says the soil needs.

beliefs.belief: If you buy good compost or bagged soil, your native ground underneath doesn't matter.
beliefs.what_is_true: Good compost or a bagged mix helps, but a thin layer of it over poor ground is not a fix. With a few inches of good soil on top, roots stay mostly in that layer, which shrinks the soil they draw water and nutrients from and means more watering and feeding. Plants do best in deep soil that is similar in texture throughout, so amendments need to be mixed down into the soil, and a raised bed shallower than 18 inches should have the original soil mixed in. Over time, roots grow down into the native soil and organic matter improves it. (For permanent plantings such as trees and shrubs the advice differs. There, topdress with mulch and don't dig amendments in.)
beliefs.response: Buying good soil doesn't let you ignore the ground underneath. A few inches of good mix over poor soil keeps roots in that thin layer, so plants need more watering and feeding. Work amendments into your soil. Don't just lay them on top, and in shallow raised beds mix in the ground below.

beliefs.belief: Seeds saved from hybrid vegetables grow true to the parent plant.
beliefs.what_is_true: You can save and grow seed from an F1 hybrid, but it will not come true. An F1 hybrid is made by crossing two distinct inbred parent lines, and its seed (the F2 generation) produces a mix of plant types with an assortment of traits, most less desirable than the hybrid parent, in combinations nobody can predict. Open-pollinated varieties are the ones to save. Seed from plants pollinated by the same variety grows into plants very similar to the parent, though different varieties of the same crop can cross and give off-types.
beliefs.response: Seeds from a hybrid won't grow true to the parent. You get a mix of plant types, most of them worse. If you want seed that comes true, save it from open-pollinated varieties, and keep them from crossing with other varieties of the same crop. Saving hybrid seed is a fun experiment, but it won't keep a variety.

beliefs.belief: Watering a little every day is the best way to water a garden.
beliefs.what_is_true: For most established plants, a light daily sprinkle is the wrong habit. Frequent shallow watering wets only the top layer of soil, so roots stay shallow, and that layer dries out quickly, leaving the plant vulnerable in dry spells. Watering slowly and deeply (in most situations about one thorough watering a week, though the weather sets the pace) encourages deep roots and better drought tolerance; water when the soil is dry to the touch an inch or two down. There are real exceptions. Young plants and new transplants have small, shallow roots and may need water every day or two in sunny, hot or windy weather, containers may need it daily by midsummer, and sandy soils and shallow-rooted crops like kohlrabi need more frequent watering.
beliefs.response: Watering a little every day usually isn't best. It keeps roots shallow, so plants struggle when it's hot and dry. Water established plants slowly and deeply, and water again when the soil is dry an inch or two down. In most situations that works out to about once a week, but the weather sets the pace, so check the soil, not the calendar. There are real exceptions. Seedlings, new transplants, containers, sandy soil and shallow-rooted crops may need water much more often.
